stem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department unresponsive after a massive intracerebral hemorrhage. He has no advance directive and no health care proxy. His wife of 40 years, two adult children, and a brother are at the bedside. Who is the most appropriate surrogate decision maker?

options.text: His wife
His brother
A hospital ethics committee
His oldest adult child

explanation: When a patient lacks capacity and has no proxy or directive, the surrogate hierarchy generally begins with the spouse, followed by adult children, then parents, then siblings. The surrogate should apply substituted judgment, deciding as the patient would have decided. His wife, as his spouse, is therefore the appropriate surrogate decision maker.
pearl: Surrogate order: health care proxy, spouse, adult children, parents, siblings. Use substituted judgment first, then best interest.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The spouse is first in the usual surrogate hierarchy.
optionExplanations.B: Siblings come after spouse, adult children, and parents.
optionExplanations.C: An ethics committee advises when conflicts arise but is not the default decision maker.
optionExplanations.D: Adult children are next in line, after the spouse, not before.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Reasonable-person standard for disclosure during informed consent
memoryAnchor: Risks, Benefits, Alternatives: RBA.
commonTrap: Equating a signed form with informed consent.
stem: A 58-year-old woman with symptomatic gallstones is scheduled for laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Before obtaining consent, the surgeon discusses the indication, expected benefits, and alternatives. Which additional element is required for the consent to be valid?

options.text: Approval from the hospital ethics committee
Disclosure of material risks that a reasonable patient would want to know
Disclosure of the surgeon personal complication rate in every case
A signed form witnessed by two family members

explanation: Valid informed consent requires disclosure of the nature of the procedure, material risks and benefits, alternatives including no treatment, and the patient capacity and voluntariness. Most jurisdictions use the reasonable-person standard for what risks must be disclosed. A signature documents consent but is not itself the process.
pearl: Elements of informed consent: capacity, voluntariness, disclosure of risks, benefits, alternatives, and understanding.

optionExplanations.A: Ethics committee approval is not required for routine consent.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Material risks, as judged by a reasonable patient, must be disclosed.
optionExplanations.C: Personal complication rates may be useful but are not universally required for validity.
optionExplanations.D: Family witnesses are not required for valid consent.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Patient may waive the right to information
memoryAnchor: Autonomy includes the right NOT to know.
commonTrap: Treating waiver as incapacity.
stem: A 65-year-old man is diagnosed with metastatic colon cancer. He tells his physician that he does not want to hear details about prognosis and prefers that his daughter receive the information and help him make decisions. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Withhold the diagnosis from both the patient and his daughter
Insist on disclosing prognosis because he must be fully informed
Respect his request and discuss details with his daughter as he designated
Document that the patient lacks decision-making capacity

explanation: Patients with capacity can waive their right to information and designate another person to receive it. The physician should confirm the wish, document it, and remain available if he changes his mind. Waiver is distinct from therapeutic privilege, which is rarely justified. The physician should respect his request and discuss details with his daughter as he designated.
pearl: Waiver is acceptable when voluntary and informed; therapeutic privilege is rare and ethically contested.

optionExplanations.A: The diagnosis should not be hidden from a designated surrogate when the patient requests it be shared with her.
optionExplanations.B: Forcing information on a patient who has waived it violates autonomy.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A voluntary waiver by a capacitated patient should be honored.
optionExplanations.D: A preference not to hear prognosis is not evidence of incapacity.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Duty to protect an identifiable victim (Tarasoff)
memoryAnchor: Tarasoff: Tell the Target.
commonTrap: Believing psychotherapy confidentiality is absolute.
stem: A 30-year-old man tells his psychiatrist during a session that he plans to kill his former girlfriend, naming her and describing how he will find her tomorrow. He appears agitated and has a history of violence. Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the psychiatrist?

options.text: Recommend anger management classes and see him next week
Obtain the patient written permission before any disclosure
Warn the identified victim and notify law enforcement
Maintain confidentiality because of the therapeutic relationship

explanation: Confidentiality can be broken when there is a serious, credible threat to an identifiable person (Tarasoff duty to protect). The physician should take reasonable steps, such as warning the victim, notifying police, and arranging evaluation or hospitalization.
pearl: Exceptions to confidentiality: threats to others, child or elder abuse, certain infectious diseases, gunshot wounds, impaired drivers.

optionExplanations.A: Delaying action a week ignores imminent danger.
optionExplanations.B: Patient permission is not required when a serious threat exists.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A specific, imminent threat to a named person triggers the duty to protect.
optionExplanations.D: Confidentiality is not absolute and yields to imminent danger to others.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Use a professional medical interpreter rather than family
memoryAnchor: Family is not a translator.
commonTrap: Using relatives for convenience.
stem: A 45-year-old woman who speaks only Vietnamese presents with abdominal pain and weight loss. Her 12-year-old son offers to interpret. A telephone interpretation service is also available in the clinic. Which of the following is the best approach to history taking?

options.text: Use the professional interpreter
Use a hospital employee who speaks a few Vietnamese words
Ask her to write her symptoms in English
Use her son because he knows her best

explanation: Professional medical interpreters improve accuracy and reduce errors. Family members, especially children, may omit or alter information, create embarrassment, and violate confidentiality.
pearl: Use trained interpreters; look at the patient, not the interpreter, when speaking.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A trained interpreter ensures accuracy and confidentiality.
optionExplanations.B: Untrained bilingual staff are not substitutes for qualified interpreters.
optionExplanations.C: Written English will not reliably reflect her symptoms.
optionExplanations.D: Children should not interpret sensitive medical information for parents.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Mandatory reporting of suspected elder abuse
memoryAnchor: Suspect it, report it.
commonTrap: Waiting for confirmation before reporting.
stem: An 82-year-old woman with dementia is brought by her son for evaluation of a fractured wrist. Examination shows bruises of different ages on her arms and back, poor hygiene, and weight loss. She appears fearful when her son answers questions. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ask the son whether he is abusing her and proceed only if he admits it
Wait for definitive proof before taking action
Discharge her home with a follow-up appointment
Report suspected abuse to adult protective services

explanation: Physicians are mandatory reporters of suspected elder abuse in most jurisdictions. Reasonable suspicion, not proof, is sufficient, and reporters are legally protected. The patient should also be interviewed alone and assessed for safe disposition.
pearl: Mandatory reporting applies to child abuse, elder abuse, and some intimate-partner violence depending on state law.

optionExplanations.A: Relying on the perpetrator admission is unreliable.
optionExplanations.B: Waiting for proof delays protection of a vulnerable patient.
optionExplanations.C: Sending her home without a report may expose her to further harm.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Suspicion is enough to trigger a report.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Elements of decision-making capacity
memoryAnchor: Choose, Understand, Appreciate, Reason.
commonTrap: Assuming refusal of recommended treatment proves incapacity.
stem: A 70-year-old man with pneumonia refuses intravenous antibiotics. Assessment shows that he can state his choice, understands that the infection could be fatal, and explains that he values comfort over prolonged hospitalization. Which of the following is the best next step?

options.text: Ask his adult children to override his refusal
Honor his decision because he has decision-making capacity
Administer antibiotics under implied consent
Seek a court order to treat him

explanation: Capacity requires the ability to express a choice, understand relevant information, appreciate the consequences, and reason about options consistent with values. Because he meets these criteria, his refusal must be respected even if the physician disagrees.
pearl: Capacity is decision-specific and assessed by the treating physician; it is not the same as competence, which is a legal determination.

optionExplanations.A: Children cannot override a capacitated patient.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A capacitated adult may refuse treatment.
optionExplanations.C: Implied consent applies only to emergencies when the patient cannot decide.
optionExplanations.D: A court order is not appropriate when the patient has capacity.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Written advance directive takes precedence over family wishes
memoryAnchor: The patient voice written down still speaks.
commonTrap: Deferring to family despite a clear directive.
stem: A 78-year-old man with end-stage COPD is intubated after respiratory failure and cannot communicate. His written advance directive, signed 1 year ago, states that he does not want prolonged mechanical ventilation. His daughter insists on continuing full support. Which of the following should guide the care team?

options.text: Follow the daughter wishes as the closest relative
Request a new directive from the daughter
Continue ventilation until the family agrees
Follow the patient written directive

explanation: A valid advance directive reflects the patient own autonomous wishes and takes precedence over family preferences. Surrogates are expected to carry out the patient stated wishes, not substitute their own. The care team should follow the patient written directive.
pearl: Hierarchy: patient directive > designated proxy > substituted judgment > best interest.

optionExplanations.A: The daughter cannot override the patient own directive.
optionExplanations.B: A directive can be created only by the patient.
optionExplanations.C: Family agreement is not required when a valid directive exists.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The patient documented wishes govern.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Disclose medical errors to the patient
memoryAnchor: Say it, own it, fix it.
commonTrap: Thinking disclosure is only needed after harm.
stem: A 52-year-old woman receives a double dose of heparin because of a nursing order transcription error. Her partial thromboplastin time is elevated but she has no bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate action by her physician?

options.text: Avoid mentioning the error because no harm occurred
Disclose only if bleeding develops
Inform the patient about the error and the plan to monitor her
Document the error only in the incident report

explanation: Physicians have an ethical duty to disclose errors, including near-misses with potential for harm, in a timely, honest manner. Disclosure should include what happened, expected consequences, and steps taken to prevent recurrence. Incident reports are internal and not a substitute for disclosure. The physician should inform the patient about the error and the plan to monitor her.
pearl: Disclose errors, apologize, and explain the corrective plan; report through safety systems separately.

optionExplanations.A: Concealing an error violates honesty even if no harm occurs.
optionExplanations.B: Disclosure is required regardless of outcome.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Honest disclosure supports trust and autonomy.
optionExplanations.D: Incident reports are not part of the patient medical record or a replacement for disclosure.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Physicians should decline significant gifts from pharmaceutical representatives
memoryAnchor: No free lunch becomes no free vacation.
commonTrap: Believing disclosure alone resolves conflicts of interest.
stem: A 41-year-old internist is offered a paid weekend vacation by a pharmaceutical company representative after prescribing the company new antihypertensive to many patients. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Decline the offer
Accept if she discloses the gift to patients
Accept if the gift is shared with her staff
Accept because it will not influence her prescribing

explanation: Gifts of significant value create conflicts of interest that may bias prescribing. Professional guidelines advise against accepting gifts with more than minimal value and against gifts tied to prescribing patterns. She should decline the offer.
pearl: Small educational items may be acceptable; gifts of substantial value are not.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A lavish gift tied to prescribing should be declined.
optionExplanations.B: Disclosure does not remove the conflict.
optionExplanations.C: Sharing the gift does not change its inappropriateness.
optionExplanations.D: Self-assessment of immunity from influence is unreliable.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Withdrawing and withholding life-sustaining treatment are ethically equivalent
memoryAnchor: Stopping equals not starting.
commonTrap: Equating withdrawal of support with euthanasia.
stem: A 68-year-old woman with advanced pancreatic cancer and respiratory failure has been on a ventilator for 5 days. Her husband, who is her proxy, says that she told him she would not want prolonged life support. Which of the following statements best describes the ethical status of stopping the ventilator?

options.text: It is ethically worse than withholding treatment
It is ethically equivalent to never starting it
It requires a court order
It is euthanasia

explanation: Withdrawing a treatment that is no longer wanted or beneficial is ethically equivalent to withholding it. Stopping life support at the informed request of a patient or surrogate is not euthanasia, which is the active administration of a lethal agent.
pearl: Withdrawal of care at the patient request is permissible; active euthanasia is not legal in most US states.

optionExplanations.A: Withdrawal is not ethically worse than never starting treatment.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Withdrawal and withholding are ethically equivalent.
optionExplanations.C: No court order is required when the surrogate carries out the patient wishes.
optionExplanations.D: Euthanasia involves actively causing death, not removing unwanted treatment.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Physicians must report suspected child abuse without parental consent
memoryAnchor: Suspicion, not proof.
commonTrap: Waiting for proof or parental agreement.
stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a spiral femur fracture. The parents give conflicting accounts, and radiographs show healing rib fractures. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Report suspected abuse to child protective services
Discharge the child with orthopedic follow-up
Obtain parental permission before reporting
Wait for repeat imaging before taking action

explanation: Physicians are mandatory reporters of suspected child abuse. Reasonable suspicion is sufficient, parental consent is not needed, and the child should be protected, usually with admission. Findings such as healing fractures of different ages and inconsistent histories are red flags.
pearl: Child abuse red flags: inconsistent history, injuries of different ages, posterior rib fractures, metaphyseal corner fractures.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Report on suspicion; consent is not required.
optionExplanations.B: Discharge could return the child to an unsafe environment.
optionExplanations.C: Parental permission is not required and could endanger the child.
optionExplanations.D: Delay leaves the child at risk.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Distinguishing beneficence from nonmaleficence
memoryAnchor: First, do no harm.
commonTrap: Thinking autonomy obliges physicians to provide any requested treatment.
stem: A 55-year-old man with a stable, asymptomatic small abdominal aortic aneurysm of 3.5 cm requests immediate surgery. His surgeon declines because the operative risk currently outweighs the benefit and surveillance is recommended. Which ethical principle most directly supports the surgeon decision?

options.text: Justice
Nonmaleficence
Autonomy
Fidelity

explanation: Nonmaleficence means avoiding harm. Performing a risky operation with no net benefit would expose the patient to harm. The surgeon should still respect autonomy by explaining the reasoning and offering surveillance and a second opinion.
pearl: Four principles: autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice. A patient cannot demand medically inappropriate treatment.

optionExplanations.A: Justice concerns fair allocation of resources, which is not the issue here.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The surgeon is avoiding unnecessary harm.
optionExplanations.C: Autonomy would favor the patient request, not the refusal to operate.
optionExplanations.D: Fidelity is faithfulness to commitments and does not specifically address avoiding harm.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Capacitated adult may refuse transfusion for religious reasons
memoryAnchor: Autonomy wins when the patient is capacitated.
commonTrap: Applying emergency implied consent when the patient has clearly refused.
stem: A 34-year-old woman who is a Jehovah Witness presents after a motor vehicle collision with a ruptured spleen and a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg. She is alert and states clearly that she refuses blood products even if she might die. Her husband asks the team to transfuse her. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Obtain her husband consent for transfusion
Transfuse because she is in a life-threatening emergency
Obtain a court order to transfuse
Honor her refusal and use alternatives such as volume expanders and surgery

explanation: A capacitated adult has the right to refuse any treatment, including life-saving transfusion. The team should continue all acceptable care, such as crystalloids, surgical control of bleeding, cell salvage if acceptable to her, and erythropoietin.
pearl: Adults with capacity may refuse life-saving treatment. Minors of Jehovah Witness parents may be transfused by court order.

optionExplanations.A: A spouse cannot override a capacitated patient.
optionExplanations.B: Implied consent applies only when the patient cannot decide and wishes are unknown.
optionExplanations.C: A court order is inappropriate for a competent adult who has refused.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Capacitated refusal must be honored; alternatives should be pursued.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Court order when parents refuse life-saving care for a child
memoryAnchor: Parents can choose, but not choose death for a curable child.
commonTrap: Over-deferring to parental autonomy.
stem: A 5-year-old girl is diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia with an excellent expected response to chemotherapy. Her parents refuse treatment because they prefer herbal remedies. Without treatment she will almost certainly die within months. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start chemotherapy without informing the parents
Accept the parents decision as their right
Seek a court order authorizing treatment
Wait until the child is old enough to decide

explanation: Parents may not refuse effective, life-saving treatment for a child. The physician should first attempt to discuss and negotiate, then seek court authorization to treat if the parents continue to refuse.
pearl: Parental refusal of life-saving care for children: involve ethics, seek court order. Emergencies may be treated under implied consent.

optionExplanations.A: Treating covertly violates honesty and parental notification duties.
optionExplanations.B: Parental authority does not extend to refusal of necessary, effective treatment.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Courts can authorize treatment when the child life is at stake.
optionExplanations.D: A 5-year-old cannot decide, and delay would be fatal.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Respecting a terminally ill patient request not to inform family
memoryAnchor: The chart belongs to the patient, not the family.
commonTrap: Sharing information with relatives out of sympathy.
stem: A 60-year-old man is diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer. He requests that his diagnosis not be shared with his wife and children because he wants to protect them. His wife calls the physician and asks about his test results. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Decline to disclose information without his permission and encourage him to share it
Disclose the diagnosis to his children instead
Tell her only the prognosis
Tell her the diagnosis because she is his spouse

explanation: Patient confidentiality applies to family members unless the patient consents or a specific exception exists. The physician should respect his wishes while exploring his reasons and encouraging him to involve his family and support systems.
pearl: Confidentiality exceptions are narrow: danger to others, abuse, reportable diseases, legal compulsion.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Without consent or an applicable exception, information is not shared.
optionExplanations.B: Children have no greater right to the information than the spouse.
optionExplanations.C: Prognosis is also protected health information.
optionExplanations.D: Spouse status does not override patient confidentiality.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Capacity is decision-specific in a patient with schizophrenia
memoryAnchor: Diagnosis is not disability: test the decision, not the diagnosis.
commonTrap: Equating schizophrenia with global incapacity.
stem: A 46-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia, well controlled on risperidone, is admitted with a diabetic foot ulcer and osteomyelitis. His temperature is 38.6 C, heart rate is 104 bpm, and white blood cell count is 17,500/mm3. MRI shows involvement of the calcaneus, and the surgeon recommends below-knee amputation to prevent sepsis. The patient refuses surgery and states that he understands that he could die from infection but believes that God will heal him and that he has no prior religious interest. Psychiatric evaluation shows no hallucinations, disorganized thought, or acute psychosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed with surgery under implied consent because of the risk of sepsis
Determine whether he can appreciate the consequences and reason about his choice before deciding on capacity
Presume that he lacks capacity because he has schizophrenia
Ask his sister to provide surrogate consent immediately

explanation: A psychiatric diagnosis does not by itself remove decision-making capacity, and capacity is specific to each decision. The evaluation must assess whether the patient can express a choice, understand information, appreciate its relevance to himself, and reason about alternatives. A sudden new belief that conflicts with prior values, or a delusional belief that prevents appreciation of risk, may indicate impaired capacity; a stable value-consistent choice does not. Only after this assessment can the team honor refusal or turn to a surrogate. Implied consent applies when the patient cannot decide in an emergency and no wishes are known, which is not established here. Because capacity is decision-specific, the physician must determine whether the refusal results in part from a delusion that impairs reasoning or reflects stable personal values; a diagnosis of incapacity must be supported by that assessment before treatment proceeds over his objection.
pearl: Psychiatric illness does not equal incapacity. Assess capacity for each specific decision.

optionExplanations.A: Implied consent does not apply while the patient is awake, communicating, and refusing; proceeding would be battery unless capacity is lacking.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Capacity is decision-specific and requires assessment of appreciation and reasoning, especially when the belief seems out of character.
optionExplanations.C: A diagnosis of schizophrenia does not equal incapacity; presuming incapacity violates the patient autonomy, whereas a proper assessment would not.
optionExplanations.D: A surrogate is used only after the patient is found to lack capacity, not before that determination, and the sister cannot consent for a capacitated adult.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Brain death is legal death and ends the obligation to continue support
memoryAnchor: Brain dead means dead: the heart beats, but the person is gone.
commonTrap: Treating brain death as a life-and-death decision that requires family consent.
stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the intensive care unit after a motorcycle collision with severe head trauma. On day 3 he is on mechanical ventilation, with a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg, a heart rate of 82 bpm, and a core temperature of 36.8 C. He has no cough or gag reflex, fixed dilated pupils, absent corneal and oculocephalic reflexes, and no respiratory effort on an apnea test with a PaCO2 of 62 mmHg. An EEG shows no activity and CT shows diffuse cerebral edema with herniation. His parents demand that all treatment continue because they believe he may still recover. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Ask a court to appoint a guardian before discontinuing support
Offer a time-limited trial of ventilation because the family disagrees
Explain that he has died by neurologic criteria and that ventilator support will be discontinued after allowing the family time to process
Continue indefinite ventilation until the parents agree to withdraw support

explanation: Brain death is irreversible loss of all brain and brainstem function and is legally and medically equivalent to death. The examination here shows coma, absent brainstem reflexes, and apnea with a PaCO2 above 60 mmHg, with imaging consistent with catastrophic injury. Once death is confirmed by standard criteria, there is no obligation to continue treatment, because the patient is no longer a living patient who can benefit. Clinicians should communicate with compassion, allow time and support for the family, involve the organ procurement organization as required, and avoid presenting withdrawal as a decision parents must make. Continuing support only prolongs physiologic function in a deceased person. Because irreversible loss of all brain function is the mechanism of death here, the diagnosis is established by standard criteria; continued ventilation can no longer benefit him, and stopping it does not cause his death, which has already occurred.
pearl: Brain death: coma, absent brainstem reflexes, and apnea. It is legal death; family consent is not required to discontinue support.

optionExplanations.A: A court is not needed because the legal determination of death has already been made by standard criteria; guardianship is for patients who lack capacity but are alive.
optionExplanations.B: A time-limited trial is meant for living patients with uncertain prognosis, and it does not apply once death has been established by neurologic criteria.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Brain death is death, so support can be stopped after compassionate communication and time for the family.
optionExplanations.D: Indefinite ventilation of a deceased patient is not required, whereas parental agreement is sought for communication but not as a condition for declaring death.

subject: Ethics
testedConcept: Duty to report an impaired physician who endangers patients
memoryAnchor: Patient safety trumps collegial loyalty.
commonTrap: Choosing confrontation or waiting to be certain.
stem: A 38-year-old surgical resident notices that a 55-year-old attending surgeon has had slurred speech, unsteady gait, and an odor of alcohol on three early-morning cases over the past month. During the last operation the attending made a technical error that required a blood transfusion for a patient with a hemoglobin of 7.4 g/dL, blood pressure of 88/56 mmHg, and heart rate of 118 bpm. The attending denies drinking when confronted privately. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the resident?

options.text: Speak to the attending privately again and take no further action
Contact the state medical board only after the attending admits to drinking
Wait until the attending makes another error to be certain
Report the concern to the hospital chief of surgery or the designated impaired-physician or patient-safety program

explanation: Physicians have an ethical, and often legal, duty to protect patients from impaired colleagues. When direct discussion fails or the risk is high, concerns should be reported promptly to the appropriate authority, such as the department chief, hospital peer review, or a physician health program, and to the state board where required. The goal is patient safety and, ideally, treatment for the impaired physician. Waiting for certainty or an admission delays protection of patients and does not fulfill the duty, because suspicion with objective supporting observations is sufficient to act. Because the risk to patients is ongoing, reporting leads to evaluation and treatment of the impaired physician, and the resident does not need to confirm a diagnosis of alcohol use before acting.
pearl: Impaired colleague: report to the appropriate authority; protect patients first and help the physician second.

optionExplanations.A: A second private conversation is inadequate when the first has failed and patients have already been harmed.
optionExplanations.B: An admission is not required before reporting, because the duty is triggered by reasonable concern, not by confession.
optionExplanations.C: Waiting for another error exposes patients to preventable harm and does not meet the duty to act.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Prompt reporting to the proper authority protects patients and can lead to treatment.

subject: Behavioral Science
testedConcept: Social smile as an early developmental milestone
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Two months, two-cheeked smile.
commonTrap: Confusing the social smile with later milestones such as babbling at 6 months.
stem: A 6-week-old boy is brought for a well-child visit. He was born at term and has been feeding well. His mother asks when he should start smiling in response to her. Which of the following is the typical age at which a social smile appears?

options.text: Around 2 months of age
Around 9 months of age
Around 12 months of age
Around 6 months of age

explanation: A social (responsive) smile typically emerges at about 2 months of age, along with cooing and following objects to the midline. Absence of a social smile by 3 to 4 months should prompt evaluation for visual, hearing, or social-communication problems.
pearl: Key milestones: social smile 2 mo; sits alone 6 mo; pincer grasp 9-10 mo; walks and 1-2 words 12 mo; two-word phrases 24 mo.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The social smile appears around 2 months of age.
optionExplanations.B: At 9 months infants typically crawl and wave bye-bye.
optionExplanations.C: At 12 months infants usually say 1 to 2 words and may cruise or walk.
optionExplanations.D: At 6 months infants typically sit with support, babble, and show stranger awareness beginning later.

subject: Behavioral Science
testedConcept: Persistence of the Moro reflex beyond infancy
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Moro disappears before the half-year mark.
commonTrap: Accepting persistence of primitive reflexes into late infancy as normal.
stem: A 7-month-old girl is evaluated for delayed motor development. Examination shows a symmetric Moro reflex with extension and adduction of the arms when her head is briefly dropped back. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Which of the following is the typical age by which the Moro reflex should disappear?

options.text: By 12 months
By 18 months
By 24 months
By 3 to 6 months

explanation: The Moro reflex is a primitive brainstem-mediated reflex that normally disappears by 3 to 6 months of age. Its persistence beyond 6 months suggests a central nervous system abnormality such as cerebral palsy or other neurologic injury and warrants further evaluation.
pearl: Primitive reflexes (Moro, rooting, palmar grasp) normally fade by about 3 to 6 months; persistence suggests CNS injury.

optionExplanations.A: By 12 months the reflex has long been absent in normal infants.
optionExplanations.B: Persistence until 18 months would be markedly abnormal.
optionExplanations.C: Persistence until 24 months would be markedly abnormal.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The Moro reflex disappears by 3 to 6 months of age.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Thelarche as the first sign of puberty in girls
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Girls: boobs, then bush, then bleeding.
commonTrap: Assuming menarche or pubic hair comes first.
stem: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because her mother noticed new breast tissue under both nipples. Examination shows breast buds and no pubic hair. She is otherwise healthy, and her growth velocity is increasing. Which of the following is the usual first sign of puberty in girls?

options.text: Axillary hair growth
Breast budding (thelarche)
Menarche
Pubic hair development (pubarche)

explanation: In most girls, the first sign of puberty is breast budding (thelarche, Tanner stage 2), driven by estrogen from the ovaries after GnRH pulsatility begins. Pubic hair, growth spurt, and then menarche follow, typically about 2 to 2.5 years after breast budding.
pearl: Girls: thelarche, then pubarche, then growth spurt, then menarche. Boys: testicular enlargement is first.

optionExplanations.A: Axillary hair appears later in puberty, driven by adrenal androgens.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Thelarche is the usual first pubertal sign in girls.
optionExplanations.C: Menarche occurs late in puberty, after the growth spurt.
optionExplanations.D: Pubic hair often follows breast development, though it can appear first in some girls.

subject: Genetics
testedConcept: Cardiovascular and gonadal findings in Turner syndrome
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Turner = Turned-down neck webbing, short, streak ovaries.
commonTrap: Overlooking cardiac screening in Turner syndrome.
stem: A 15-year-old girl is evaluated for primary amenorrhea. She is 140 cm tall and has a webbed neck, a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, and no breast development. Blood pressure is 150/70 mmHg in the arms and 100/60 mmHg in the legs. Which of the following karyotypes is most likely?

options.text: 47,XXY
46,XY

explanation: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes short stature, a webbed neck, shield chest, streak ovaries with primary amenorrhea and elevated FSH, and left-sided cardiac defects such as bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta. The arm-leg blood pressure difference suggests coarctation.
pearl: Turner: bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation; horseshoe kidney; high FSH; no Barr body.

optionExplanations.A: 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome, which occurs in males.
optionExplanations.B: Trisomy 21 is Down syndrome, not associated with streak ovaries.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. 45,X is Turner syndrome.
optionExplanations.D: 46,XY in a phenotypic female suggests androgen insensitivity or gonadal dysgenesis without these somatic features.

subject: Genetics
testedConcept: Hormonal profile of Klinefelter syndrome
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: XXY: tall, small testes, sky-high FSH.
commonTrap: Mistaking primary for secondary hypogonadism.
stem: A 24-year-old man is evaluated for infertility. He is 190 cm tall with long limbs, mild gynecomastia, and small firm testes. Semen analysis shows azoospermia. Which of the following hormone patterns is most likely?

options.text: Low testosterone, low FSH, low LH
Normal testosterone, normal FSH, low LH
High testosterone, low FSH, low LH
Low testosterone, high FSH, high LH

explanation: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes primary testicular failure. Seminiferous tubule dysgenesis lowers inhibin B and sperm production, raising FSH. Leydig cell dysfunction lowers testosterone, raising LH. The result is hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. Klinefelter syndrome therefore produces low testosterone with high FSH and high LH.
pearl: Klinefelter: 47,XXY, Barr body, tall, gynecomastia, increased risk of breast cancer and autoimmune disease.

optionExplanations.A: Low gonadotropins indicate secondary hypogonadism, such as Kallmann syndrome.
optionExplanations.B: A normal profile would not explain small firm testes and azoospermia.
optionExplanations.C: High testosterone would not cause infertility and gynecomastia in this pattern.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Primary testicular failure leads to low testosterone with elevated FSH and LH.

subject: Anatomy
testedConcept: First pharyngeal arch derivatives and Treacher Collins syndrome
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: First arch: jaw and ear bones, chewing muscles.
commonTrap: Confusing first-arch derivatives with second-arch stapes and facial muscles.
stem: A newborn girl has hypoplastic mandible and zygomatic bones, downward-slanting palpebral fissures, and malformed external ears. Hearing screening shows conductive hearing loss. The structures affected are derived from neural crest cells of which of the following?

options.text: First pharyngeal arch
Third pharyngeal arch
Second pharyngeal arch
Fourth pharyngeal arch

explanation: Treacher Collins syndrome results from failure of neural crest migration into the first pharyngeal arch, causing mandibular and maxillary hypoplasia, ear malformations, and conductive hearing loss. The first arch gives rise to the mandible, maxilla, malleus, incus, and muscles of mastication (CN V).
pearl: Arch nerves: 1 = CN V; 2 = CN VII; 3 = CN IX; 4 and 6 = CN X.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. First arch neural crest forms the mandible, maxilla, and malleus and incus.
optionExplanations.B: The third arch forms the stylopharyngeus muscle and part of the hyoid (CN IX).
optionExplanations.C: The second arch forms the stapes, styloid process, and muscles of facial expression (CN VII).
optionExplanations.D: The fourth arch forms laryngeal cartilages and pharyngeal constrictors (CN X).

subject: Immunology
testedConcept: Third and fourth pharyngeal pouch maldevelopment in 22q11 deletion
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Third pouch = Thymus and inferior parathyroids (3 below 4).
commonTrap: Attributing the hypocalcemia to a vitamin D deficiency.
stem: A 5-day-old boy has a tetanic seizure. Serum calcium is 6.1 mg/dL and phosphate is elevated. Examination shows a harsh holosystolic murmur and a low-set, notched ear. Chest radiograph shows an absent thymic shadow. Failure of which embryologic structures best explains the hypocalcemia?

options.text: Second pharyngeal cleft
Third and fourth pharyngeal pouches
Neural plate
First and second pharyngeal arches

explanation: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) results from abnormal development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, causing thymic hypoplasia (T-cell deficiency), absent inferior and superior parathyroid glands (hypocalcemia), and conotruncal cardiac defects.
pearl: DiGeorge: CATCH-22 (cardiac, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcemia, 22q11).

optionExplanations.A: The second pharyngeal cleft normally disappears; persistence causes branchial cysts.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The third pouch gives the thymus and inferior parathyroids; the fourth gives the superior parathyroids.
optionExplanations.C: The neural plate forms the nervous system.
optionExplanations.D: First and second arches form facial and ear structures, not the parathyroids.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Omphalocele versus gastroschisis
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Omphalocele has a Sac and Syndromes; gastroschisis has Guts Showing.
commonTrap: Missing the covering membrane that distinguishes omphalocele.
stem: A newborn boy has intestines and liver protruding through the umbilicus, covered by a thin translucent membrane. Echocardiography shows a ventricular septal defect, and the karyotype shows trisomy 18. Which of the following best describes the defect?

options.text: Meckel diverticulum
Gastroschisis
Omphalocele
Umbilical hernia

explanation: Omphalocele results from failure of the midgut to return to the abdomen and is covered by a membrane (amnion and peritoneum) at the umbilical ring. It is often associated with other anomalies and chromosomal disorders such as trisomy 18 and 13. Gastroschisis is a paraumbilical defect without a covering sac and is rarely associated with other anomalies.
pearl: Omphalocele: covered, midline, associated anomalies. Gastroschisis: uncovered, paraumbilical, elevated maternal AFP.

optionExplanations.A: Meckel diverticulum is a remnant of the vitelline duct in the ileum, not an abdominal wall defect.
optionExplanations.B: Gastroschisis lacks a covering membrane and is lateral to the umbilicus.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A membrane-covered defect at the umbilicus with associated anomalies is omphalocele.
optionExplanations.D: An umbilical hernia is covered by skin and usually closes spontaneously.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Facial features and growth effects of fetal alcohol syndrome
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Smooth philtrum, thin lip, small head: Fetal Alcohol Face.
commonTrap: Confusing the facial features with congenital rubella or hydantoin syndromes.
stem: A 4-year-old girl is evaluated for developmental delay and poor growth. Examination shows microcephaly, short palpebral fissures, a smooth philtrum, and a thin upper lip. Her mother was heavy alcohol user during pregnancy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Congenital hypothyroidism
Fetal alcohol syndrome
Congenital rubella
Fetal hydantoin syndrome

explanation: Fetal alcohol syndrome is a leading preventable cause of intellectual disability and presents with prenatal and postnatal growth restriction, microcephaly, characteristic facial features (short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip), and neurodevelopmental deficits. Cardiac defects such as ventricular septal defect may also occur.
pearl: No safe level of alcohol in pregnancy is established; FAS is the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability in the US.

optionExplanations.A: Congenital hypothyroidism causes macroglossia, umbilical hernia, and lethargy.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The facial pattern with maternal alcohol exposure defines FAS.
optionExplanations.C: Congenital rubella causes cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and patent ductus arteriosus.
optionExplanations.D: Fetal hydantoin syndrome causes nail and digit hypoplasia and cleft lip or palate.

subject: Behavioral Science
testedConcept: Object permanence in the sensorimotor stage
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Peekaboo means the object still exists.
commonTrap: Assigning conservation to infancy.
stem: A 10-month-old girl watches her mother hide a toy under a blanket and immediately lifts the blanket to find it. Previously she lost interest when objects were hidden. Which of the following cognitive concepts has she developed?

options.text: Egocentrism
Conservation
Object permanence
Abstract reasoning

explanation: Object permanence, the understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight, develops during Piaget sensorimotor stage (birth to about 2 years), usually by 8 to 12 months. Conservation appears in the concrete operational stage and abstract reasoning in the formal operational stage.
pearl: Piaget: sensorimotor (0-2), preoperational (2-7), concrete operational (7-11), formal operational (11+).

optionExplanations.A: Egocentrism is prominent in the preoperational stage, ages 2 to 7.
optionExplanations.B: Conservation develops around 7 years in the concrete operational stage.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Searching for hidden objects shows object permanence.
optionExplanations.D: Abstract reasoning develops after age 11.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Serum creatinine and glomerular filtration in normal aging
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Small muscles, small creatinine, same kidney problem.
commonTrap: Trusting a normal creatinine in a frail older adult.
stem: An 80-year-old woman who weighs 48 kg has a serum creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL, which is within the laboratory reference range. She is prescribed an antibiotic that requires renal dose adjustment. Which of the following best explains why her creatinine may underestimate renal impairment?

options.text: Creatinine is produced by the kidney and falls as renal mass falls
Aging increases creatinine clearance by hyperfiltration
Tubular secretion of creatinine increases with age
Reduced muscle mass lowers creatinine production while GFR declines with age

explanation: Glomerular filtration rate falls by roughly 1 mL/min per year after about age 40, yet serum creatinine often stays normal because older adults have less muscle mass and produce less creatinine. Estimating GFR with the Cockcroft-Gault or CKD-EPI equations is therefore essential for drug dosing.
pearl: Use eGFR or Cockcroft-Gault rather than serum creatinine alone in elderly, cachectic, and low-muscle-mass patients.

optionExplanations.A: Creatinine is a product of muscle metabolism, not renal production.
optionExplanations.B: Aging reduces rather than increases glomerular filtration.
optionExplanations.C: Tubular secretion does not increase with age.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Reduced muscle mass keeps creatinine deceptively normal despite a lower GFR.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia in bilateral renal agenesis
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: No pee, no fluid, no lungs.
commonTrap: Attributing respiratory failure to surfactant deficiency alone.
stem: A male newborn has severe respiratory distress immediately after birth. He has a flattened nose, low-set ears, a receding chin, and limb contractures. Prenatal ultrasonography showed oligohydramnios. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his respiratory failure?

options.text: Pulmonary hypoplasia due to bilateral renal agenesis
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
Meconium aspiration syndrome
Surfactant deficiency from prematurity

explanation: Potter sequence is caused by oligohydramnios, most often from bilateral renal agenesis, because fetal urine is the main source of amniotic fluid after about 16 weeks. Lack of fluid compresses the fetus, causing the characteristic facies, limb deformities, and pulmonary hypoplasia that is usually fatal.
pearl: Potter sequence: oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, limb deformities, Potter facies. Cause: bilateral renal agenesis or posterior urethral valves.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Oligohydramnios from absent kidneys causes lung hypoplasia.
optionExplanations.B: Diaphragmatic hernia causes lung hypoplasia but does not cause oligohydramnios.
optionExplanations.C: Meconium aspiration occurs after fetal distress in post-term infants and does not explain the facies and limb contractures.
optionExplanations.D: Surfactant deficiency affects premature infants and does not explain the facies and contractures.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Neural crest migration failure causing Hirschsprung disease
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: No ganglia, no peristalsis, no poop.
commonTrap: Confusing aganglionosis with duodenal atresia in a neonate with vomiting.
stem: A 2-day-old term boy has not passed meconium and has a distended abdomen with bilious vomiting. A rectal examination is followed by explosive release of stool and gas. A contrast enema shows a narrowed rectum with a dilated proximal colon. Failure of which of the following processes is responsible?

options.text: Neural crest cell migration to the distal colon
Rotation of the midgut
Closure of the processus vaginalis
Recanalization of the duodenum

explanation: Hirschsprung disease results from failure of neural crest cells to migrate into the distal colon, causing an aganglionic segment that remains contracted. It is associated with RET mutations and Down syndrome. Biopsy shows absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal and myenteric plexuses.
pearl: Hirschsprung: no meconium in 48 hours, transition zone on enema, RET mutation, rectal suction biopsy diagnostic.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Aganglionosis results from failed neural crest migration.
optionExplanations.B: Failed midgut rotation causes malrotation and volvulus.
optionExplanations.C: A patent processus vaginalis causes an indirect inguinal hernia or hydrocele.
optionExplanations.D: Failed duodenal recanalization causes duodenal atresia and a double-bubble sign.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Failure of spiral septum rotation in transposition of the great arteries
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: No spiral, no switch: aorta and pulmonary artery swapped.
commonTrap: Expecting a murmur or oxygen responsiveness.
stem: A 6-hour-old term boy born to a mother with diabetes is cyanotic. His oxygen saturation is 70% and does not improve with 100% oxygen. A single loud S2 is heard without a murmur, and chest radiograph shows an egg-shaped heart with a narrow mediastinum. Which of the following embryologic abnormalities is the most likely cause?

options.text: Incomplete fusion of the endocardial cushions
Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close
Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral
Malalignment of the infundibular septum

explanation: Transposition of the great arteries results from failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral, so the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle. The two circulations run in parallel, and survival depends on mixing through a patent ductus arteriosus, foramen ovale, or ventricular septal defect. Prostaglandin E1 maintains ductal patency before surgical correction.
pearl: TGA: maternal diabetes, no murmur, egg on a string; give prostaglandin E1 and arrange an arterial switch.

optionExplanations.A: Endocardial cushion defects cause atrioventricular septal defects, often in Down syndrome.
optionExplanations.B: A patent ductus would cause a continuous murmur and not cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Lack of spiraling produces parallel circulations.
optionExplanations.D: Anterior displacement of the infundibular septum causes tetralogy of Fallot with a systolic murmur.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Impaired GnRH neuron migration in Kallmann syndrome
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: No smell, no puberty: the GnRH neurons never arrived.
commonTrap: Interpreting low gonadotropins as constitutional delay without testing smell.
stem: A 17-year-old boy is evaluated because he has not entered puberty. He cannot smell coffee or perfume. Testes are 3 mL bilaterally and he has no pubic hair. Serum testosterone, LH, and FSH are all low, and MRI of the brain shows hypoplastic olfactory bulbs. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?

options.text: Primary testicular failure
Failed migration of GnRH-secreting neurons
Excess prolactin secretion
Aromatase deficiency

explanation: Kallmann syndrome is a form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism caused by failed migration of GnRH-secreting neurons from the olfactory placode to the hypothalamus. It causes anosmia, low LH, FSH, and testosterone, and delayed puberty. Treatment is gonadotropin or testosterone replacement.
pearl: Delayed puberty with anosmia and low LH/FSH is Kallmann syndrome (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism).

optionExplanations.A: Primary testicular failure would show elevated LH and FSH.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Anosmia with low gonadotropins indicates impaired GnRH neuron migration.
optionExplanations.C: Hyperprolactinemia could lower gonadotropins but would not cause anosmia and olfactory bulb hypoplasia.
optionExplanations.D: Aromatase deficiency impairs estrogen synthesis and causes tall stature and delayed bone age, not anosmia.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Weeks 3 to 8 as the period of greatest teratogenic susceptibility
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Three to eight: the building weeks.
commonTrap: Applying the all-or-none rule to the fifth week.
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 5 weeks of gestation takes isotretinoin for 2 weeks before learning that she is pregnant. She asks about the risk of congenital malformations. Which of the following best describes this stage of fetal development?

options.text: It is the fetal period, when exposure mainly affects growth and function
It is the all-or-none period, when exposure either kills the embryo or causes no harm
It is the period before implantation, when exposure causes no risk
It is the period of organogenesis, when teratogens cause the greatest structural malformations

explanation: Weeks 3 through 8 of gestation constitute embryogenesis (organogenesis), when organ systems form and teratogen exposure causes the greatest risk of major structural malformations. Isotretinoin causes craniofacial, cardiac, thymic, and CNS defects. The first 2 weeks are the all-or-none period, and later exposure primarily affects growth and functional development.
pearl: Weeks 0-2: all or none. Weeks 3-8: organogenesis, highest teratogenic risk. Week 9 onward: growth and function.

optionExplanations.A: The fetal period begins at week 9 and affects growth more than structure.
optionExplanations.B: The all-or-none period is weeks 1 to 2, before the stage described.
optionExplanations.C: Pre-implantation occurs in the first week and does not describe week 5.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Weeks 3 to 8 is the period of maximum structural vulnerability.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Failure of duodenal recanalization and the double-bubble sign
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Duodenum did not Dig a tunnel: failed recanalization.
commonTrap: Confusing midgut malrotation with duodenal atresia in a bilious neonate.
stem: A 12-hour-old term girl has bilious vomiting after her first feeding. Her prenatal course was notable for polyhydramnios. On examination she has upslanting palpebral fissures, a single palmar crease, and a flat nasal bridge. The abdomen is scaphoid with mild epigastric fullness. Abdominal radiography shows two gas-filled bubbles in the upper abdomen with no distal gas. Her temperature is 36.9 C, heart rate is 150 bpm, and sodium is 134 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of her obstruction?

options.text: Vascular accident of the superior mesenteric artery during fetal life
Failure of recanalization of the duodenal lumen
Failure of the midgut loop to rotate during return to the abdomen
Failure of neural crest cell migration into the colon

explanation: Duodenal atresia results from failure of the solid duodenal lumen to recanalize during weeks 8 to 10 of development. Polyhydramnios occurs because the fetus cannot absorb swallowed amniotic fluid past the obstruction. The double-bubble sign represents a dilated stomach and proximal duodenum with absent distal gas, and bilious vomiting occurs when the obstruction is distal to the ampulla of Vater. About 30% of cases occur in patients with Down syndrome, which fits the dysmorphic features here. Treatment is surgical duodenoduodenostomy after fluid resuscitation and decompression, and the cause is developmental, not infectious.
pearl: Double bubble plus polyhydramnios equals duodenal atresia; look for Down syndrome and other VACTERL-type anomalies.

optionExplanations.A: A mesenteric vascular accident causes jejunoileal atresia, which typically shows multiple dilated bowel loops and air-fluid levels rather than a double-bubble sign confined to the upper abdomen.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Failed recanalization produces duodenal atresia with a double-bubble sign, polyhydramnios, and an association with Down syndrome.
optionExplanations.C: Midgut malrotation causes volvulus and may produce bilious vomiting, but it does not cause a double-bubble sign with absent distal gas or polyhydramnios.
optionExplanations.D: Failed neural crest migration causes Hirschsprung disease, which produces distal colonic obstruction with a transition zone rather than a double-bubble sign and bilious proximal obstruction.

subject: Genetics
testedConcept: Androgen receptor defect causing 46,XY complete androgen insensitivity
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Androgens knock, but the receptor does not answer.
commonTrap: Confusing AIS with Turner syndrome because of primary amenorrhea.
stem: A 16-year-old girl is evaluated for primary amenorrhea. She has normal breast development, scant axillary and pubic hair, and a blind-ending vagina. Pelvic ultrasonography shows no uterus or ovaries, and bilateral inguinal masses are palpated. Her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and serum potassium is 4.0 mEq/L. Serum luteinizing hormone is elevated at 22 mIU/mL and serum testosterone is 600 ng/dL (male reference range 300-1000). Karyotype analysis is pending. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her condition?

options.text: Deficiency of 5-alpha-reductase type 2
Deficiency of 21-hydroxylase
Mutation of the androgen receptor gene
Deletion of the SHOX gene

explanation: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder from loss-of-function mutations in the androgen receptor, in a 46,XY individual. Testes produce normal or high testosterone and anti-Mullerian hormone, so there is no uterus, fallopian tubes, or upper vagina. Because tissues cannot respond to androgens, external genitalia are female, pubic and axillary hair are scant, and testosterone is aromatized to estrogen, producing breast development. Elevated LH reflects loss of negative feedback by androgen. The testes carry a risk of malignancy and are usually removed after puberty. Because the receptor is nonfunctional, the karyotype is 46,XY despite a female phenotype; aromatization of the abundant testosterone results in estrogen-driven breast development, while LH increases because androgen feedback is lost.
pearl: AIS: 46,XY, female phenotype, no uterus, normal or high testosterone, high LH, testes should be removed after puberty.

optionExplanations.A: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency causes ambiguous genitalia at birth with virilization at puberty because testosterone converts poorly to dihydrotestosterone, and breast development would not occur.
optionExplanations.B: 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes virilization of 46,XX females with a uterus and ovaries and low cortisol, which would not explain the absent uterus here.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. An androgen receptor defect gives a female phenotype with testes, high testosterone, and elevated LH in a 46,XY patient.
optionExplanations.D: SHOX deletion causes short stature as in Turner syndrome, whereas this patient has normal puberty-related breast development with a male karyotype.

subject: Genetics
testedConcept: CGG repeat expansion and FMR1 methylation in fragile X syndrome
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Fragile X: X, big testes, big ears, big jaw, CGG.
commonTrap: Choosing a CAG repeat disorder because both are trinucleotide expansions.
stem: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for developmental delay and hyperactivity. He has a long narrow face, large ears, and a prominent jaw. He avoids eye contact and has repetitive hand-flapping. His maternal uncle also has intellectual disability. His mother is of normal intelligence. Echocardiography shows mitral valve prolapse. His blood pressure is 98/60 mmHg, heart rate is 92 bpm, and serum thyroid-stimulating hormone is normal at 2.1 mIU/L. Which of the following genetic findings is most likely in this patient?

options.text: CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion with hypermethylation of FMR1
CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene
Deletion of the maternally inherited region of chromosome 15q11-q13
Nondisjunction producing an extra copy of chromosome 21

explanation: Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and is caused by expansion of a CGG repeat in the 5 prime untranslated region of FMR1 on the X chromosome. More than 200 repeats cause hypermethylation and silencing of the gene, reducing FMRP, a protein that regulates synaptic function. Features include a long face, large ears, a prominent jaw, macroorchidism after puberty, autistic features, and mitral valve prolapse. Anticipation occurs because repeat expansion increases during maternal meiosis, which explains the family pattern in which carrier mothers are unaffected but affected sons and maternal relatives are seen. Because the diagnosis is confirmed by DNA analysis of the CGG repeat number, genetic counseling matters: the risk of expansion to a full mutation increases with the size of a maternal premutation, and silencing of the gene results in decreased FMRP.
pearl: Fragile X: CGG repeats, FMR1, macroorchidism, long face, mitral valve prolapse; anticipation through maternal transmission.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. FMR1 CGG expansion above 200 repeats with methylation silences the gene and causes fragile X syndrome.
optionExplanations.B: A CAG expansion in the huntingtin gene causes Huntington disease, which presents in adulthood with chorea and dementia, not childhood developmental delay.
optionExplanations.C: Deletion of maternal 15q11-q13 causes Angelman syndrome with severe delay, seizures, and ataxia, whereas the facial features and family history here point away from it.
optionExplanations.D: Trisomy 21 would show upslanting palpebral fissures, a single palmar crease, and a heart defect such as an endocardial cushion defect, and it would not cluster in maternal male relatives.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Laboratory pattern of iron deficiency anemia
memoryAnchor: Ferritin and TIBC move in opposite directions in iron deficiency.
commonTrap: Mixing up iron deficiency and anemia of chronic disease patterns.
stem: A 29-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has fatigue and pallor. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume is 71 fL, and red cell distribution width is elevated. Which of the following laboratory patterns is most likely?

options.text: Low ferritin, low total iron-binding capacity, high serum iron
High ferritin, low total iron-binding capacity, low serum iron
High ferritin, high total iron-binding capacity, high serum iron
Low ferritin, high total iron-binding capacity, low serum iron

explanation: Iron deficiency anemia causes a microcytic anemia with low serum iron and ferritin and compensatory high TIBC (transferrin). RDW is elevated because of anisocytosis. Anemia of chronic disease shows high ferritin and low TIBC.
pearl: Iron deficiency: low ferritin, high TIBC, low transferrin saturation. Chronic disease: high ferritin, low TIBC.

optionExplanations.A: This combination does not fit any common pattern of iron disorder.
optionExplanations.B: High ferritin with low TIBC suggests anemia of chronic disease.
optionExplanations.C: High iron and ferritin suggest iron overload such as hemochromatosis.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Low iron and ferritin with high TIBC define iron deficiency.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Methylmalonic acid elevation distinguishes B12 from folate deficiency
memoryAnchor: MMA means B12.
commonTrap: Giving folate for macrocytic anemia without excluding B12 deficiency.
stem: A 68-year-old man has fatigue, glossitis, and numbness in both feet. Examination shows decreased vibration sense in the lower extremities. Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL, MCV is 112 fL, and the smear shows hypersegmented neutrophils. Which of the following laboratory findings would best confirm the cause of his neurologic symptoms?

options.text: Elevated serum iron
Low serum folate with normal methylmalonic acid
Elevated serum methylmalonic acid
Low reticulocyte count with normal homocysteine

explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts. Both homocysteine and methylmalonic acid rise in B12 deficiency, whereas only homocysteine rises in folate deficiency. Neurologic findings support B12, not folate, deficiency.
pearl: B12 deficiency: increased MMA and homocysteine; folate deficiency: increased homocysteine only. Treating with folate alone can worsen neurologic damage.

optionExplanations.A: Serum iron is not elevated in megaloblastic anemia.
optionExplanations.B: Folate deficiency has normal methylmalonic acid and does not cause neurologic findings.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Elevated methylmalonic acid is specific for B12 deficiency.
optionExplanations.D: Homocysteine is elevated in both B12 and folate deficiency.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Heinz bodies and bite cells in G6PD deficiency
memoryAnchor: No NADPH, no shield: fava beans burn the red cells.
commonTrap: Interpreting Heinz bodies as evidence of immune hemolysis.
stem: A 9-year-old boy of Mediterranean descent develops dark urine, jaundice, and back pain 2 days after eating fava beans. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL, indirect bilirubin is elevated, and a peripheral smear shows bite cells and blue inclusions on supravital staining. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

options.text: Autoantibody-mediated red cell destruction
Defective spectrin in the red cell membrane
Pyruvate kinase deficiency
Impaired generation of NADPH and reduced glutathione

explanation: G6PD deficiency, X-linked, impairs the pentose phosphate pathway, reducing NADPH and glutathione, so oxidative stress from fava beans, sulfa drugs, or infection precipitates hemolysis. Denatured hemoglobin forms Heinz bodies, which are removed by splenic macrophages to produce bite cells.
pearl: G6PD: Heinz bodies, bite cells, episodic hemolysis after oxidants; X-linked recessive.

optionExplanations.A: Autoimmune hemolysis would have a positive Coombs test and spherocytes.
optionExplanations.B: Spectrin defects cause hereditary spherocytosis with spherocytes and no Heinz bodies.
optionExplanations.C: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic extravascular hemolysis, not oxidant-triggered episodes.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Reduced NADPH leaves red cells vulnerable to oxidative damage.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Osmotic fragility and spectrin defects in hereditary spherocytosis
memoryAnchor: Spheres burst in salt-poor water.
commonTrap: Confusing hereditary spherocytosis with autoimmune hemolysis.
stem: A 7-year-old boy has episodic jaundice, splenomegaly, and an aplastic crisis after parvovirus B19 infection. His father had a splenectomy for anemia. Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration is elevated, and the smear shows spherocytes without central pallor. The Coombs test is negative. Which of the following findings is most likely?

options.text: Increased osmotic fragility
Positive direct antiglobulin test
Absent glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity
Decreased osmotic fragility

explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis, usually autosomal dominant, results from defects in ankyrin, spectrin, or band 3, producing spheroid cells that are trapped and destroyed by the spleen. Osmotic fragility is increased and MCHC is elevated. Splenectomy is curative of the anemia.
pearl: Hereditary spherocytosis: increased MCHC, osmotic fragility, EMA binding test abnormal; treated by splenectomy.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Spherocytes lyse easily in hypotonic solution.
optionExplanations.B: A positive DAT indicates autoimmune hemolysis, which is Coombs-negative here.
optionExplanations.C: G6PD deficiency causes oxidant-triggered hemolysis, not spherocytes with a family history.
optionExplanations.D: Decreased fragility occurs in thalassemia and sickle cell disease with target cells.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Hemoglobin electrophoresis in beta-thalassemia major
memoryAnchor: Beta zero: no A, only F.
commonTrap: Confusing beta-thalassemia major with the milder trait.
stem: A 14-month-old boy of Greek descent has pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, and frontal bossing. Hemoglobin is 5.8 g/dL with an MCV of 62 fL, and the smear shows target cells and nucleated red cells. Which of the following hemoglobin electrophoresis results is expected?

options.text: Predominant hemoglobin S
Markedly elevated hemoglobin F with absent hemoglobin A
Hemoglobin Barts as the predominant hemoglobin
Normal hemoglobin A with elevated hemoglobin A2 only

explanation: Beta-thalassemia major results from absent beta-globin synthesis, so hemoglobin A is absent and compensatory hemoglobin F and A2 are increased. Ineffective erythropoiesis causes marrow expansion (frontal bossing, crew-cut skull), extramedullary hematopoiesis, and iron overload from transfusions.
pearl: Beta-thal major: transfusion dependence, chelation, marrow expansion; beta-thal minor: mildly increased A2.

optionExplanations.A: Hemoglobin S predominance indicates sickle cell disease.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Without beta chains, HbA is absent and HbF predominates.
optionExplanations.C: Hemoglobin Barts occurs with severe alpha-thalassemia (hydrops fetalis).
optionExplanations.D: Normal HbA with high A2 describes beta-thalassemia minor.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Immune thrombocytopenia presentation and pathogenesis
memoryAnchor: ITP: isolated low platelets in an otherwise well patient.
commonTrap: Confusing ITP with TTP or DIC.
stem: A 5-year-old girl develops petechiae and bruising 2 weeks after a viral upper respiratory illness. She appears well, and the spleen is not palpable. Platelet count is 14,000/mm3, hemoglobin is 12.2 g/dL, and white blood cell count is normal. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?

options.text: Platelet consumption by disseminated intravascular coagulation
Decreased thrombopoietin from hepatic failure
Autoantibodies against platelet glycoproteins IIb/IIIa leading to splenic clearance
Deficiency of ADAMTS13 with microthrombi

explanation: Childhood immune thrombocytopenia is typically post-viral and caused by IgG autoantibodies against platelet glycoproteins that cause splenic macrophage destruction. Bone marrow shows increased megakaryocytes. Most children recover spontaneously.
pearl: ITP: isolated thrombocytopenia, normal PT/aPTT, increased megakaryocytes; adults often chronic, children usually self-limited.

optionExplanations.A: DIC would show prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, and an ill patient.
optionExplanations.B: Hepatic failure would produce coagulopathy and other features not seen here.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. IgG against GpIIb/IIIa leads to platelet clearance in the spleen.
optionExplanations.D: ADAMTS13 deficiency causes TTP with fever, anemia, and neurologic findings.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Laboratory profile of von Willebrand disease
memoryAnchor: vWF sticks platelets and shelters factor VIII.
commonTrap: Missing that vWD can prolong the aPTT through low factor VIII.
stem: A 19-year-old woman has recurrent epistaxis and menorrhagia since menarche. Her mother has similar symptoms. Platelet count is normal, prothrombin time is normal, and activated partial thromboplastin time is mildly prolonged. Bleeding time is prolonged. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Vitamin K deficiency
von Willebrand disease
Hemophilia A
Glanzmann thrombasthenia

explanation: von Willebrand factor mediates platelet adhesion via GpIb and carries factor VIII, so deficiency causes mucocutaneous bleeding, prolonged bleeding time, normal platelet count, and a prolonged aPTT. It is usually autosomal dominant. Desmopressin releases stored vWF and is first-line for mild type 1 disease.
pearl: vWD: increased bleeding time and aPTT, abnormal ristocetin cofactor assay; treat with desmopressin.

optionExplanations.A: Vitamin K deficiency prolongs PT first and does not affect bleeding time.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Mucosal bleeding with prolonged aPTT and bleeding time suggests vWD.
optionExplanations.C: Hemophilia A causes hemarthroses, X-linked inheritance, and a normal bleeding time.
optionExplanations.D: Glanzmann thrombasthenia has a defect in GpIIb/IIIa with normal aPTT.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: ADAMTS13 deficiency in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
memoryAnchor: ADAMTS13 trims the vWF; without it, clots form.
commonTrap: Treating suspected TTP with platelet transfusion.
stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with fever, confusion, and petechiae. Temperature is 38.4 C, hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL, platelet count is 18,000/mm3, and creatinine is 1.9 mg/dL. The smear shows schistocytes. Prothrombin time and fibrinogen are normal. Which of the following best explains this disorder?

options.text: Shiga toxin-mediated endothelial injury
Heparin-induced platelet factor 4 antibodies
Deficiency of factor VIII
Deficiency of ADAMTS13 causing large von Willebrand multimers

explanation: TTP is caused by deficient or autoantibody-inhibited ADAMTS13, which normally cleaves ultra-large von Willebrand multimers. Persistent multimers promote platelet microthrombi, producing thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, fever, renal dysfunction, and neurologic symptoms. Coagulation tests are normal and plasma exchange is first-line treatment.
pearl: TTP pentad: fever, MAHA, thrombocytopenia, renal failure, neurologic changes; treat with plasma exchange.

optionExplanations.A: Shiga toxin causes HUS, typically in children after bloody diarrhea, with prominent renal failure.
optionExplanations.B: HIT occurs after heparin exposure and causes thrombosis, not schistocytes.
optionExplanations.C: Factor VIII deficiency causes hemophilia A with prolonged aPTT.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. ADAMTS13 deficiency leaves large vWF multimers that cause platelet microthrombi.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: BCR-ABL fusion and imatinib in chronic myeloid leukemia
memoryAnchor: Philadelphia: 9 meets 22; imatinib blocks the kinase.
commonTrap: Choosing ATRA because both are leukemia-targeted therapies.
stem: A 48-year-old man has fatigue, early satiety, and left upper quadrant fullness. White blood cell count is 120,000/mm3 with immature granulocytes and basophilia. Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase is low. Cytogenetic analysis shows t(9;22). Which of the following drugs targets the molecular abnormality responsible?

options.text: Imatinib
Rituximab
All-trans retinoic acid
Methotrexate

explanation: The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) creates the BCR-ABL fusion, a constitutively active tyrosine kinase driving CML. Imatinib and other tyrosine kinase inhibitors block ABL and induce remission. A low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase distinguishes CML from a leukemoid reaction.
pearl: CML: t(9;22), BCR-ABL, basophilia, low LAP; blast crisis can be myeloid or lymphoid.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Imatinib inhibits the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase.
optionExplanations.B: Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells.
optionExplanations.C: All-trans retinoic acid targets the PML-RARA fusion of acute promyelocytic leukemia.
optionExplanations.D: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and is not targeted at BCR-ABL.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Reed-Sternberg cells and CD15/CD30 markers in Hodgkin lymphoma
memoryAnchor: Owl eyes: CD15 and CD30.
commonTrap: Assuming CD20 positivity in classic Hodgkin lymphoma.
stem: A 24-year-old man has painless cervical lymphadenopathy, night sweats, and a 5-kg weight loss. Chest radiography shows a mediastinal mass. Lymph node biopsy shows large binucleate cells with owl-eye nucleoli in a mixed inflammatory background. Which of the following immunophenotypes is most likely?

options.text: CD15 and CD30 positive
CD10 positive and BCL-2 positive
CD20 positive and CD5 positive
TdT positive

explanation: Reed-Sternberg cells of classic Hodgkin lymphoma express CD15 and CD30 and are CD45 negative. The mixed inflammatory background includes eosinophils, T cells, and plasma cells. Nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype in young adults.
pearl: Hodgkin: Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15, CD30), bimodal age, contiguous spread, B symptoms.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Classic Reed-Sternberg cells are CD15+ and CD30+.
optionExplanations.B: CD10 with BCL-2 indicates follicular lymphoma with t(14;18).
optionExplanations.C: CD20+ CD5+ cells are typical of mantle cell lymphoma or chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
optionExplanations.D: TdT positivity marks precursor lymphoblasts of acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Rouleaux and M spike in multiple myeloma
memoryAnchor: Casts of light chains clog the distal tubules.
commonTrap: Attributing renal failure only to hypercalcemia or dehydration.
stem: A 66-year-old woman has back pain and fatigue. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL, calcium is 12.1 mg/dL, creatinine is 2.3 mg/dL, and serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal spike. A peripheral smear shows red cells stacked like coins. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her renal failure?

options.text: Ischemic acute tubular necrosis from hypovolemia
Immune complex deposition in the glomerulus
Precipitation of light chains in the distal tubules
Amyloid beta deposition in the mesangium
