explanation: In multiple myeloma, excess monoclonal light chains (Bence Jones proteins) precipitate in the distal tubules with Tamm-Horsfall protein as casts, causing cast nephropathy. Hypercalcemia and dehydration worsen renal injury. Lytic bone lesions, anemia, and rouleaux are classic.
pearl: Myeloma: CRAB (calcium, renal, anemia, bone), M spike, rouleaux, Bence Jones protein, bone marrow plasma cells over 10 percent.

optionExplanations.A: Hypovolemia can contribute but does not explain the monoclonal protein pathology.
optionExplanations.B: Immune complex disease is not characteristic of myeloma.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Light-chain casts obstruct distal tubules.
optionExplanations.D: Myeloma-related amyloid is AL type, not amyloid beta.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Warfarin-induced skin necrosis and protein C deficiency
memoryAnchor: Protein C falls first: warfarin begins by clotting.
commonTrap: Thinking warfarin is immediately anticoagulant.
stem: A 55-year-old man with a pulmonary embolism is started on warfarin without bridging heparin. On day 4 he develops painful, well-demarcated erythematous patches on the thighs that evolve to hemorrhagic necrosis. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the skin lesions?

options.text: Deficiency of vitamin K-dependent factor VII only
Early decline of protein C causing transient hypercoagulability
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
Direct toxicity of warfarin to dermal fibroblasts

explanation: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S. Protein C has the shortest half-life, so its early fall produces a transient prothrombotic state and microvascular thrombosis of the skin, especially in protein C deficiency. Bridging with heparin prevents this.
pearl: Start warfarin with heparin overlap to avoid skin necrosis; INR monitors the extrinsic pathway.

optionExplanations.A: Factor VII has a short half-life but its decline is anticoagulant, not thrombotic.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Early protein C depletion causes transient hypercoagulability.
optionExplanations.C: HIT requires heparin exposure and typically occurs 5 to 10 days later with thrombocytopenia.
optionExplanations.D: Warfarin necrosis is thrombotic, not due to direct fibroblast toxicity.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Extrinsic pathway monitoring with prothrombin time
memoryAnchor: Seven is first, so PT is first.
commonTrap: Attributing PT prolongation to intrinsic pathway factors.
stem: A 74-year-old woman taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation has an INR of 6.5 after starting a new antibiotic. She has no bleeding. Which of the following coagulation factors is most responsible for the early prolongation of the prothrombin time?

options.text: Factor XII
Factor VIII
Factor XI
Factor VII

explanation: Prothrombin time evaluates the extrinsic and common pathways (factors VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen). Factor VII has the shortest half-life of the vitamin K-dependent factors, about 6 hours, so it falls first and drives early PT prolongation. aPTT reflects the intrinsic pathway.
pearl: PT measures extrinsic (VII) and common pathways; PTT measures intrinsic (VIII, IX, XI, XII).

optionExplanations.A: Factor XII is intrinsic and not vitamin K-dependent.
optionExplanations.B: Factor VIII is intrinsic and is not vitamin K-dependent.
optionExplanations.C: Factor XI is intrinsic and not vitamin K-dependent.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Factor VII is in the extrinsic pathway and has the shortest half-life.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction from ABO incompatibility
memoryAnchor: Wrong blood, immediate fire.
commonTrap: Confusing febrile nonhemolytic reaction with a hemolytic reaction.
stem: A 60-year-old man receiving a red blood cell transfusion develops fever, flank pain, hypotension, and dark urine within 15 minutes. The direct antiglobulin test is positive and plasma free hemoglobin is elevated. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?

options.text: Recipient IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies
Preformed antibodies against donor red cell ABO antigens
Donor antibodies against recipient neutrophil antigens
Cytokines released from stored donor leukocytes

explanation: Acute hemolytic transfusion reactions result from ABO incompatibility, usually through clerical error, in which recipient IgM antibodies bind donor red cells, activate complement, and cause intravascular hemolysis. Management includes stopping the transfusion, supporting blood pressure and urine output, and rechecking compatibility.
pearl: Acute hemolytic reaction: type II hypersensitivity; stop transfusion immediately.

optionExplanations.A: IgA deficiency causes anaphylaxis, not hemolysis with a positive DAT.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Preformed anti-A or anti-B antibodies cause immediate intravascular hemolysis.
optionExplanations.C: Donor anti-neutrophil antibodies cause transfusion-related acute lung injury.
optionExplanations.D: Cytokines from leukocytes cause febrile nonhemolytic reactions, which are mild.

subject: Immunology
testedConcept: Type IV hypersensitivity in tuberculin skin testing
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Type IV: Four letters of T-cell Time delay.
commonTrap: Attributing the reaction to antibodies.
stem: A 35-year-old nurse has an induration of 12 mm at the site of a purified protein derivative injection 48 hours after placement. Which of the following is the primary effector mechanism of this reaction?

options.text: Immune complex deposition with complement activation
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation
Sensitized T cells releasing cytokines and activating macrophages
IgG binding to cell surface antigens

explanation: The tuberculin reaction is a delayed type (type IV) hypersensitivity mediated by sensitized CD4 T cells that release interferon-gamma, activating macrophages and causing induration 48 to 72 hours after exposure. No antibodies are involved.
pearl: Type IV: delayed, T cell, no antibody (PPD, contact dermatitis, graft rejection).

optionExplanations.A: Immune complex deposition characterizes type III reactions such as serum sickness.
optionExplanations.B: IgE-mediated type I reactions occur within minutes.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Type IV is T cell-mediated and delayed.
optionExplanations.D: IgG binding to cells characterizes type II reactions.

subject: Immunology
testedConcept: Recurrent Neisseria infections in terminal complement deficiency
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: MAC kills Neisseria.
commonTrap: Choosing C3 deficiency because it also causes infection.
stem: A 20-year-old man has a second episode of meningococcal meningitis in 3 years. Total hemolytic complement activity (CH50) is absent, while C3 and C4 levels are normal. Which of the following is the most likely defect?

options.text: Deficiency of a terminal complement component (C5-C9)
Deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor
Deficiency of C3
Deficiency of decay-accelerating factor

explanation: The membrane attack complex (C5b-C9) is needed to lyse Neisseria. Deficiency of C5 through C9 causes recurrent Neisseria infections, with normal C3 and C4 and absent CH50. C3 deficiency would cause severe recurrent bacterial infections of many organisms.
pearl: Terminal complement deficiency: recurrent Neisseria infections; C3 deficiency: severe recurrent pyogenic infections.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Terminal component deficiency impairs MAC-mediated lysis of Neisseria.
optionExplanations.B: C1 inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema with low C4.
optionExplanations.C: C3 deficiency produces low C3 and recurrent infections with many pyogenic organisms.
optionExplanations.D: DAF deficiency causes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.

subject: Immunology
testedConcept: Absent B cells and BTK mutation in X-linked agammaglobulinemia
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Bruton: B cells are Bruised and missing.
commonTrap: Choosing hyper-IgM syndrome, where IgM is elevated.
stem: A 9-month-old boy has had recurrent otitis media and two episodes of pneumonia since 6 months of age. Tonsils are absent and lymph nodes are not palpable. Flow cytometry shows absent CD19+ B cells, and serum immunoglobulins of all classes are markedly decreased. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.text: Mutation in the adenosine deaminase gene
Mutation in CD40 ligand
Deletion at 22q11.2
Mutation in Bruton tyrosine kinase

explanation: X-linked agammaglobulinemia is caused by BTK mutations that block maturation of pre-B cells to mature B cells. Symptoms appear after maternal IgG wanes at about 6 months, with recurrent bacterial infections by encapsulated organisms and enteroviruses. Patients lack tonsils and lymph node germinal centers. The defect is a mutation in Bruton tyrosine kinase.
pearl: XLA: male infant, symptoms after 6 months, absent B cells, absent tonsils, low all immunoglobulins; treat with IVIG.

optionExplanations.A: ADA deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency with absent T and B cells.
optionExplanations.B: CD40L mutation causes hyper-IgM syndrome with elevated IgM and normal B cell numbers.
optionExplanations.C: A 22q11.2 deletion causes DiGeorge syndrome with T-cell deficiency.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. BTK mutation blocks B cell maturation.

subject: Immunology
testedConcept: NADPH oxidase deficiency and catalase-positive infections
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: No burst, no kill: catalase-positive bugs thrive.
commonTrap: Confusing CGD with leukocyte adhesion deficiency.
stem: A 6-year-old boy has recurrent abscesses of the skin, lungs, and liver caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus species. Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry shows no oxidative burst. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

options.text: Defective NADPH oxidase
Defective myeloperoxidase
Defective LFA-1 integrin
Defective lysosomal trafficking regulator protein

explanation: Chronic granulomatous disease results from NADPH oxidase deficiency, preventing production of reactive oxygen species. Catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Burkholderia) are not killed because they destroy their own hydrogen peroxide. Dihydrorhodamine test shows absent oxidative burst.
pearl: CGD: catalase-positive infections, granulomas, abnormal DHR test; treat with interferon-gamma and prophylactic antibiotics.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. NADPH oxidase deficiency prevents the respiratory burst.
optionExplanations.B: Myeloperoxidase deficiency usually causes few infections and abnormal DHR with a different pattern.
optionExplanations.C: LFA-1 deficiency causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency with delayed cord separation and no pus.
optionExplanations.D: LYST defects cause Chediak-Higashi syndrome with giant lysosomal granules.

subject: Immunology
testedConcept: Hyperacute rejection from preformed antibodies
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Hyperacute means hyper-fast antibody.
commonTrap: Attributing immediate graft failure to T cells.
stem: A 45-year-old man undergoes renal transplantation. Within minutes of vascular anastomosis the kidney becomes cyanotic and mottled, and no urine is produced. Biopsy shows fibrinoid necrosis of vessels and neutrophil infiltration. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?

options.text: Recipient CD8 T cells attacking donor parenchyma
Donor T cells attacking recipient tissues
Chronic proliferation of intimal smooth muscle
Preformed recipient antibodies against donor antigens

explanation: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to hours from preformed antibodies against donor ABO or HLA antigens, activating complement and causing thrombosis and necrosis. It is prevented by ABO matching and cross-matching and cannot be treated; the graft must be removed.
pearl: Hyperacute: minutes, antibody; acute: weeks, T cells; chronic: months to years, vascular fibrosis.

optionExplanations.A: CD8 T-cell attack characterizes acute cellular rejection over days to weeks.
optionExplanations.B: Donor T cells attacking recipient tissue define graft-versus-host disease.
optionExplanations.C: Intimal proliferation is chronic rejection occurring months to years later.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Preformed antibodies cause immediate type II hypersensitivity.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies in lupus nephritis
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: Double strand, double specific.
commonTrap: Choosing antihistone because of the drug-induced lupus association.
stem: A 26-year-old woman has a malar rash, arthralgias, and proteinuria. Serum C3 and C4 are low. Which of the following antibodies is most specific for her likely diagnosis?

options.text: Anti-centromere
Antihistone
Anti-double-stranded DNA
Anti-Jo-1

explanation: Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies are highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus, and anti-dsDNA correlates with lupus nephritis. Complement consumption by immune complexes lowers C3 and C4. ANA is sensitive but not specific. Anti-double-stranded DNA is therefore the most specific antibody here.
pearl: SLE: ANA (sensitive), anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith (specific); low complement in active nephritis.

optionExplanations.A: Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited scleroderma (CREST).
optionExplanations.B: Antihistone antibodies are associated with drug-induced lupus.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Anti-dsDNA is highly specific for SLE and tracks nephritis.
optionExplanations.D: Anti-Jo-1 is associated with polymyositis and dermatomyositis.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: JAK2 V617F mutation and low erythropoietin in polycythemia vera
memoryAnchor: Low EPO plus high hemoglobin means JAK2.
commonTrap: Missing that secondary polycythemia has high EPO.
stem: A 58-year-old man has headaches, pruritus after hot showers, and a ruddy complexion. Examination shows splenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 19.4 g/dL, platelet count is 640,000/mm3, and serum erythropoietin is low. Oxygen saturation is normal. Which of the following mutations is most likely present?

options.text: Calreticulin deletion only
JAK2 V617F
BCR-ABL fusion
PML-RARA fusion

explanation: Polycythemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by JAK2 V617F in most patients, causing erythropoietin-independent red cell production, with elevated hemoglobin, low EPO, and often thrombocytosis and splenomegaly. Treatment includes phlebotomy and aspirin, with hydroxyurea in higher-risk patients.
pearl: PV: low EPO, JAK2 mutation, aquagenic pruritus, risk of thrombosis and Budd-Chiari.

optionExplanations.A: Calreticulin mutations occur in essential thrombocythemia and myelofibrosis, not typically PV.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. JAK2 V617F is present in over 95 percent of polycythemia vera.
optionExplanations.C: BCR-ABL defines chronic myeloid leukemia.
optionExplanations.D: PML-RARA defines acute promyelocytic leukemia.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: GPI anchor deficiency and complement-mediated hemolysis in PNH
memoryAnchor: No GPI, no brakes: complement burns red cells at night.
commonTrap: Expecting a positive Coombs test in PNH.
stem: A 33-year-old woman has episodes of dark morning urine, abdominal pain, and hepatic vein thrombosis. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase is elevated, and the direct antiglobulin test is negative. Flow cytometry shows loss of CD55 and CD59 on red cells. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

options.text: Mutation in G6PD
Mutation in PIGA causing absent GPI anchors
Mutation in the spectrin gene
Autoantibody against red cell antigens

explanation: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria results from acquired PIGA mutation in a hematopoietic stem cell, causing loss of GPI-anchored proteins DAF (CD55) and MIRL (CD59). Red cells are lysed by complement, and patients have intravascular hemolysis, thrombosis, and cytopenias. Eculizumab inhibits C5.
pearl: PNH: Coombs-negative hemolysis, thrombosis, loss of CD55/CD59; treat with eculizumab.

optionExplanations.A: G6PD deficiency causes oxidant-triggered hemolysis in males.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. PIGA mutation removes complement inhibitors from the cell surface.
optionExplanations.C: Spectrin defects cause hereditary spherocytosis with a positive family history.
optionExplanations.D: Autoantibodies would produce a positive DAT.

subject: Immunology
testedConcept: CD40 ligand defect preventing immunoglobulin class switching
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: CD40L is the switch handle for class switching.
commonTrap: Missing the elevated IgM in a patient with recurrent infections.
stem: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent sinopulmonary infections and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Serum IgM is elevated, whereas IgG and IgA are very low. B cell numbers are normal. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

options.text: Defective adenosine deaminase
Defective Bruton tyrosine kinase
Defective IL-2 receptor gamma chain
Defective CD40 ligand on helper T cells

explanation: Hyper-IgM syndrome, usually X-linked, results from CD40 ligand (CD154) deficiency on activated helper T cells, which blocks CD40 signaling needed for isotype switching and germinal center formation. IgM is high while IgG and IgA are low, and defective T cell macrophage activation predisposes to opportunistic infection.
pearl: Hyper-IgM: high IgM, low other isotypes, CD40L defect; opportunistic infections can occur.

optionExplanations.A: ADA deficiency causes SCID with low T and B cells.
optionExplanations.B: BTK defect lowers all immunoglobulins with absent B cells.
optionExplanations.C: IL-2 receptor gamma chain defect causes X-linked SCID.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. CD40L deficiency prevents class switching.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Tissue factor release and consumption coagulopathy in DIC
memoryAnchor: Tissue factor sets off the cascade everywhere.
commonTrap: Confusing DIC with TTP because of schistocytes and thrombocytopenia.
stem: A 30-year-old woman at 37 weeks of gestation is brought to the hospital with vaginal bleeding after placental abruption. Her blood pressure is 82/50 mmHg, heart rate is 124 bpm, and bleeding continues from intravenous sites. Hemoglobin is 7.1 g/dL, platelet count is 38,000/mm3, prothrombin time is 24 seconds, aPTT is 58 seconds, fibrinogen is 90 mg/dL, and D-dimer is markedly elevated. The smear shows schistocytes. Which of the following best explains the coagulopathy?

options.text: Release of tissue factor into the circulation activating widespread coagulation
Deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors from poor intake
Autoantibody against platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa
Deficiency of ADAMTS13 with ultra-large multimers

explanation: Placental abruption releases tissue factor (thromboplastin) into the maternal circulation, activating the extrinsic pathway and causing disseminated fibrin deposition in small vessels. Platelets and clotting factors are consumed, so PT and aPTT prolong, fibrinogen falls, D-dimer rises, and schistocytes form because fibrin strands shear red cells. The result is both thrombosis and bleeding. Treatment addresses the underlying cause, here delivery, and replaces platelets, cryoprecipitate, and plasma while maintaining perfusion.
pearl: DIC: low platelets, low fibrinogen, prolonged PT/aPTT, high D-dimer, schistocytes; causes include sepsis, obstetric complications, malignancy.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Tissue factor release triggers consumptive coagulopathy, giving prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, and schistocytes.
optionExplanations.B: Vitamin K deficiency prolongs PT and later aPTT but fibrinogen remains normal, the platelet count is preserved, and D-dimer is not markedly elevated.
optionExplanations.C: Anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies cause isolated thrombocytopenia with normal PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen, and they would not produce schistocytes.
optionExplanations.D: ADAMTS13 deficiency causes TTP with thrombocytopenia and hemolysis but normal PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen because coagulation factors are not consumed.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: ATRA induced differentiation of promyelocytes in acute promyelocytic leukemia
memoryAnchor: ATRA turns promyelocytes into mature cells.
commonTrap: Delaying ATRA until the translocation is confirmed.
stem: A 41-year-old woman has gum bleeding, ecchymoses, and fatigue for 1 week. Hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL, white blood cell count is 3,200/mm3, platelet count is 22,000/mm3, prothrombin time is 19 seconds, and fibrinogen is 110 mg/dL. Peripheral smear shows abnormal promyelocytes with multiple Auer rods. Cytogenetics show t(15;17). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment mechanism for this patient?

options.text: Hydroxyurea inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase
Rituximab depleting CD20-positive B cells
All-trans retinoic acid promoting differentiation of promyelocytes
Imatinib blocking the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase

explanation: Acute promyelocytic leukemia is caused by t(15;17) producing the PML-RARA fusion protein, which blocks myeloid differentiation at the promyelocyte stage. Granules release tissue factor and cause a high risk of DIC, as shown by low fibrinogen and prolonged PT. All-trans retinoic acid overcomes the differentiation block and, with arsenic trioxide, achieves very high remission rates. Treatment should start immediately upon suspicion because of the bleeding risk, even before cytogenetic confirmation, and it increases the differentiation of leukemic cells into mature neutrophils.
pearl: APL: t(15;17), PML-RARA, Auer rods, DIC; treat with ATRA plus arsenic trioxide, start immediately.

optionExplanations.A: Hydroxyurea is cytoreductive for myeloproliferative disease and does not reverse the differentiation block or correct the coagulopathy of APL.
optionExplanations.B: Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells, but leukemic promyelocytes are myeloid cells and are not CD20 dependent.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. ATRA overcomes the PML-RARA differentiation block and treats the underlying leukemia, reducing the DIC risk.
optionExplanations.D: Imatinib targets BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukemia, which is not driven by t(15;17), and it would not treat the promyelocytic block.

subject: Immunology
testedConcept: Absent T cells and thymic shadow in severe combined immunodeficiency
physicianTask: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
memoryAnchor: No T cells, no thymus shadow, transplant early.
commonTrap: Treating SCID with immunoglobulin alone.
stem: A 4-month-old boy has persistent oral candidiasis, chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. His temperature is 38.2 C, respiratory rate is 58/min, and oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. Chest radiography shows diffuse interstitial infiltrates and an absent thymic shadow. Absolute lymphocyte count is 450/mm3, and flow cytometry shows markedly decreased CD3-positive T cells. A maternal uncle died in infancy of infections. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment?

options.text: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
Thymus transplantation for all cases
Lifelong intravenous immunoglobulin alone
Interferon-gamma and prophylactic antibiotics only

explanation: This infant has severe combined immunodeficiency, most commonly X-linked from an IL-2 receptor gamma chain (common gamma chain) mutation, which impairs signaling for T and natural killer cell development and causes absent B cell function secondary to absent T cell help. Early opportunistic infections, failure to thrive, lymphopenia, and an absent thymic shadow suggest the diagnosis. Live vaccines are contraindicated. The only definitive treatment is early hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and gene therapy is an option for some forms, while IVIG and prophylaxis provide only temporary support because the T cell defect results in persistent risk.
pearl: SCID: absent thymic shadow, lymphopenia, opportunistic infections; no live vaccines; treat with HSCT.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Stem cell transplantation replaces the defective lymphoid lineage and is the only definitive treatment for SCID.
optionExplanations.B: Thymus transplantation is used for complete DiGeorge syndrome, whereas SCID is due to an intrinsic lymphocyte defect, so a thymus graft would not restore function.
optionExplanations.C: IVIG replaces antibody but does not correct the T cell deficiency, so opportunistic infections and mortality would persist without transplantation.
optionExplanations.D: Interferon-gamma and prophylaxis help in chronic granulomatous disease, which involves a phagocyte oxidative defect rather than a lymphocyte deficiency.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Chronic lithium adverse effects including nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
memoryAnchor: Lithium makes kidneys deaf to ADH.
commonTrap: Expecting a response to desmopressin.
stem: A 35-year-old woman with bipolar disorder who has taken lithium for 3 years reports polyuria, polydipsia, and fatigue. Serum sodium is 148 mEq/L, urine osmolality is low, and she does not respond to desmopressin. TSH is elevated. Which of the following best explains her urinary findings?

options.text: Primary polydipsia causing water intoxication
Resistance of the collecting duct to antidiuretic hormone
Excess secretion of antidiuretic hormone
Osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia

explanation: Lithium accumulates in principal cells of the collecting duct and impairs aquaporin-2 insertion in response to ADH, causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus that does not respond to desmopressin. Lithium also causes hypothyroidism, tremor, and teratogenic cardiac defects (Ebstein anomaly). Treatment includes amiloride and discontinuing lithium.
pearl: Lithium: tremor, hypothyroidism, nephrogenic DI, Ebstein anomaly; avoid with NSAIDs, thiazides, and ACE inhibitors.

optionExplanations.A: Primary polydipsia causes hyponatremia and dilute urine, not hypernatremia.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by blocking ADH effect.
optionExplanations.C: Excess ADH (SIADH) would cause hyponatremia and concentrated urine.
optionExplanations.D: Hyperglycemia would produce glucosuria and high urine osmolality.

subject: Behavioral Science
testedConcept: Duration criteria distinguishing schizophrenia from schizophreniform disorder
memoryAnchor: One, Six: the clock decides the name.
commonTrap: Diagnosing schizophrenia before 6 months.
stem: A 22-year-old man has experienced auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions, and social withdrawal for 3 months. He has no mood episode, and urine toxicology is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizophrenia
Brief psychotic disorder
Schizophreniform disorder
Schizoaffective disorder

explanation: Schizophreniform disorder is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms last at least 1 month but less than 6 months. Schizophrenia requires at least 6 months of illness. Brief psychotic disorder lasts less than 1 month, and schizoaffective disorder requires a concurrent major mood episode.
pearl: Brief psychotic less than 1 month; schizophreniform 1 to 6 months; schizophrenia 6 months or more.

optionExplanations.A: Schizophrenia requires 6 months of symptoms.
optionExplanations.B: Brief psychotic disorder lasts less than 1 month.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Symptoms for 3 months fit schizophreniform disorder.
optionExplanations.D: Schizoaffective disorder includes mood episodes, which are absent.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: First-line long-term treatment of panic disorder
memoryAnchor: Panic: SSRI first, benzos for a bridge.
commonTrap: Choosing a benzodiazepine as first-line long-term therapy.
stem: A 28-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of palpitations, sweating, chest tightness, and fear of dying that peak within 10 minutes. She worries about future attacks and avoids driving. Cardiac evaluation is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Propranolol alone
Alprazolam alone
Buspirone
Sertraline

explanation: SSRIs and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, combined with cognitive-behavioral therapy, are first-line long-term treatment for panic disorder. Benzodiazepines act quickly but carry risk of dependence and are used only short term or as a bridge.
pearl: Panic disorder: SSRI or SNRI plus CBT; benzodiazepines only as short-term bridge.

optionExplanations.A: Propranolol does not prevent panic attacks.
optionExplanations.B: Alprazolam alone risks dependence and is not first-line long term.
optionExplanations.C: Buspirone is used for generalized anxiety and is ineffective for panic disorder.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Sertraline, an SSRI, is first-line for panic disorder.

subject: Behavioral Science
testedConcept: Splitting as the defense mechanism in borderline personality disorder
memoryAnchor: Split: all good or all bad.
commonTrap: Mistaking projection for splitting.
stem: A 24-year-old woman with unstable relationships, recurrent self-cutting, and chronic emptiness describes her new therapist as perfect on Monday and cruel and incompetent by Friday. Which of the following defense mechanisms is she using?

options.text: Reaction formation
Rationalization
Projection
Splitting

explanation: Splitting, viewing people as all good or all bad, is characteristic of borderline personality disorder. First-line treatment is dialectical behavior therapy. Projection attributes unacceptable feelings to others, reaction formation replaces an impulse with its opposite, and rationalization justifies behavior with logical-sounding reasons.
pearl: Borderline PD: splitting, impulsivity, self-harm, fear of abandonment; treat with DBT.

optionExplanations.A: Reaction formation converts an unacceptable impulse into its opposite behavior.
optionExplanations.B: Rationalization explains unacceptable behavior with plausible reasons.
optionExplanations.C: Projection attributes one own feelings to someone else.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Alternating idealization and devaluation is splitting.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal and delirium tremens
memoryAnchor: Withdrawal needs benzos; sobriety drugs come later.
commonTrap: Using antipsychotics as monotherapy for delirium tremens.
stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic alcohol use is hospitalized for pneumonia. On day 3 he develops tremor, visual hallucinations of insects, disorientation, temperature of 38.3 C, heart rate of 124 bpm, and blood pressure of 168/96 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Lorazepam
Disulfiram
Haloperidol alone
Naltrexone

explanation: Delirium tremens typically begins 48 to 96 hours after the last drink and includes autonomic hyperactivity, hallucinations, and confusion. Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam (preferred in liver disease) or diazepam are the treatment of choice and reduce mortality and seizures. Haloperidol alone can lower the seizure threshold. Thiamine should be given before glucose.
pearl: Alcohol withdrawal: 6-24 h tremor; 12-48 h seizures; 48-96 h delirium tremens. Give benzodiazepines and thiamine.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Benzodiazepines treat alcohol withdrawal and prevent seizures.
optionExplanations.B: Disulfiram causes aversive reactions to alcohol and is not a withdrawal treatment.
optionExplanations.C: Antipsychotics alone do not prevent seizures and may worsen them.
optionExplanations.D: Naltrexone reduces cravings but does not treat withdrawal.

subject: Behavioral Science
testedConcept: Refeeding syndrome with hypophosphatemia in anorexia nervosa
memoryAnchor: Feed slowly: insulin pulls phosphate into cells.
commonTrap: Overlooking electrolyte monitoring during refeeding.
stem: A 17-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa and a BMI of 14 kg/m2 is hospitalized and started on aggressive enteral nutrition. On day 3 she develops weakness, confusion, and respiratory muscle fatigue. Which of the following laboratory abnormalities is most likely?

options.text: Hypercalcemia
Hyperphosphatemia
Hypophosphatemia
Hypernatremia

explanation: Refeeding syndrome results from insulin-driven intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium when carbohydrates are reintroduced to a malnourished patient. Hypophosphatemia causes muscle weakness, respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmias, and hemolysis. Electrolytes should be monitored and repleted, and calories advanced slowly.
pearl: Refeeding syndrome: low phosphate, potassium, magnesium; give thiamine; advance calories slowly.

optionExplanations.A: Hypercalcemia is not characteristic.
optionExplanations.B: Hyperphosphatemia is not expected with refeeding.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Phosphate shifts into cells and levels fall.
optionExplanations.D: Hypernatremia is not the hallmark of refeeding syndrome.

subject: Anatomy
testedConcept: Clinical deficits of middle cerebral artery occlusion
memoryAnchor: MCA: face and arm; ACA: leg.
commonTrap: Mixing the MCA and ACA territories.
stem: A 68-year-old right-handed man with atrial fibrillation has sudden right-sided facial droop and arm weakness with expressive speech difficulty but intact comprehension. Leg strength is relatively spared. Which of the following arteries is most likely occluded?

options.text: Left anterior cerebral artery
Left middle cerebral artery
Right middle cerebral artery
Basilar artery

explanation: The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral cerebral convexity, including the motor and sensory cortex for the face and arm. A left MCA stroke in a right-handed patient causes right face and arm weakness with aphasia, here Broca (expressive). Anterior cerebral artery strokes spare the face and cause leg weakness.
pearl: MCA: face and arm weakness, aphasia (dominant), neglect (nondominant); ACA: leg weakness; PCA: visual field loss.

optionExplanations.A: The ACA causes contralateral leg weakness with relative sparing of the arm and face.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The left MCA causes right face and arm weakness with aphasia.
optionExplanations.C: A right MCA stroke would cause left-sided deficits and neglect.
optionExplanations.D: Basilar occlusion causes bilateral deficits, cranial nerve palsies, and altered consciousness.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Thiamine administration before glucose in Wernicke encephalopathy
memoryAnchor: Thiamine first, then sugar.
commonTrap: Treating hypoglycemia with glucose before thiamine in alcohol use disorder.
stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic alcohol use is brought in confused, with a wide-based gait and horizontal nystagmus. Serum glucose is 68 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous naloxone
Oral folate
Intravenous thiamine before glucose
Intravenous glucose alone

explanation: Wernicke encephalopathy causes confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia from thiamine deficiency. Giving glucose before thiamine can precipitate or worsen the disorder because thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase. Untreated, it can progress to Korsakoff syndrome with irreversible memory loss and confabulation.
pearl: Wernicke triad: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; give thiamine before glucose.

optionExplanations.A: Naloxone treats opioid overdose, which is not suggested.
optionExplanations.B: Folate does not treat thiamine deficiency.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Thiamine must be given before or with glucose.
optionExplanations.D: Glucose alone can precipitate acute thiamine depletion.

subject: Anatomy
testedConcept: Lower motor neuron facial palsy involves the forehead
memoryAnchor: Forehead involved means peripheral.
commonTrap: Misinterpreting forehead sparing as peripheral.
stem: A 34-year-old woman wakes with right facial drooping, inability to close the right eye, and loss of forehead wrinkling on the right. Taste is decreased on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue on that side, and sounds seem louder. Which of the following lesions best explains these findings?

options.text: Right abducens nerve lesion
Right trigeminal nerve lesion
Left motor cortex lesion
Right facial nerve lesion in the facial canal proximal to the chorda tympani

explanation: A peripheral (lower motor neuron) facial nerve lesion, as in Bell palsy, paralyzes the entire ipsilateral face including the forehead. A lesion proximal to the chorda tympani reduces anterior tongue taste, and a lesion proximal to the stapedius branch causes hyperacusis. A central lesion spares the forehead because of bilateral upper motor neuron input.
pearl: Bell palsy: LMN facial weakness; treat with oral steroids; upper motor neuron lesions spare the forehead.

optionExplanations.A: The abducens nerve controls lateral gaze.
optionExplanations.B: The trigeminal nerve mediates facial sensation and mastication, not facial expression.
optionExplanations.C: A left cortical lesion causes contralateral lower facial weakness with forehead sparing.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Forehead involvement with taste loss and hyperacusis indicates a peripheral facial nerve lesion.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Substantia nigra degeneration and Lewy bodies in Parkinson disease
memoryAnchor: Lose the dopamine, lose the movement.
commonTrap: Confusing Lewy bodies with Alzheimer tangles.
stem: A 66-year-old man has a resting tremor of the right hand, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and a shuffling gait. Which of the following pathologic findings is most likely at autopsy?

options.text: Loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert with neurofibrillary tangles
Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta with Lewy bodies
Atrophy of the caudate nucleus with CAG repeats
Demyelinating plaques in the periventricular white matter

explanation: Parkinson disease results from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, with intracellular alpha-synuclein inclusions (Lewy bodies). The loss of dopamine disinhibits the indirect pathway and reduces thalamic excitation of the motor cortex, causing bradykinesia and rigidity.
pearl: Parkinson: resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability; treat with levodopa/carbidopa.

optionExplanations.A: Nucleus basalis loss and tangles describe Alzheimer disease.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Nigral dopaminergic loss with Lewy bodies defines Parkinson disease.
optionExplanations.C: Caudate atrophy with CAG expansion describes Huntington disease.
optionExplanations.D: Periventricular plaques describe multiple sclerosis.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Ethosuximide for absence seizures through T-type calcium channel blockade
memoryAnchor: Ethosuximide: Ethically, T channels in the thalamus.
commonTrap: Using sodium channel blockers for absence seizures.
stem: A 7-year-old girl has frequent episodes of staring and unresponsiveness lasting 10 seconds, with eyelid fluttering. She has no postictal confusion. EEG shows 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges. Hyperventilation reproduces an episode. Which of the following is the drug of choice?

options.text: Ethosuximide
Phenytoin
Carbamazepine
Phenobarbital

explanation: Absence seizures show 3-Hz spike-and-wave on EEG and brief staring without postictal state. Ethosuximide blocks thalamic T-type calcium channels and is first-line. Valproate is an alternative when generalized tonic-clonic seizures also occur. Phenytoin and carbamazepine can worsen absence seizures.
pearl: Absence: ethosuximide; adverse effects: GI distress, headache, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons.
optionExplanations.B: Phenytoin does not help and may worsen absence seizures.
optionExplanations.C: Carbamazepine can aggravate absence seizures.
optionExplanations.D: Phenobarbital is not first-line for absence seizures.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Oligoclonal bands and periventricular plaques in multiple sclerosis
memoryAnchor: MS: lesions separated in time and space; CSF bands.
commonTrap: Confusing albuminocytologic dissociation of GBS with MS.
stem: A 29-year-old woman has had 2 episodes of neurologic dysfunction: 6 months ago she had painful visual loss in the right eye that resolved, and now she has leg weakness and urinary urgency. MRI shows multiple periventricular white matter lesions. Which of the following findings in cerebrospinal fluid is most likely?

options.text: Albuminocytologic dissociation
Oligoclonal IgG bands
Xanthochromia
Markedly elevated neutrophils with low glucose

explanation: Multiple sclerosis involves immune-mediated demyelination of CNS white matter separated in time and space. CSF shows oligoclonal IgG bands and mildly elevated protein, with normal glucose. Interferon-beta, glatiramer, and other disease-modifying therapies reduce relapses.
pearl: MS: optic neuritis, INO, spasticity; MRI periventricular plaques; treat relapses with high-dose steroids.

optionExplanations.A: Albuminocytologic dissociation is typical of Guillain-Barre syndrome.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Oligoclonal bands reflect intrathecal IgG synthesis.
optionExplanations.C: Xanthochromia indicates subarachnoid hemorrhage.
optionExplanations.D: Neutrophils with low glucose indicate bacterial meningitis.

subject: Anatomy
testedConcept: Hemisection of the spinal cord and crossed sensory loss
memoryAnchor: Pain crosses early, touch crosses late.
commonTrap: Assuming all sensory modalities cross at the same level.
stem: A 26-year-old man is stabbed in the back at the T10 level. Examination shows right leg weakness with loss of vibration and proprioception on the right and loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left below the level of the lesion. Which of the following best explains the contralateral loss of pain and temperature?

options.text: The spinothalamic tract crosses within a few segments of its entry into the cord
The dorsal columns cross at the spinal level of entry
The anterior horn cells project contralaterally
The corticospinal tract decussates in the cervical cord

explanation: In Brown-Sequard syndrome, hemisection causes ipsilateral upper motor neuron weakness (corticospinal tract, crossed in the medulla), ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception (dorsal columns, crossed in the medulla), and contralateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic fibers cross in the anterior white commissure one or two levels above entry).
pearl: Brown-Sequard: ipsilateral weakness and loss of fine touch/proprioception; contralateral loss of pain and temperature.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Spinothalamic fibers cross near their level of entry.
optionExplanations.B: Dorsal column fibers ascend ipsilaterally and cross in the medulla.
optionExplanations.C: Anterior horn cells project ipsilaterally to muscle.
optionExplanations.D: The corticospinal tract crosses in the medullary pyramids, not the cervical cord.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Differentiating serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome
weakSpotCategory: Serotonin Syndrome and Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
topic: Serotonin Syndrome and Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
memoryAnchor: Serotonin: Shaky and Spasming; NMS: Stiff and Slow.
commonTrap: Treating serotonin syndrome with dantrolene as if it were NMS.
stem: A 44-year-old woman taking sertraline for depression is prescribed linezolid for a skin infection. Within 12 hours she develops agitation, diarrhea, diaphoresis, and muscle twitching. Temperature is 39.4 C, heart rate is 134 bpm, and blood pressure is 168/98 mmHg. Examination shows dilated pupils, hyperreflexia, and inducible ankle clonus. Serum creatine kinase is 1,800 U/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose
Administer haloperidol for agitation
Administer dantrolene and bromocriptine
Discontinue serotonergic drugs and administer cyproheptadine with benzodiazepines

explanation: This presentation is serotonin syndrome from combining an SSRI with linezolid, a weak MAO inhibitor. Clinical features include autonomic instability, neuromuscular excitation with hyperreflexia and clonus, mydriasis, diarrhea, and altered mental status, with onset within hours. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome instead develops over days with lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, and normal pupils. Management is to stop all serotonergic agents, give benzodiazepines, supportive cooling and fluids, and cyproheptadine, a 5-HT2A antagonist, for moderate to severe cases. Because the mechanism is excess serotonergic stimulation, treatment removes the cause by stopping the serotonergic agents, and benzodiazepines with cooling help decrease muscle activity and the risk of rhabdomyolysis.
pearl: Serotonin syndrome: rapid onset, clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhea, mydriasis; NMS: slow onset, lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia.

optionExplanations.A: Increasing sertraline would raise serotonergic toxicity and worsen the syndrome.
optionExplanations.B: Haloperidol blocks dopamine and can worsen hyperthermia and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome in a patient with this presentation.
optionExplanations.C: Dantrolene and bromocriptine treat neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which has rigidity and hyporeflexia rather than clonus and mydriasis.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Stop the serotonergic drugs and give benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine for serotonin syndrome.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies and thymic abnormalities in myasthenia gravis
memoryAnchor: Myasthenia: weaker as the day goes on.
commonTrap: Confusing myasthenia gravis with Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
stem: A 31-year-old woman has drooping eyelids and double vision that worsen by evening and improve with rest. She has difficulty chewing and climbing stairs late in the day. Strength is normal in the morning. Edrophonium administration transiently improves ptosis. Chest CT shows an anterior mediastinal mass. Heart rate is 84 bpm, blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, serum potassium is 4.1 mEq/L, and forced vital capacity is 3.1 L. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of her symptoms?

options.text: Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
Antibodies against myelin proteins in peripheral nerves
Antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
Botulinum toxin blocking acetylcholine release

explanation: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease with IgG antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, causing fatigable weakness of ocular, bulbar, and proximal limb muscles. Thymic hyperplasia or thymoma is common, and the mediastinal mass here suggests a thymoma. Edrophonium or neostigmine, acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, temporarily improve strength by increasing acetylcholine in the cleft. Treatment includes pyridostigmine, immunosuppression, and thymectomy, and the respiratory function must be monitored because myasthenic crisis can cause respiratory failure. The diagnosis rests on a reduced number of functional receptors, because the antibodies cause receptor internalization and complement-mediated damage; this results in fatigable weakness, and a thymoma, when present, is removed surgically.
pearl: Myasthenia gravis: worsens with use, anti-AChR antibodies, thymoma, improves with edrophonium; Lambert-Eaton improves with use.

optionExplanations.A: Presynaptic calcium channel antibodies cause Lambert-Eaton syndrome, which improves with repeated use and is associated with small cell lung cancer.
optionExplanations.B: Antibodies against peripheral myelin cause Guillain-Barre syndrome, with ascending areflexic weakness rather than fatigable ocular weakness.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors cause fatigable weakness and are associated with thymoma.
optionExplanations.D: Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release and causes descending paralysis with dilated pupils and does not improve with edrophonium.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Bisphosphonate mechanism and esophageal precautions
memoryAnchor: Bisphosphonates bind bone and kill osteoclasts.
commonTrap: Confusing the actions of denosumab and teriparatide with alendronate.
stem: A 64-year-old postmenopausal woman has a T-score of -2.9 at the femoral neck after a wrist fracture. Her physician starts alendronate. Which of the following is the mechanism of this drug and an important counseling point?

options.text: Stimulates osteoblasts; inject daily
Blocks RANK ligand; take with milk
Induces osteoclast apoptosis; take upright with water to avoid esophagitis
Increases intestinal calcium absorption; take at bedtime

explanation: Bisphosphonates are pyrophosphate analogs that bind hydroxyapatite and inhibit osteoclast function by blocking farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase, inducing osteoclast apoptosis. They should be taken fasting with a full glass of water and the patient should remain upright for 30 minutes to avoid pill esophagitis. Rare adverse effects include osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fractures.
pearl: Bisphosphonates: take fasting with water and remain upright; risk of osteonecrosis of jaw and atypical fractures.

optionExplanations.A: Teriparatide stimulates osteoblasts when given intermittently by injection.
optionExplanations.B: Denosumab blocks RANK ligand and is given by injection.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Bisphosphonates induce osteoclast apoptosis and can cause esophagitis.
optionExplanations.D: Calcitriol or vitamin D increase intestinal calcium absorption and are not bisphosphonates.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals in pseudogout
memoryAnchor: Pseudogout: Positive, Pyrophosphate, Parallel blue.
commonTrap: Reversing the birefringence of urate and pyrophosphate crystals.
stem: A 78-year-old woman has acute swelling and pain in the right knee after hospitalization for pneumonia. Radiograph shows linear calcification of the articular cartilage. Joint aspiration shows rhomboid-shaped crystals. Which of the following findings on polarized light microscopy is expected?

options.text: Strongly negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals
No crystals but many gram-positive cocci
Cholesterol clefts
Weakly positively birefringent crystals

explanation: Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease) produces rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals and chondrocalcinosis. Acute attacks often follow illness or surgery. Treatment includes NSAIDs, colchicine, or intra-articular steroids. Gout shows needle-shaped negatively birefringent urate crystals.
pearl: Gout: negative birefringence, yellow when parallel; pseudogout: positive birefringence, blue when parallel.

optionExplanations.A: Needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals are urate crystals of gout.
optionExplanations.B: Gram-positive cocci would indicate septic arthritis, not crystalline arthritis.
optionExplanations.C: Cholesterol clefts are not a feature of pseudogout.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. CPPD crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Methotrexate as first-line DMARD in rheumatoid arthritis
memoryAnchor: RA starts with methotrexate and folate.
commonTrap: Using steroids as the sole long-term therapy.
stem: A 45-year-old woman has 3 months of symmetric swelling and morning stiffness lasting 90 minutes in the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints. Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial disease-modifying therapy?

options.text: Long-term prednisone alone
Methotrexate
Hydroxychloroquine as sole therapy for severe disease
Allopurinol

explanation: Methotrexate, a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor, is the first-line DMARD for rheumatoid arthritis and should be started early to prevent joint destruction. Folate supplementation reduces toxicity. TNF inhibitors are added if disease control is inadequate. Allopurinol treats gout.
pearl: RA: anti-CCP, rheumatoid factor, pannus; methotrexate first, then biologics such as TNF inhibitors.

optionExplanations.A: Chronic steroids alone are not disease modifying and cause toxicity.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Methotrexate is the anchor DMARD in RA.
optionExplanations.C: Hydroxychloroquine is reserved for mild disease or combination therapy.
optionExplanations.D: Allopurinol lowers uric acid and has no role in RA.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Heberden and Bouchard nodes in osteoarthritis
memoryAnchor: OA: wear and tear; RA: attack by antibodies.
commonTrap: Treating bony nodes as inflammatory arthritis.
stem: A 62-year-old woman has bony enlargements of the distal interphalangeal joints and knee pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest. Morning stiffness lasts 10 minutes. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is normal. Which of the following is the most likely underlying process?

options.text: Cartilage degeneration with osteophyte formation
Autoimmune synovial proliferation with pannus
Urate crystal deposition in the synovium
Bacterial invasion of the joint space

explanation: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative disease with progressive loss of articular cartilage, subchondral sclerosis, and osteophytes. Heberden nodes affect the distal interphalangeal joints and Bouchard nodes the proximal ones. Brief morning stiffness and a normal ESR help distinguish it from inflammatory arthritis.
pearl: OA: DIP (Heberden) and PIP (Bouchard); RA spares the DIP.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Cartilage degeneration with osteophytes defines OA.
optionExplanations.B: Pannus formation characterizes rheumatoid arthritis with prolonged stiffness.
optionExplanations.C: Urate crystal deposition causes gout with acute inflammation.
optionExplanations.D: Bacterial invasion causes septic arthritis with fever and an acutely hot joint.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Salmonella osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease
memoryAnchor: Sickle cell: Salmonella in the bone.
commonTrap: Excluding S. aureus or omitting Salmonella in sickle cell disease.
stem: A 9-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has fever and severe pain over the right tibia for 4 days. The area is warm and tender. Temperature is 39 C and ESR is elevated. MRI shows marrow edema and periosteal elevation. Which organism is most likely in addition to Staphylococcus aureus in this population?

options.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Salmonella species
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Pasteurella multocida

explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of osteomyelitis overall. Patients with sickle cell disease have functional asplenia and bone infarcts, which predispose to Salmonella osteomyelitis. Pseudomonas is seen after puncture wounds through shoes or in injection drug users. Salmonella species are therefore the additional organism to consider in sickle cell osteomyelitis.
pearl: Osteomyelitis: S. aureus overall; Salmonella with sickle cell; Pseudomonas with puncture or IV drug use.

optionExplanations.A: Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes vertebral osteomyelitis (Pott disease) with a more indolent course.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Salmonella is characteristic of osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease.
optionExplanations.C: Pseudomonas is associated with puncture wounds and intravenous drug use.
optionExplanations.D: Pasteurella multocida follows cat or dog bites.

subject: Anatomy
testedConcept: Supraspinatus function in shoulder abduction
memoryAnchor: Supraspinatus Starts abduction.
commonTrap: Choosing the deltoid, which abducts after the first 15 degrees.
stem: A 58-year-old painter has shoulder pain and difficulty initiating abduction of the right arm. When the examiner passively abducts the arm to 90 degrees, the patient cannot hold it there and it drops slowly. Which muscle is most likely torn?

options.text: Subscapularis
Teres minor
Supraspinatus
Infraspinatus

explanation: The supraspinatus initiates the first 15 degrees of abduction and is the most commonly injured rotator cuff muscle, with a positive drop-arm test. The infraspinatus and teres minor externally rotate, and the subscapularis internally rotates the arm.
pearl: Rotator cuff: SITS (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis); supraspinatus most injured.

optionExplanations.A: The subscapularis is an internal rotator.
optionExplanations.B: The teres minor is an external rotator.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The supraspinatus initiates abduction.
optionExplanations.D: The infraspinatus is an external rotator.

subject: Anatomy
testedConcept: Median nerve compression in carpal tunnel syndrome
memoryAnchor: Median nerve: Thumb, index, middle.
commonTrap: Confusing median and ulnar sensory territories.
stem: A 40-year-old woman who works as a typist has nocturnal tingling of the thumb, index, and middle fingers. Tapping over the volar wrist reproduces symptoms. Thenar muscle bulk is slightly reduced. Compression of which nerve is the most likely cause?

options.text: Musculocutaneous nerve
Radial nerve
Ulnar nerve
Median nerve

explanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome is compression of the median nerve under the flexor retinaculum. It causes numbness of the lateral three and a half fingers, thenar atrophy, and positive Tinel and Phalen signs. Risk factors include pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, and rheumatoid arthritis.
pearl: Carpal tunnel: median nerve; Tinel and Phalen signs; splinting and steroid injection, then release.

optionExplanations.A: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies forearm flexion muscles and lateral forearm sensation.
optionExplanations.B: The radial nerve supplies the dorsum of the hand and extensors.
optionExplanations.C: The ulnar nerve supplies the little finger and medial ring finger.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The median nerve supplies the thumb, index, and middle fingers and the thenar muscles.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis in obese adolescents
memoryAnchor: Ice cream cone slips off the cone.
commonTrap: Missing hip pathology because the pain is felt in the knee.
stem: A 13-year-old obese boy has a 2-month history of right knee and groin pain and a limp. Examination shows limited internal rotation of the right hip, and the leg externally rotates when the hip is flexed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Osgood-Schlatter disease
Legg-Calve-Perthes disease
Transient synovitis

explanation: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is a Salter-Harris type I fracture through the proximal femoral physis in obese adolescents, causing hip or referred knee pain and limited internal rotation. Frog-leg lateral radiographs show posterior and inferior slip of the epiphysis. Treatment is non-weight bearing and surgical pinning.
pearl: SCFE: obese adolescent, referred knee pain, externally rotated leg; pin surgically.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Obese adolescent with hip pain and limited internal rotation indicates SCFE.
optionExplanations.B: Osgood-Schlatter disease causes tibial tubercle pain from traction apophysitis.
optionExplanations.C: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease affects younger children (4 to 8 years) with avascular necrosis.
optionExplanations.D: Transient synovitis follows a viral illness in younger children with resolving symptoms.

subject: Genetics
testedConcept: Type I collagen defect in osteogenesis imperfecta
memoryAnchor: Type ONE: BONE.
commonTrap: Concluding child abuse without considering osteogenesis imperfecta.
stem: A 3-year-old boy has had four long bone fractures after minor falls. He has blue sclerae, hearing loss, and poorly formed teeth. His parents have no history of abuse. Which of the following proteins is defective?

options.text: Type III collagen
Type I collagen
Type II collagen
Fibrillin-1

explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta results from defects in type I collagen (COL1A1 and COL1A2), usually autosomal dominant. Features include brittle bones, blue sclerae from thin collagen over the choroid, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and hearing loss from ossicle abnormalities. Multiple fractures with normal development and family history help distinguish it from child abuse.
pearl: Type I collagen = bone: osteogenesis imperfecta. Blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, hearing loss.

optionExplanations.A: Type III collagen defects cause vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Type I collagen is the structural protein of bone, sclera, and dentin.
optionExplanations.C: Type II collagen is in cartilage and the vitreous.
optionExplanations.D: Fibrillin-1 defects cause Marfan syndrome.

subject: Genetics
testedConcept: Frameshift dystrophin mutation in Duchenne muscular dystrophy
memoryAnchor: Duchenne: Deleted, frameshift, Dead dystrophin.
commonTrap: Reversing the genetic mechanisms of Duchenne and Becker.
stem: A 5-year-old boy has difficulty climbing stairs and uses his hands to push up on his thighs when rising from the floor. His calves appear enlarged. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated. Which of the following best describes the underlying genetic abnormality?

options.text: In-frame deletion producing a truncated but partly functional dystrophin
Trinucleotide repeat expansion in a myotonin gene
Mutation in the acid alpha-glucosidase gene
Frameshift mutation causing absent dystrophin

explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is X-linked recessive and results from a frameshift (out-of-frame) deletion in the dystrophin gene, producing absent dystrophin and progressive muscle necrosis, Gowers sign, pseudohypertrophy of calves, and cardiomyopathy. In-frame mutations cause the milder Becker form.
pearl: Duchenne: frameshift, X-linked, Gowers sign, high CK; Becker: in-frame, milder.

optionExplanations.A: An in-frame deletion leads to Becker muscular dystrophy.
optionExplanations.B: A trinucleotide repeat in myotonin kinase causes myotonic dystrophy.
optionExplanations.C: Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency causes Pompe disease with cardiomegaly in infancy.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A frameshift leads to no functional dystrophin in Duchenne.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation in Paget disease of bone
memoryAnchor: Paget: Plenty of ALP, normal calcium.
commonTrap: Expecting abnormal calcium and phosphate in Paget disease.
stem: A 70-year-old man has increasing hat size, bone pain, and hearing loss. Radiograph of the pelvis shows thickened, sclerotic cortices. Serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly elevated, whereas calcium and phosphate are normal. Which of the following complications is he at increased risk for?

options.text: Osteosarcoma
Hypercalcemia of malignancy
Osteoid osteoma
Multiple myeloma

explanation: Paget disease of bone involves excessive osteoclastic resorption followed by disorganized osteoblastic formation (mosaic pattern), producing enlarged, weak bones, bone pain, high-output heart failure, and cranial nerve compression with hearing loss. Alkaline phosphatase is high with normal calcium and phosphate. Bisphosphonates are first-line, and secondary osteosarcoma is a feared complication.
pearl: Paget: high ALP, normal Ca and phosphate, mosaic bone, high-output heart failure, osteosarcoma risk.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Pagetic bone can transform into osteosarcoma.
optionExplanations.B: Hypercalcemia of malignancy is not typical in Paget disease.
optionExplanations.C: Osteoid osteoma is a benign tumor of young adults.
optionExplanations.D: Myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm not related to Paget disease.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Arthrocentesis in acute monoarticular arthritis in a sexually active young adult
memoryAnchor: Diplococci in the joint: ceftriaxone.
commonTrap: Missing the gonococcal cause in a young sexually active adult.
stem: A 22-year-old sexually active man has 2 days of fever, a swollen, warm, painful left knee, and a few pustules on the hands. Temperature is 38.5 C. Gram stain of joint fluid shows gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following organism-targeted treatments is most appropriate?

options.text: Intra-articular corticosteroids
Vancomycin alone
Ceftriaxone
Oral doxycycline alone

explanation: Disseminated gonococcal infection causes migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, dermatitis, or purulent arthritis in sexually active adults. Gram-negative diplococci in the joint indicate Neisseria gonorrhoeae, treated with ceftriaxone with joint drainage. Doxycycline or azithromycin is added for possible chlamydial coinfection.
pearl: Septic arthritis: S. aureus is most common overall; N. gonorrhoeae in sexually active young adults.

optionExplanations.A: Steroids are contraindicated in an infected joint.
optionExplanations.B: Vancomycin covers gram-positive organisms and would not treat gram-negative diplococci.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Ceftriaxone treats gonococcal septic arthritis.
optionExplanations.D: Doxycycline alone is not adequate therapy for gonococcal arthritis.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: HLA-B27 and sacroiliitis in ankylosing spondylitis
memoryAnchor: B27: bamboo spine and uveitis.
commonTrap: Associating spondyloarthropathy with rheumatoid factor.
stem: A 24-year-old man has 6 months of low back pain and stiffness that is worse in the morning and improves with exercise. Chest expansion is reduced. Radiographs show sacroiliac joint erosions. He has had an episode of anterior uveitis. Which of the following is most likely associated with his condition?

options.text: Anti-CCP antibodies
HLA-B27
HLA-DR4
HLA-DR3

explanation: Ankylosing spondylitis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy associated with HLA-B27, causing sacroiliitis, spinal fusion (bamboo spine), enthesitis, anterior uveitis, aortic regurgitation, and reduced chest expansion. NSAIDs and TNF inhibitors are treatments.
pearl: Seronegative spondyloarthropathies (PAIR): psoriatic, ankylosing, IBD-associated, reactive; all HLA-B27.

optionExplanations.A: Anti-CCP is specific for rheumatoid arthritis.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. HLA-B27 is the characteristic association.
optionExplanations.C: HLA-DR4 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis.
optionExplanations.D: HLA-DR3 is associated with several autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes and SLE.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: EWS-FLI1 translocation and onion-skin periosteal reaction in Ewing sarcoma
memoryAnchor: Ewing: Eleven-twenty-two, Onion skin.
commonTrap: Mistaking Ewing sarcoma for osteomyelitis because of fever and elevated ESR.
stem: A 12-year-old boy has 2 months of left thigh pain, low-grade fever, and a tender swelling over the mid-femur. Temperature is 38.1 C, hemoglobin is 11.4 g/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 62 mm/h. Radiograph shows a lytic lesion in the diaphysis with layered lamellated periosteal reaction. Biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells with glycogen-rich cytoplasm. Which of the following genetic abnormalities is most likely present?

options.text: t(11;22) producing the EWS-FLI1 fusion
Loss of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene
t(12;16) producing a FUS-DDIT3 fusion
t(8;14) involving MYC

explanation: Ewing sarcoma is a small round blue cell tumor of children with t(11;22) producing the EWS-FLI1 transcription factor fusion. It arises in the diaphysis of long bones, with an onion-skin periosteal reaction, systemic symptoms such as fever and elevated ESR that mimic osteomyelitis, and glycogen-positive (PAS) cells. Treatment includes chemotherapy, with surgery or radiation, because the tumor is aggressive and metastasizes to lung and bone, and prognosis depends on stage at diagnosis. Because the fusion transcription factor drives proliferation, cytogenetic confirmation supports the diagnosis, and treatment combines chemotherapy with local control, as micrometastases result in a high risk of relapse if systemic therapy is omitted.
pearl: Ewing: t(11;22), diaphysis, onion skin, small round blue cells; osteosarcoma: metaphysis, sunburst, Codman triangle.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. t(11;22) EWS-FLI1 is the defining abnormality of Ewing sarcoma.
optionExplanations.B: RB1 loss is associated with retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma, which typically involves the metaphysis with a sunburst pattern rather than the diaphysis.
optionExplanations.C: t(12;16) occurs in myxoid liposarcoma, a soft tissue tumor, and does not cause a lytic diaphyseal bone lesion.
optionExplanations.D: t(8;14) involves MYC and occurs in Burkitt lymphoma, which is a B-cell tumor and not a primary bone sarcoma with onion-skin reaction.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Urgent glucocorticoids for suspected giant cell arteritis to prevent vision loss
weakSpotCategory: Polymyalgia Rheumatica with Giant Cell Arteritis
topic: Polymyalgia Rheumatica with Giant Cell Arteritis
memoryAnchor: Suspect GCA: steroids first, biopsy second.
commonTrap: Waiting for biopsy results before starting treatment.
stem: A 72-year-old woman has 3 weeks of bilateral shoulder and hip stiffness that is worse in the morning, along with a new unilateral temporal headache, scalp tenderness, and jaw pain with chewing. Last night she had brief monocular vision loss. Temperature is 37.9 C, heart rate is 84 bpm, blood pressure is 134/80 mmHg, hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL, ESR is 98 mm/h, and C-reactive protein is elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Start low-dose aspirin and observe
Prescribe NSAIDs and schedule follow-up in 2 weeks
Start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately and arrange temporal artery biopsy
Delay treatment until the temporal artery biopsy is completed

explanation: This patient has polymyalgia rheumatica overlapping with giant cell arteritis, as shown by jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and amaurosis fugax with markedly elevated ESR. Giant cell arteritis is an ophthalmologic emergency because ischemic optic neuropathy can cause permanent blindness, and the risk of irreversible vision loss increases with delay. Treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids must begin immediately upon suspicion, and temporal artery biopsy can still be positive for days to weeks after steroids because skip lesions require an adequate specimen. Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with giant cells, and the response to steroids is rapid.
pearl: GCA: age over 50, headache, jaw claudication, high ESR; treat immediately with steroids; biopsy afterward.

optionExplanations.A: Aspirin alone does not treat the underlying arteritis and does not prevent ischemic optic neuropathy adequately.
optionExplanations.B: NSAIDs do not control giant cell arteritis, and a 2-week delay exposes her to the risk of permanent blindness.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Start glucocorticoids immediately to prevent blindness and do the biopsy afterward.
optionExplanations.D: Delaying treatment for biopsy risks permanent vision loss, whereas biopsy yield remains acceptable after starting steroids.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Auspitz sign and Koebner phenomenon in plaque psoriasis
memoryAnchor: Silver scale, bleeding dots.
commonTrap: Confusing psoriasis with eczema.
stem: A 32-year-old man has well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales on the elbows and knees, and pitting of the fingernails. Removing a scale causes pinpoint bleeding. New plaques appear at sites of scratching. Which of the following histologic findings is most likely?

options.text: Subepidermal blister with eosinophils
Intraepidermal acantholysis with a tombstone appearance
Spongiosis with perivascular lymphocytes only
Epidermal hyperplasia with parakeratosis and neutrophils in the stratum corneum

explanation: Psoriasis shows marked epidermal hyperplasia (acanthosis), parakeratosis, loss of the granular layer, and neutrophil collections (Munro microabscesses) in the stratum corneum. The Auspitz sign is bleeding on removal of scale and the Koebner phenomenon is lesion formation at sites of trauma. Associated findings include nail pitting and psoriatic arthritis.
pearl: Psoriasis: Auspitz sign, Koebner phenomenon, nail pitting, psoriatic arthritis; avoid beta blockers and lithium.

optionExplanations.A: Subepidermal blisters with eosinophils are characteristic of bullous pemphigoid.
optionExplanations.B: Acantholysis with a tombstone pattern describes pemphigus vulgaris.
optionExplanations.C: Spongiosis is typical of eczematous dermatitis.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Parakeratosis and Munro microabscesses define psoriasis.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Anti-desmoglein antibodies in pemphigus vulgaris
memoryAnchor: Pemphigus Pops, pemphigoid Persists.
commonTrap: Confusing the location and immunofluorescence patterns of pemphigus and pemphigoid.
stem: A 48-year-old woman has painful oral erosions and flaccid blisters on the trunk that rupture easily. Gentle lateral pressure on normal-appearing skin causes the epidermis to separate. Immunofluorescence shows a net-like pattern of IgG around keratinocytes. Which of the following is the target antigen?

options.text: Transglutaminase
Type VII collagen
Desmoglein 3
BP180 hemidesmosomal protein

explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris is a type II hypersensitivity with IgG against desmoglein 3 (and sometimes desmoglein 1), causing acantholysis within the epidermis. Flaccid blisters, mucosal involvement, and a positive Nikolsky sign are typical. Bullous pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomes with tense blisters and a linear IgG pattern.
pearl: Pemphigus: intraepidermal, flaccid, Nikolsky positive, net-like IgG; pemphigoid: subepidermal, tense, linear IgG.

optionExplanations.A: Transglutaminase is targeted in dermatitis herpetiformis (celiac disease).
optionExplanations.B: Type VII collagen is targeted in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Desmoglein 3 antibodies cause intraepidermal blistering.
optionExplanations.D: BP180 is targeted in bullous pemphigoid.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Pearly nodule with rolled borders of basal cell carcinoma
memoryAnchor: BCC: Basal, Beautiful pearly, Best prognosis.
commonTrap: Confusing BCC with SCC in sun-exposed ulcerated lesions.
stem: A 66-year-old farmer has a slowly enlarging 8-mm pearly papule with rolled borders and telangiectasias on the nose. A central ulcer has persisted for 6 months. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Basal cell carcinoma
Melanoma
Squamous cell carcinoma
Seborrheic keratosis

explanation: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer. It presents as a pearly papule with telangiectasias on sun-exposed skin, especially the face. Histology shows basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artifact. It rarely metastasizes, and Mohs surgery is preferred for facial lesions.
pearl: BCC: palisading nuclei, rarely metastasizes; SCC: keratin pearls, can metastasize.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A pearly nodule with rolled borders and telangiectasias is classic for BCC.
optionExplanations.B: Melanoma has asymmetric pigmentation and irregular borders.
optionExplanations.C: Squamous cell carcinoma is often scaly or crusted and arises from actinic keratosis.
optionExplanations.D: Seborrheic keratosis is a stuck-on waxy plaque, not ulcerated.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Breslow depth as the strongest prognostic factor in melanoma
memoryAnchor: Breslow = Depth.
commonTrap: Using horizontal size rather than depth for prognosis.
stem: A 52-year-old man has a pigmented lesion on the back that has changed in size and color, with asymmetry and irregular borders. Excisional biopsy confirms melanoma. Which of the following histologic features is the most important predictor of prognosis?

options.text: Patient sex
Presence of lymphocytes in the dermis
Lesion diameter alone
Tumor thickness (Breslow depth)

explanation: Breslow thickness, the vertical depth of invasion in millimeters, is the strongest prognostic factor in localized melanoma and guides excision margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy. Ulceration and mitotic rate also affect staging. BRAF V600E mutations are targeted by vemurafenib.
pearl: Melanoma: ABCDE; Breslow thickness determines margins; BRAF V600E treated with vemurafenib or dabrafenib.

optionExplanations.A: Sex has a minor effect and is not the main determinant.
optionExplanations.B: Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes have a minor prognostic role.
optionExplanations.C: Diameter is part of the ABCDE criteria but is not the main prognostic marker.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Breslow depth is the best predictor of metastasis and survival.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: Honey-colored crusts of nonbullous impetigo
memoryAnchor: Honey crusts: Staph and Strep.
commonTrap: Attributing rheumatic fever to skin infection.
stem: A 5-year-old boy has honey-colored crusted lesions around the nose and mouth that spread to his hands over 3 days. He is afebrile. Which of the following organisms most commonly causes this condition?

options.text: Herpes simplex virus
Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes
Candida albicans
Pseudomonas aeruginosa

explanation: Nonbullous impetigo, the most common form, is caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes and shows honey-colored crusts on the face and extremities. Topical mupirocin is used for limited disease. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, but not rheumatic fever, can follow streptococcal skin infection.
pearl: Streptococcal skin infection can cause glomerulonephritis but not rheumatic fever.

optionExplanations.A: HSV causes grouped vesicles on an erythematous base.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. S. aureus and S. pyogenes cause honey-crusted impetigo.
optionExplanations.C: Candida causes erythematous patches with satellite lesions.
optionExplanations.D: Pseudomonas causes hot-tub folliculitis and swimmer ear.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Autoimmune melanocyte destruction in vitiligo
memoryAnchor: Vitiligo kills the pigment cells.
commonTrap: Confusing vitiligo with albinism.
stem: A 25-year-old woman has well-demarcated depigmented patches on the hands and around the eyes that have enlarged over 2 years. She has hypothyroidism. A Wood lamp examination shows accentuation of the patches. Which of the following mechanisms best explains her skin findings?

options.text: Reduced number of keratinocytes
Fungal invasion of the stratum corneum
Decreased tyrosinase activity from a genetic mutation
Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes

explanation: Vitiligo results from autoimmune destruction of melanocytes, causing depigmented macules and patches. It is associated with other autoimmune diseases such as autoimmune thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes. Albinism is a tyrosinase defect with normal melanocyte numbers and diffuse hypopigmentation.
pearl: Vitiligo: absent melanocytes; albinism: normal number but no melanin synthesis.

optionExplanations.A: Keratinocyte number is not decreased in vitiligo.
optionExplanations.B: Tinea versicolor causes scaly hypopigmentation from fungal infection and does not destroy melanocytes.
