optionExplanations.C: Decreased tyrosinase activity causes oculocutaneous albinism with generalized depigmentation.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Melanocytes are destroyed in vitiligo.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Stevens-Johnson syndrome after sulfonamide exposure
memoryAnchor: Stop the drug first.
commonTrap: Treating a severe cutaneous reaction as a simple rash.
stem: A 34-year-old woman develops fever, mucosal erosions, and painful targetoid skin lesions with epidermal detachment 10 days after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Less than 10 percent of body surface area is involved. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the drug with topical steroids
Discontinue the offending drug and provide supportive care
Treat with ultraviolet light therapy
Start oral antifungals

explanation: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are severe delayed drug reactions with keratinocyte apoptosis, causing mucocutaneous erosions and epidermal detachment. Common triggers include sulfonamides, allopurinol, anticonvulsants, and nevirapine. Management is immediate drug withdrawal and supportive burn-unit care.
pearl: SJS less than 10% BSA; TEN more than 30%; common culprits: sulfa drugs, allopurinol, antiepileptics.

optionExplanations.A: Continuing the drug would worsen the reaction.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Stop the offending drug and give supportive care.
optionExplanations.C: Phototherapy can worsen skin injury.
optionExplanations.D: Antifungals are not indicated.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Cutibacterium acnes and follicular plugging in acne vulgaris
memoryAnchor: Plug, grease, bug, burn.
commonTrap: Blaming S. aureus or fungal overgrowth.
stem: A 16-year-old boy has facial comedones, inflammatory papules, and pustules. Which of the following factors is most directly involved in the inflammatory lesions?

options.text: Malassezia furfur overgrowth
Staphylococcus aureus toxin production
Cutibacterium acnes colonization of obstructed follicles
Sarcoptes scabiei infestation

explanation: Acne vulgaris involves follicular hyperkeratinization, increased sebum production under androgen influence, and colonization of the plugged follicle by Cutibacterium acnes, which triggers inflammation. Topical retinoids address plugging and benzoyl peroxide reduces bacteria, while isotretinoin treats severe disease.
pearl: Acne: retinoids for comedones, benzoyl peroxide and antibiotics for inflammatory lesions, isotretinoin for severe disease.

optionExplanations.A: Malassezia causes tinea versicolor and seborrheic dermatitis.
optionExplanations.B: S. aureus is not the primary agent in acne.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. C. acnes in obstructed follicles drives the inflammatory phase.
optionExplanations.D: Sarcoptes scabiei causes scabies with burrows and intense pruritus.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Leser-Trelat sign and sudden appearance of seborrheic keratoses
memoryAnchor: Sudden crop of keratoses: look for cancer.
commonTrap: Dismissing seborrheic keratoses as always benign.
stem: A 70-year-old man develops dozens of waxy, stuck-on brown plaques on his trunk over 2 months. He has also lost 7 kg unintentionally. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Evaluate for an underlying gastrointestinal malignancy
Reassure and provide no further evaluation
Start topical antifungal therapy
Refer for cryotherapy only

explanation: Seborrheic keratoses are common benign lesions of older adults. A sudden eruption of many lesions with weight loss is the Leser-Trelat sign, a paraneoplastic phenomenon associated with gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma, so malignancy screening is required. Acanthosis nigricans is another paraneoplastic skin sign of gastric cancer.
pearl: Leser-Trelat: sudden multiple seborrheic keratoses with GI adenocarcinoma.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Sudden eruption with weight loss suggests an underlying malignancy.
optionExplanations.B: Reassurance is appropriate for isolated lesions but not for the Leser-Trelat sign.
optionExplanations.C: Antifungal therapy is not indicated for stuck-on plaques.
optionExplanations.D: Cryotherapy treats individual lesions but does not address possible cancer.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: KOH preparation findings in dermatophyte infection
memoryAnchor: Ringworm: ring of hyphae.
commonTrap: Confusing the KOH appearance of tinea versicolor with that of dermatophytes.
stem: A 14-year-old wrestler has an annular scaly erythematous plaque with central clearing and a raised border on the shoulder. Which of the following is expected on potassium hydroxide preparation of skin scrapings?

options.text: Gram-positive cocci in clusters
Budding yeast with pseudohyphae
Spaghetti and meatballs pattern
Septate hyphae

explanation: Tinea corporis is caused by dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) that infect keratinized tissue, producing annular plaques with central clearing. KOH preparation shows branching septate hyphae. Tinea versicolor (Malassezia) shows spaghetti and meatballs, and Candida shows budding yeast with pseudohyphae.
pearl: Dermatophytes: KOH shows hyphae; treat with topical terbinafine, or oral for nails and scalp.

optionExplanations.A: Gram-positive cocci would suggest bacterial infection.
optionExplanations.B: Budding yeast with pseudohyphae describes Candida.
optionExplanations.C: Spaghetti and meatballs describes Malassezia furfur in tinea versicolor.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Dermatophytes appear as septate hyphae on KOH.

subject: Immunology
testedConcept: Atopic triad and filaggrin mutations in atopic dermatitis
memoryAnchor: Atopy: leaky skin, Th2, IgE.
commonTrap: Treating atopic dermatitis as a contact reaction.
stem: A 3-year-old girl has a pruritic eczematous rash on the flexural surfaces of the elbows and knees. Her father has asthma and her mother has allergic rhinitis. Serum IgE is elevated. Which of the following is the most likely underlying abnormality?

options.text: Type IV hypersensitivity to nickel
Autoantibodies against desmoglein
Skin barrier dysfunction with filaggrin loss-of-function mutations
Deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor

explanation: Atopic dermatitis is associated with filaggrin mutations that impair the skin barrier, together with a Th2-skewed immune response producing IgE. It is part of the atopic triad with asthma and allergic rhinitis. Treatment includes emollients and topical corticosteroids.
pearl: Atopic triad: eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis; flexural in children, face and extensor in infants.

optionExplanations.A: Nickel allergy causes allergic contact dermatitis and does not explain the flexural pattern.
optionExplanations.B: Desmoglein antibodies cause pemphigus.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Barrier dysfunction and filaggrin mutations are central.
optionExplanations.D: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Permethrin treatment of scabies and household contacts
memoryAnchor: Scabies itches at night; treat everyone.
commonTrap: Treating only the symptomatic patient.
stem: A 9-year-old boy has intense nocturnal itching with linear burrows between the fingers and papules on the wrists. Several family members are also itching. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral acyclovir
Topical permethrin for the patient and household contacts
Topical mupirocin
Oral fluconazole

explanation: Scabies is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei mites that burrow into the stratum corneum, producing intense nocturnal pruritus and linear burrows. Treatment is topical permethrin applied to the entire body, with simultaneous treatment of household contacts and washing of bedding. Oral ivermectin is an alternative.
pearl: Scabies: permethrin or ivermectin; treat all close contacts simultaneously.

optionExplanations.A: Acyclovir treats herpesvirus infections.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Permethrin kills the mite, and contacts are treated simultaneously.
optionExplanations.C: Mupirocin treats localized bacterial skin infections.
optionExplanations.D: Fluconazole treats fungal infections.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Subepidermal blistering with hemidesmosome antibodies in bullous pemphigoid
memoryAnchor: Hemidesmosome, hemisphere below: subepidermal.
commonTrap: Confusing desmosomes with hemidesmosomes.
stem: A 78-year-old man has tense, pruritic bullae on the flexor surfaces and trunk for 3 weeks. The mouth is spared and Nikolsky sign is negative. Biopsy shows a subepidermal blister with eosinophils, and direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane. Which of the following is the target of the autoantibodies?

options.text: Hemidesmosomes
Tight junctions
Desmosomes
Gap junctions

explanation: Bullous pemphigoid involves IgG against BP180 and BP230 in hemidesmosomes, causing subepidermal blisters with tense bullae, eosinophils, and linear basement membrane deposits. Mucosal involvement is uncommon. Pemphigus targets desmosomes and causes intraepidermal flaccid blisters with positive Nikolsky sign.
pearl: Pemphigoid: subepidermal, tense bullae, mouth usually spared, linear IgG at the basement membrane.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomal proteins.
optionExplanations.B: Tight junctions are not the target.
optionExplanations.C: Desmosomes are the target in pemphigus.
optionExplanations.D: Gap junctions are not targeted.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Actinic keratosis as a precursor of squamous cell carcinoma
weakSpotCategory: Actinic Keratosis and Squamous Cell Carcinoma
topic: Actinic Keratosis and Squamous Cell Carcinoma
memoryAnchor: Rough sun-damaged patch: could become SCC.
commonTrap: Calling in situ disease invasive carcinoma.
stem: A 71-year-old fair-skinned man has a 1-cm rough, scaly erythematous patch on the scalp that has become thickened and tender over 3 months. He has had many years of sun exposure. Biopsy shows atypical keratinocytes extending through the full thickness of the epidermis without dermal invasion. Which of the following is the best description of this lesion?

options.text: Invasive melanoma
Squamous cell carcinoma in situ
Benign seborrheic keratosis
Basal cell carcinoma

explanation: Actinic keratosis is a precursor lesion caused by UV-induced p53 mutations. Full-thickness epidermal atypia without dermal invasion defines squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen disease). Invasive SCC shows keratin pearls and dermal invasion and can metastasize. Treatment of in situ disease is excision, curettage, or topical therapy.
pearl: UV light causes pyrimidine dimers and p53 mutations; actinic keratosis can progress to SCC.

optionExplanations.A: Melanoma arises from melanocytes, not keratinocytes.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Full-thickness atypia without invasion is SCC in situ.
optionExplanations.C: Seborrheic keratosis is benign and has horn cysts.
optionExplanations.D: Basal cell carcinoma shows basaloid nests with palisading.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Management priorities in toxic epidermal necrolysis
memoryAnchor: Skin burns without a fire: treat like a burn.
commonTrap: Treating with steroids and continuing the culprit drug.
stem: A 43-year-old man with gout starts allopurinol and 3 weeks later develops fever, painful mucosal erosions of the mouth and eyes, and widespread skin detachment involving 40% of his body surface area. Blood pressure is 92/58 mmHg, heart rate is 124 bpm, serum creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL, and serum bicarbonate is 17 mEq/L. Nikolsky sign is positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop allopurinol and transfer to a burn unit for fluid resuscitation and wound care
Start oral antifungal therapy for the erosions
Treat with oral prednisone and continue allopurinol
Apply topical antibiotics only and discharge

explanation: Toxic epidermal necrolysis involves keratinocyte apoptosis mediated by cytotoxic T cells, with more than 30% body surface area detachment, positive Nikolsky sign, and mucosal involvement. Allopurinol, sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, and nevirapine are common causes, and HLA-B*58:01 increases the risk with allopurinol. The mechanism of fluid loss leads to hypovolemia, renal injury, and sepsis risk, so the treatment is immediate drug withdrawal and supportive care in a burn or intensive care unit, with fluid resuscitation, wound care, ophthalmology consultation, and consideration of cyclosporine or IVIG.
pearl: SJS/TEN: stop the culprit, supportive care in a burn unit; HLA-B*58:01 and allopurinol; HLA-B*15:02 and carbamazepine.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Withdraw the causative drug and give burn-unit supportive care, because mortality increases with delay.
optionExplanations.B: Antifungal therapy treats infection and does not address an immune-mediated drug reaction.
optionExplanations.C: Continuing allopurinol would increase injury and systemic steroids are not proven to decrease mortality, whereas stopping the trigger is essential.
optionExplanations.D: Topical antibiotics and discharge ignore the risk of hypovolemia, sepsis, and organ failure, and the patient requires intensive monitoring.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Dynamic outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
memoryAnchor: HCM: less blood, more obstruction.
commonTrap: Applying aortic stenosis maneuver rules to HCM.
stem: A 19-year-old basketball player collapses during practice. Examination shows a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border that increases when he stands up quickly or performs the Valsalva maneuver. His father died suddenly at age 40. Which of the following maneuvers would decrease the intensity of the murmur?

options.text: Standing from a squat
Valsalva strain phase
Squatting
Amyl nitrite inhalation

explanation: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, usually autosomal dominant from sarcomere gene mutations (beta-myosin heavy chain), causes dynamic left ventricular outflow obstruction. Maneuvers that decrease preload or afterload (standing, Valsalva, amyl nitrite) intensify the murmur, while squatting increases venous return and afterload and decreases the murmur. Beta blockers are first-line treatment and competitive sports are restricted.
pearl: HCM murmur: louder with standing and Valsalva; softer with squatting and handgrip. Leading cause of sudden death in young athletes.

optionExplanations.A: Standing decreases venous return and increases the murmur.
optionExplanations.B: The Valsalva strain phase decreases preload and increases the murmur.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Squatting increases preload and afterload, which decreases the murmur of HCM.
optionExplanations.D: Amyl nitrite decreases afterload and increases the murmur.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Opening snap and left atrial enlargement in rheumatic mitral stenosis
memoryAnchor: Mitral stenosis: big atrium, small ventricle.
commonTrap: Expecting left ventricular enlargement in pure mitral stenosis.
stem: A 42-year-old woman who immigrated from a region with limited health care has dyspnea on exertion and palpitations. Examination shows an irregularly irregular pulse, an opening snap, and a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her arrhythmia?

options.text: Aortic root dilation
Right ventricular infarction
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left atrial enlargement

explanation: Mitral stenosis, most often from rheumatic heart disease, obstructs left atrial emptying and increases left atrial pressure, causing left atrial enlargement and atrial fibrillation. Findings include an opening snap and a diastolic rumble, and the shorter A2-to-opening-snap interval indicates more severe disease. Anticoagulation reduces thromboembolic risk.
pearl: Mitral stenosis: opening snap, diastolic rumble, AF, left atrial thrombus, dysphagia from enlarged atrium.

optionExplanations.A: Aortic root dilation is seen in Marfan syndrome or syphilis.
optionExplanations.B: Right ventricular infarction is unrelated.
optionExplanations.C: Left ventricular hypertrophy is not the main change in isolated mitral stenosis.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Left atrial enlargement predisposes to atrial fibrillation.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: Viridans streptococci endocarditis after dental procedures on damaged valves
memoryAnchor: Dental work plus damaged valve equals viridans.
commonTrap: Choosing S. pneumoniae because it is also alpha-hemolytic.
stem: A 38-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic mitral valve disease has 3 weeks of low-grade fever and fatigue after a dental extraction. Examination shows a new regurgitant murmur, splinter hemorrhages, and Osler nodes. Blood cultures grow alpha-hemolytic streptococci that are optochin resistant. Which organism is the most likely cause?

options.text: Streptococcus viridans group
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Staphylococcus aureus
Enterococcus faecalis

explanation: Subacute endocarditis on previously damaged valves after dental procedures is most commonly caused by viridans group streptococci from the oral flora. S. aureus instead causes acute endocarditis on normal valves, often in injection drug users.
pearl: Viridans: subacute, damaged valves, dental; S. aureus: acute, IV drug use, tricuspid; Enterococcus: GU/GI procedures.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Viridans streptococci cause subacute endocarditis on damaged valves.
optionExplanations.B: S. pneumoniae is bile soluble and causes pneumonia and meningitis rather than subacute endocarditis.
optionExplanations.C: S. aureus causes acute, aggressive endocarditis and is catalase positive.
optionExplanations.D: Enterococcus is associated with gastrointestinal or urinary procedures.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression in acute pericarditis
memoryAnchor: Pericarditis: lean forward, NSAID and colchicine.
commonTrap: Treating as STEMI with reperfusion therapy.
stem: A 27-year-old man has sharp pleuritic chest pain that improves when leaning forward, 1 week after a viral illness. A pericardial friction rub is heard. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?

options.text: Immediate cardiac catheterization
Intravenous heparin infusion
Ibuprofen and colchicine
Intravenous alteplase

explanation: Acute pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, commonly viral. Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression, a friction rub, and positional chest pain are characteristic. First-line treatment is an NSAID such as ibuprofen plus colchicine, which decreases recurrence. Corticosteroids are avoided as first-line therapy.
pearl: Pericarditis: pleuritic pain, friction rub, diffuse ST elevation and PR depression; NSAIDs plus colchicine.

optionExplanations.A: Catheterization is for ST-elevation myocardial infarction with regional changes.
optionExplanations.B: Heparin would increase the risk of hemorrhagic effusion.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. NSAID plus colchicine treats pericarditis and reduces recurrence.
optionExplanations.D: Thrombolysis is contraindicated and risks hemopericardium.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Pulsus paradoxus and Beck triad in cardiac tamponade
memoryAnchor: Tamponade: the heart is squeezed, so inspiration steals from the left.
commonTrap: Confusing pulsus paradoxus with Kussmaul sign.
stem: A 55-year-old man with lung cancer develops dyspnea and lightheadedness. Blood pressure is 88/62 mmHg and heart sounds are distant. Jugular veins are distended. Systolic blood pressure falls by 18 mmHg during inspiration. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of the pulse finding?

options.text: Inspiratory decrease in intrathoracic pressure that raises left ventricular preload
Inspiratory increase in right ventricular filling that compresses the left ventricle
Aortic regurgitation with a wide pulse pressure
Constrictive pericarditis with Kussmaul sign

explanation: In cardiac tamponade, fluid in the fixed pericardial space limits total cardiac volume. During inspiration, increased venous return expands the right ventricle and bows the interventricular septum into the left ventricle, decreasing left ventricular filling and stroke volume. This produces pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory drop in systolic pressure greater than 10 mmHg), Beck triad, and electrical alternans. Treatment is pericardiocentesis.
pearl: Tamponade: Beck triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds), pulsus paradoxus, electrical alternans.

optionExplanations.A: Inspiration decreases left ventricular preload in tamponade, not increases it.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Competition for limited space reduces left ventricular filling during inspiration.
optionExplanations.C: Aortic regurgitation causes a wide pulse pressure, not pulsus paradoxus.
optionExplanations.D: Kussmaul sign is paradoxical JVP rise with inspiration and occurs in constrictive disease; the stem describes pulsus paradoxus.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Digoxin toxicity with hypokalemia and antidote
memoryAnchor: Low K, high toxicity.
commonTrap: Giving calcium or cardioverting a patient with digoxin toxicity.
stem: A 76-year-old woman with heart failure and atrial fibrillation taking digoxin and furosemide has nausea, blurred yellow vision, and palpitations. Serum potassium is 3.0 mEq/L and ECG shows frequent premature ventricular beats and atrial tachycardia with block. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Atropine and electrical cardioversion
Intravenous calcium gluconate
Hemodialysis
Digoxin immune Fab and potassium repletion

explanation: Digoxin inhibits the Na/K-ATPase, increasing intracellular calcium and vagal tone. Toxicity causes nausea, visual changes with yellow halos, and arrhythmias, and it is worsened by hypokalemia (digoxin competes with potassium at the pump). Treatment includes digoxin immune Fab for life-threatening arrhythmias and correction of potassium and magnesium.
pearl: Digoxin: hypokalemia, renal failure, quinidine, and verapamil increase toxicity; antidote is Fab fragments.

optionExplanations.A: Cardioversion is hazardous in digoxin toxicity and can cause refractory ventricular arrhythmias.
optionExplanations.B: Calcium can worsen digoxin-induced arrhythmias in toxicity.
optionExplanations.C: Digoxin is not removed by dialysis because of its large volume of distribution.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Digoxin immune Fab neutralizes the drug, and hypokalemia is corrected.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Anticoagulation to prevent stroke in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation
memoryAnchor: Atrial fibrillation: anticoagulate by score, not by rhythm.
commonTrap: Choosing aspirin because it seems safer.
stem: A 74-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes, and heart failure has new nonvalvular atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular rate. His CHA2DS2-VASc score is 5. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce his risk of stroke?

options.text: Start aspirin alone
Prescribe digoxin to restore sinus rhythm
Start apixaban
Perform electrical cardioversion without anticoagulation

explanation: In nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, left atrial stasis promotes thrombus formation and cardioembolic stroke. A CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or more in men warrants oral anticoagulation, preferably with a direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban, which is superior to warfarin in many patients. Aspirin is much less effective for stroke prevention. The next step is therefore to start apixaban.
pearl: AF: rate or rhythm control plus anticoagulation based on CHA2DS2-VASc; warfarin or a DOAC.

optionExplanations.A: Aspirin alone is inadequate for stroke prevention in high-risk AF.
optionExplanations.B: Digoxin controls rate but does not restore rhythm or prevent thrombosis.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Apixaban reduces the risk of cardioembolic stroke.
optionExplanations.D: Cardioversion without anticoagulation increases embolic risk.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Mobitz type II block requires pacing
memoryAnchor: Mobitz II drops without warning.
commonTrap: Treating Mobitz II like benign Wenckebach.
stem: A 70-year-old man has intermittent dizziness. ECG shows a constant PR interval of 0.20 seconds with occasional nonconducted P waves and a wide QRS complex. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Permanent pacemaker
Atropine as long-term therapy
Observation only
Digoxin

explanation: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block features constant PR intervals with sudden nonconducted P waves, reflecting disease below the AV node (His-Purkinje system). It can progress to complete heart block, so a permanent pacemaker is indicated. Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) shows progressive PR prolongation and is usually benign.
pearl: Mobitz I: progressive PR lengthening, benign; Mobitz II: fixed PR with dropped beats, pacemaker.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A permanent pacemaker is needed for Mobitz II.
optionExplanations.B: Atropine is a temporary measure and often ineffective in infranodal block.
optionExplanations.C: Observation is appropriate for asymptomatic Wenckebach, not Mobitz II.
optionExplanations.D: Digoxin slows AV conduction and would worsen block.

subject: Anatomy
testedConcept: Inferior myocardial infarction and bradycardia from right coronary artery occlusion
memoryAnchor: RCA feeds the nodes and the floor.
commonTrap: Overlooking nodal blood supply from the RCA.
stem: A 58-year-old man has crushing chest pain. ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF, and heart rate is 42/min with a PR interval of 0.30 seconds. Which of the following arteries is most likely occluded?

options.text: Left circumflex artery only
Left main coronary artery
Left anterior descending artery
Right coronary artery

explanation: Inferior ST elevation indicates occlusion of the right coronary artery in most patients (right-dominant circulation). The RCA supplies the SA and AV nodes in most people, so occlusion often causes bradycardia and AV block. The left anterior descending artery supplies the anterior wall and septum.
pearl: RCA: inferior MI, SA and AV nodes, right ventricle; LAD: anterior wall and septum; LCx: lateral wall.

optionExplanations.A: The circumflex supplies the lateral wall and rarely is solely responsible for this pattern.
optionExplanations.B: Left main occlusion causes widespread, often catastrophic, ischemia.
optionExplanations.C: LAD occlusion causes anterior ST elevation in V1 to V4.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. RCA occlusion causes inferior infarction with nodal ischemia.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Molecular mimicry and Aschoff bodies in acute rheumatic fever
memoryAnchor: Strep mimics the heart.
commonTrap: Attributing rheumatic fever to direct bacterial infection of the heart.
stem: A 9-year-old girl has fever, migratory joint pain, and a new holosystolic apical murmur 3 weeks after pharyngitis. Antistreptolysin O titer is elevated. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of her cardiac disease?

options.text: Immune complex deposition in glomeruli
Antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac antigens
Direct invasion of the myocardium by Streptococcus pyogenes
Streptococcal exotoxin acting as a superantigen

explanation: Acute rheumatic fever is a type II hypersensitivity caused by molecular mimicry between group A streptococcal M protein and cardiac myosin and valvular antigens. Pancarditis includes Aschoff bodies (granulomas with Anitschkow cells), and the mitral valve is most affected. Jones criteria and penicillin prophylaxis guide care.
pearl: Rheumatic fever: Jones criteria (joints, carditis, nodules, erythema marginatum, chorea); mitral valve most affected.

optionExplanations.A: Immune complexes in glomeruli describe poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Cross-reactive antibodies from molecular mimicry damage the heart.
optionExplanations.C: The organism does not invade the myocardium in rheumatic fever.
optionExplanations.D: Superantigens cause toxic shock syndrome and scarlet fever.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Statin myopathy and rhabdomyolysis risk
memoryAnchor: Macrolides block the statin metabolizer.
commonTrap: Attributing the myopathy to allergy rather than drug interaction.
stem: A 60-year-old man taking atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia starts clarithromycin for pneumonia. One week later he has diffuse muscle pain and dark urine. Serum creatine kinase is 12,000 U/L. Which of the following best explains this reaction?

options.text: Induction of CYP2C9 decreased statin levels
Inhibition of CYP3A4 increased statin levels
Allergic hypersensitivity to atorvastatin
Direct hepatic necrosis from clarithromycin

explanation: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, and atorvastatin is metabolized by CYP3A4. Macrolides such as clarithromycin inhibit CYP3A4, raising statin levels and increasing the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Other risk factors include fibrates, niacin, and renal impairment. Management is stopping the statin and giving fluids.
pearl: Statin plus CYP3A4 inhibitor (macrolides, azole antifungals, grapefruit juice) raises myopathy risk.

optionExplanations.A: Induction would lower statin levels and decrease the risk.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. CYP3A4 inhibition raises atorvastatin levels and risk of rhabdomyolysis.
optionExplanations.C: Statin myopathy is dose related and not an allergic reaction.
optionExplanations.D: Clarithromycin hepatotoxicity would produce elevated transaminases rather than CK elevation.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Bradykinin accumulation causing ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema
memoryAnchor: ACE inhibitors keep bradykinin around.
commonTrap: Thinking the cough reflects direct airway toxicity or high angiotensin II.
stem: A 55-year-old man with hypertension has had a dry, persistent cough for 3 weeks since starting lisinopril. Chest radiograph is normal. Which of the following best explains his cough?

options.text: Accumulation of bradykinin
Direct toxicity to airway epithelium
Histamine release from mast cells
Increased circulating angiotensin II

explanation: ACE inhibitors block the breakdown of bradykinin, which accumulates and causes dry cough and angioedema. Switching to an agent that does not affect bradykinin resolves the cough. ACE inhibitors also cause hyperkalemia, first-dose hypotension, and teratogenicity, and are contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis.
pearl: ACE inhibitors: cough, angioedema, hyperkalemia, teratogenic; an angiotensin receptor blocker avoids the bradykinin effect.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Accumulation of bradykinin causes the dry cough.
optionExplanations.B: The cough is mediated by bradykinin and not by direct epithelial toxicity.
optionExplanations.C: Histamine release causes IgE-mediated allergic reactions with urticaria, whereas ACE inhibitor cough is not allergic and is mediated by bradykinin instead.
optionExplanations.D: Angiotensin II is decreased, not increased, by ACE inhibition.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Doxorubicin cardiotoxicity causing dilated cardiomyopathy
memoryAnchor: Doxorubicin Dilates the heart.
commonTrap: Confusing dilated and restrictive cardiomyopathy.
stem: A 45-year-old woman treated for breast cancer with doxorubicin 2 years ago has progressive dyspnea and orthopnea. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 25%. Which of the following best explains her cardiomyopathy?

options.text: Pressure overload hypertrophy
Autoimmune myocarditis
Free radical injury to cardiomyocytes
Amyloid deposition in the interstitium

explanation: Doxorubicin generates free radicals and causes dose-dependent cardiotoxicity, producing dilated cardiomyopathy with systolic dysfunction. Dexrazoxane, an iron chelator, can reduce the risk. Other causes of dilated cardiomyopathy include alcohol, coxsackievirus, Chagas disease, peripartum state, and cobalt.
pearl: Doxorubicin: dilated cardiomyopathy, preventable with dexrazoxane; trastuzumab also causes cardiotoxicity.

optionExplanations.A: Pressure overload causes concentric hypertrophy, not dilation.
optionExplanations.B: Autoimmune myocarditis is not the mechanism here.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Free radical damage underlies doxorubicin cardiomyopathy.
optionExplanations.D: Amyloid causes restrictive cardiomyopathy with a stiff, non-dilated ventricle.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Wide pulse pressure and early diastolic murmur in aortic regurgitation
memoryAnchor: Root dilates, leaflets leak.
commonTrap: Attributing the diastolic murmur to mitral disease.
stem: A 36-year-old man with Marfan syndrome has dyspnea. Blood pressure is 160/45 mmHg, and a bounding pulse and head bobbing with each heartbeat are noted. A high-pitched early diastolic decrescendo murmur is heard at the left sternal border. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this valvular lesion?

options.text: Rheumatic fever of the mitral valve
Bicuspid valve calcification in a 30-year-old
Papillary muscle rupture
Aortic root dilation

explanation: Aortic regurgitation produces a wide pulse pressure from large stroke volume and diastolic run-off, with a bounding pulse, head bobbing (de Musset sign), and an early diastolic decrescendo murmur. Aortic root dilation, as in Marfan syndrome, syphilitic aortitis, and aortic dissection, prevents leaflet coaptation. Vasodilators reduce afterload.
pearl: AR: wide pulse pressure, water-hammer pulse, de Musset sign, Austin Flint murmur.

optionExplanations.A: Mitral rheumatic disease would cause an apical murmur and not a wide pulse pressure.
optionExplanations.B: Bicuspid calcification typically causes stenosis later in life.
optionExplanations.C: Papillary muscle rupture causes acute mitral regurgitation after infarction.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Root dilation in Marfan syndrome causes aortic regurgitation.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Coronary artery aneurysm prevention with IVIG and aspirin in Kawasaki disease
memoryAnchor: Kawasaki: protect the coronaries with IVIG.
commonTrap: Treating the fever as a bacterial infection.
stem: A 3-year-old boy has 6 days of fever, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, cervical lymphadenopathy, and a polymorphous rash with swelling of the hands and feet. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment to prevent the major complication?

options.text: Systemic corticosteroids alone
Intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin
Oral amoxicillin
Intravenous acyclovir

explanation: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis of young children. The most serious complication is coronary artery aneurysm with thrombosis or rupture. Treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin reduces the risk and should begin within 10 days of fever. Echocardiography monitors coronary involvement.
pearl: Kawasaki: fever over 5 days, CRASH (conjunctivitis, rash, adenopathy, strawberry tongue, hand-foot changes); IVIG and aspirin.

optionExplanations.A: Corticosteroids alone are not first-line therapy.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. IVIG plus aspirin reduces coronary aneurysms.
optionExplanations.C: Amoxicillin does not treat this vasculitis.
optionExplanations.D: Acyclovir treats herpesvirus infections.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Coronary vasospasm treated with calcium channel blockers
memoryAnchor: Variant angina: spasm, not plaque.
commonTrap: Using beta blockers for vasospastic angina.
stem: A 44-year-old woman who smokes has episodes of chest pain at rest, always between 2 and 4 AM. During an episode, ECG shows transient ST elevation that resolves with sublingual nitroglycerin. Coronary angiography shows no fixed stenosis. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate for prevention?

options.text: Alteplase
Aspirin alone
Amlodipine
Propranolol

explanation: Prinzmetal (variant) angina results from episodic coronary vasospasm, causing transient ST elevation at rest, often at night, without fixed obstruction. Calcium channel blockers and nitrates relieve and prevent vasospasm. Nonselective beta blockers can worsen vasospasm through unopposed alpha stimulation. Smoking cessation is essential.
pearl: Prinzmetal: rest pain, transient ST elevation, treat with calcium channel blockers and nitrates.

optionExplanations.A: Alteplase treats thrombotic occlusion, not vasospasm.
optionExplanations.B: Aspirin does not prevent vasospasm and may not help.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine prevent coronary vasospasm.
optionExplanations.D: Nonselective beta blockers can worsen vasospasm.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Squatting relief of cyanotic spells in tetralogy of Fallot
memoryAnchor: Squat to raise systemic resistance.
commonTrap: Thinking squatting acts by lowering pulmonary resistance.
stem: A 2-year-old boy has episodes of cyanosis during crying that resolve when he squats. Examination shows a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border and a single S2. Chest radiograph shows a boot-shaped heart. Which of the following best explains why squatting relieves his cyanosis?

options.text: Increased systemic vascular resistance decreases the right-to-left shunt
Increased heart rate improves ventricular filling
Decreased venous return reduces shunt flow
Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance increases the shunt

explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot consists of pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, an overriding aorta, and a ventricular septal defect. Squatting increases systemic vascular resistance, which reduces the right-to-left shunt across the VSD and sends more blood to the lungs. The severity of right ventricular outflow obstruction determines cyanosis. Early surgical repair is definitive.
pearl: Tet spells: squatting, knee-chest position; Tetralogy: PROVe (pulmonary stenosis, RVH, overriding aorta, VSD).

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Higher systemic resistance reduces right-to-left shunting.
optionExplanations.B: Heart rate does not mediate this effect.
optionExplanations.C: Squatting increases venous return, not decreases it.
optionExplanations.D: Squatting does not decrease pulmonary resistance.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Cyanide toxicity from prolonged nitroprusside infusion
memoryAnchor: Nitroprusside plus time equals cyanide.
commonTrap: Overlooking drug-induced cyanide toxicity in a patient with lactic acidosis.
stem: A 63-year-old man with a hypertensive emergency receives sodium nitroprusside infusion for 48 hours. He develops confusion, headache, and metabolic acidosis with an elevated lactate. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning
Serotonin syndrome
Methemoglobinemia from dapsone
Cyanide toxicity

explanation: Nitroprusside releases nitric oxide and cyanide as it is metabolized. Prolonged or high-dose infusion can overwhelm hepatic rhodanese and cause cyanide toxicity, with lactic acidosis, confusion, and bright red venous blood. Treatment is stopping the infusion and giving sodium nitrite, sodium thiosulfate, or hydroxocobalamin.
pearl: Nitroprusside: cyanide toxicity; treat with thiosulfate, nitrite, or hydroxocobalamin.

optionExplanations.A: Carbon monoxide poisoning requires exposure to combustion products.
optionExplanations.B: Serotonin syndrome requires serotonergic drugs.
optionExplanations.C: Dapsone causes methemoglobinemia and is not part of the history.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Nitroprusside metabolism releases cyanide.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Preload-dependent hypotension in right ventricular infarction
memoryAnchor: Right heart is preload dependent: fill it.
commonTrap: Giving nitroglycerin to a hypotensive patient with inferior MI.
stem: A 61-year-old man has crushing chest pain and diaphoresis. Blood pressure is 78/50 mmHg and heart rate is 54/min. Jugular venous distention is prominent, lungs are clear to auscultation, and no S3 is heard. ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF, and in right-sided lead V4R. Serum troponin I is 14 ng/mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous nitroglycerin infusion titrated to pain
Intravenous morphine for pain control
Intravenous normal saline bolus for volume loading
Intravenous furosemide to reduce congestion

explanation: Inferior ST elevation with hypotension, clear lungs, and jugular venous distention suggests right ventricular infarction from proximal right coronary artery occlusion, confirmed by ST elevation in V4R. The failing right ventricle is preload dependent, so hypotension is treated with intravenous fluid resuscitation to maintain filling pressure. Nitrates, diuretics, and morphine decrease preload and can cause profound hypotension. Reperfusion with percutaneous coronary intervention remains the definitive treatment, and bradycardia may need atropine or pacing because of nodal ischemia. An intravenous normal saline bolus is therefore the most appropriate next step in management.
pearl: RV infarction: inferior MI, hypotension, JVD, clear lungs, V4R elevation; give fluids, avoid nitrates and diuretics.

optionExplanations.A: Nitroglycerin decreases preload and could cause severe hypotension, whereas this right ventricle depends on adequate filling instead of vasodilation.
optionExplanations.B: Morphine causes venodilation, which would decrease preload and lower blood pressure further rather than support it.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A normal saline bolus increases right ventricular preload and treats hypotension in RV infarction.
optionExplanations.D: Furosemide would decrease preload, whereas the lungs are clear and no pulmonary congestion exists to treat.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Aldosterone antagonist mortality benefit and hyperkalemia monitoring in heart failure
memoryAnchor: Spironolactone saves lives and raises potassium.
commonTrap: Forgetting hyperkalemia when adding an aldosterone antagonist to an ACE inhibitor.
stem: A 58-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 30% has class III heart failure symptoms despite taking lisinopril and carvedilol. Blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg, heart rate is 68 bpm, serum creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL, and serum potassium is 4.2 mEq/L. His physician adds spironolactone. Which of the following is the most important monitoring consideration after starting this drug?

options.text: Thyroid function tests
Complete blood count for agranulocytosis
Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone
Serum potassium and renal function

explanation: Aldosterone antagonists such as spironolactone and eplerenone decrease mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction by blocking aldosterone-mediated sodium retention and cardiac fibrosis. Because spironolactone blocks the aldosterone receptor in the collecting duct, it decreases potassium secretion, and in combination with an ACE inhibitor it increases the risk of hyperkalemia, especially in renal impairment. Potassium and creatinine should be checked within the first week and at intervals thereafter. Spironolactone also causes gynecomastia through antiandrogen effects, and eplerenone is an alternative that avoids it.
pearl: HFrEF drugs with mortality benefit: ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta blockers, aldosterone antagonists, SGLT2 inhibitors; monitor K and creatinine.

optionExplanations.A: Thyroid function is monitored with amiodarone, not with aldosterone antagonists.
optionExplanations.B: Agranulocytosis is a risk with drugs such as clozapine and carbamazepine, not with spironolactone.
optionExplanations.C: Calcium and PTH monitoring is not needed with spironolactone, which does not primarily affect calcium handling, unlike loop and thiazide diuretics.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Hyperkalemia and renal function must be monitored because of aldosterone blockade combined with an ACE inhibitor drug.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Kussmaul sign and pericardial calcification in constrictive pericarditis
memoryAnchor: A stiff shell: JVP rises when he breathes in.
commonTrap: Treating constrictive pericarditis with drainage as if it were tamponade.
stem: A 52-year-old man from a region where tuberculosis is endemic has 6 months of progressive abdominal distention, peripheral edema, and fatigue. Blood pressure is 106/72 mmHg, heart rate is 92 bpm, and jugular venous pressure rises with inspiration. A high-pitched early diastolic knock is heard. The liver is enlarged and ascites is present. Chest CT shows a thickened, calcified pericardium. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment?

options.text: Surgical pericardiectomy with removal of the thickened pericardium
Long-term oral anticoagulation with warfarin
Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing
Emergency pericardiocentesis to drain the effusion

explanation: Constrictive pericarditis is caused by a rigid, scarred pericardium that restricts diastolic filling, most often after tuberculosis in endemic regions, radiation, or cardiac surgery. Findings include Kussmaul sign, a pericardial knock, right-sided heart failure with edema and ascites, and a calcified pericardium on imaging. Ventricular filling is limited, so cardiac output decreases, and echocardiography shows septal bounce. Diuretics give temporary relief, and pericardiectomy is the definitive treatment because the underlying mechanism is mechanical constraint. Surgical pericardiectomy with removal of the thickened pericardium is therefore the definitive treatment.
pearl: Constrictive pericarditis: Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, calcification; tamponade has pulsus paradoxus and no Kussmaul sign.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Surgical pericardiectomy is definitive for symptomatic constrictive pericarditis.
optionExplanations.B: Anticoagulation does not address pericardial constraint and is not a treatment for constrictive pericarditis.
optionExplanations.C: Biventricular pacing treats dyssynchrony in systolic heart failure and does not relieve mechanical constraint by a rigid pericardium.
optionExplanations.D: Pericardiocentesis treats effusion and tamponade, whereas constriction results from a thick, scarred pericardium without a drainable fluid collection.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: Staphylococcus aureus tricuspid valve endocarditis in injection drug use
memoryAnchor: Needles to the right heart, then the lungs.
commonTrap: Missing the tricuspid valve as the source of pulmonary nodules.
stem: A 29-year-old man who injects heroin has 5 days of fever, pleuritic chest pain, and cough with hemoptysis. Temperature is 39.5 C, heart rate is 118 bpm, and blood pressure is 102/60 mmHg. A holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border increases with inspiration. Chest radiograph shows multiple peripheral nodular opacities with cavitation. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in clusters that are coagulase positive. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his chest findings?

options.text: Aspiration pneumonia from a lung abscess in the dependent segments
Septic emboli from tricuspid valve vegetations
Primary tuberculosis with miliary spread
Pulmonary infarction from deep vein thrombosis

explanation: Injection drug use predisposes to Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis of the normal tricuspid valve, because skin flora and particulate matter injure the right-sided endocardium. Right-sided vegetations embolize to the lungs, causing multiple peripheral nodules with cavitation, fever, and hemoptysis, and the tricuspid regurgitation murmur increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign). Diagnosis uses repeated blood cultures and echocardiography under the Duke criteria. Treatment includes prolonged intravenous antistaphylococcal antibiotics, such as vancomycin pending susceptibilities, and surgery for refractory infection or large vegetations that increase embolic risk.
pearl: IV drug use: S. aureus, tricuspid valve, septic pulmonary emboli; murmur louder on inspiration.

optionExplanations.A: Aspiration abscesses localize to dependent lung segments and would not cause multiple peripheral nodules with a tricuspid murmur.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Right-sided vegetations send septic emboli to the lungs, causing nodular cavitary lesions.
optionExplanations.C: Primary tuberculosis would not produce coagulase-positive cocci in blood cultures or a tricuspid regurgitation murmur.
optionExplanations.D: Pulmonary infarction from DVT would not cause bacteremia with gram-positive cocci and cavitary nodules.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Beta-2 agonist mechanism in acute asthma
memoryAnchor: Beta-2 agonists raise cAMP and open the airways.
commonTrap: Confusing the mechanisms of albuterol, montelukast, and ipratropium.
stem: A 17-year-old girl with asthma has wheezing and shortness of breath after cold exercise. Her peak expiratory flow is 55% of predicted. She is treated with inhaled albuterol and improves within minutes. Which of the following is the mechanism by which albuterol relieves bronchospasm?

options.text: Increases intracellular cyclic AMP in airway smooth muscle
Blocks muscarinic receptors in the vagal efferent pathway
Blocks leukotriene receptors on bronchial smooth muscle
Inhibits phosphodiesterase in mast cells only

explanation: Albuterol is a selective beta-2 adrenergic agonist. Activation of the Gs-coupled receptor increases adenylyl cyclase activity and cyclic AMP, relaxing airway smooth muscle. Adverse effects include tremor, tachycardia, and hypokalemia. Long-acting beta agonists should not be used alone in asthma because of increased risk of exacerbation.
pearl: Albuterol: Gs, cAMP, bronchodilation; side effects: tremor, tachycardia, hypokalemia.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Beta-2 stimulation raises cAMP and relaxes bronchial smooth muscle.
optionExplanations.B: Muscarinic antagonists such as ipratropium block cholinergic bronchoconstriction.
optionExplanations.C: Leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast block leukotriene receptors.
optionExplanations.D: Phosphodiesterase inhibition is the action of theophylline.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Panacinar emphysema in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
memoryAnchor: Panacinar for Pan-lung, lower lobes, nonsmoker.
commonTrap: Assuming all emphysema is smoking-related and upper-lobe predominant.
stem: A 38-year-old nonsmoking man has progressive dyspnea. Chest radiograph shows hyperinflation with lower lobe predominance, and pulmonary function testing shows a decreased FEV1/FVC ratio. His father died of cirrhosis. Which of the following pathologic patterns is most likely?

options.text: Interstitial fibrosis with honeycombing
Noncaseating granulomas
Panacinar emphysema
Centriacinar emphysema in the upper lobes

explanation: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency allows unopposed neutrophil elastase to destroy alveolar walls, causing panacinar emphysema that is lower-lobe predominant. Liver disease results from accumulation of misfolded protein in hepatocytes (PAS-positive globules). Smoking-related emphysema instead predominates at the apices.
pearl: AAT deficiency: panacinar, lower lobes, liver cirrhosis, PAS-positive globules.

optionExplanations.A: Honeycombing indicates interstitial fibrosis and a restrictive pattern.
optionExplanations.B: Noncaseating granulomas indicate sarcoidosis.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Panacinar emphysema is characteristic of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
optionExplanations.D: Centriacinar emphysema is related to smoking and favors the upper lobes.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch with dead space in pulmonary embolism
memoryAnchor: PE: air goes in, blood does not.
commonTrap: Describing PE as a shunt.
stem: A 48-year-old woman has sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea 5 days after a long flight. Heart rate is 112 bpm, respiratory rate is 26/min, and oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. Chest radiograph is clear. Which of the following best describes the physiologic abnormality?

options.text: Perfusion of lung units that receive no ventilation
Decreased diffusion capacity because of alveolar edema
Decreased total lung capacity from fibrosis
Ventilation of lung units that receive no perfusion

explanation: Pulmonary embolism obstructs pulmonary arterial flow, producing ventilation of unperfused alveoli (dead space, high V/Q ratio) and, through reflex and regional effects, areas of low V/Q that cause hypoxemia. A clear chest radiograph is typical. CT pulmonary angiography confirms the diagnosis, and anticoagulation with heparin is the treatment.
pearl: PE: high V/Q (dead space); shunt: V/Q of zero; treat PE with heparin then oral anticoagulation.

optionExplanations.A: Perfusion without ventilation (shunt) occurs in conditions like atelectasis or pneumonia.
optionExplanations.B: Alveolar edema is not present on the clear radiograph.
optionExplanations.C: Fibrosis decreases lung volumes and would not appear suddenly.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Ventilated but unperfused lung units create dead space.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Noncaseating granulomas and hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis
memoryAnchor: Granulomas make their own active vitamin D.
commonTrap: Attributing hypercalcemia to PTH or PTHrP.
stem: A 32-year-old Black woman has dry cough, fatigue, and tender red nodules on the shins. Chest radiograph shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Serum calcium is 11.4 mg/dL and angiotensin-converting enzyme is elevated. Which of the following best explains the hypercalcemia?

options.text: Secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide
Activation of vitamin D by macrophages in granulomas
Excess parathyroid hormone from adenoma
Osteolytic bone metastases

explanation: Sarcoidosis is characterized by non-caseating granulomas. Activated macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active calcitriol, increasing intestinal calcium absorption and causing hypercalcemia. Erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar adenopathy are typical, and corticosteroids are first-line treatment.
pearl: Sarcoid: noncaseating granulomas, ACE elevation, hypercalcemia from 1-alpha-hydroxylase; treat with steroids.

optionExplanations.A: PTHrP is produced by squamous cell carcinomas.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Granuloma macrophages activate vitamin D.
optionExplanations.C: A parathyroid adenoma causes primary hyperparathyroidism with high PTH.
optionExplanations.D: Bone metastases are not suggested here.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Immediate needle decompression for tension pneumothorax
memoryAnchor: Needle first, film later.
commonTrap: Ordering a radiograph in an unstable patient.
stem: A 24-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle crash. He is in severe respiratory distress with a blood pressure of 78/50 mmHg and heart rate of 134 bpm. Breath sounds are absent on the left, the trachea is deviated to the right, and neck veins are distended. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Needle decompression of the left chest
Intubation and observation
Chest radiograph before intervention
Pericardiocentesis

explanation: Tension pneumothorax causes progressive intrapleural air accumulation, mediastinal shift away from the affected side, decreased venous return, and obstructive shock. It is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate needle decompression in the second intercostal space midclavicular line (or fifth intercostal space anterior axillary line), followed by chest tube insertion.
pearl: Tension pneumothorax: hypotension, JVD, tracheal deviation away, absent breath sounds; treat before imaging.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Decompress the left chest immediately.
optionExplanations.B: Positive-pressure ventilation without decompression can worsen tension physiology.
optionExplanations.C: Waiting for imaging delays lifesaving treatment.
optionExplanations.D: Pericardiocentesis treats tamponade, which does not cause absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes in ARDS
memoryAnchor: ARDS: leaky capillaries, normal wedge.
commonTrap: Treating ARDS as cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
stem: A 45-year-old man with severe pancreatitis develops hypoxemia that does not improve with oxygen. Chest radiograph shows bilateral diffuse infiltrates, and the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 10 mmHg. Which of the following histologic findings is expected?

options.text: Neutrophilic bronchiolitis with mucus plugs
Honeycombing with fibroblast foci
Hyaline membranes lining the alveoli
Noncaseating granulomas

explanation: ARDS results from diffuse alveolar damage with increased permeability of the alveolar-capillary barrier, producing noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and hyaline membranes composed of fibrin and necrotic cells. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is normal, distinguishing it from cardiogenic edema. Treatment is low-tidal-volume ventilation with PEEP.
pearl: ARDS: PaO2/FiO2 of 300 or less, bilateral infiltrates, wedge 18 mmHg or less; low tidal volume and PEEP.

optionExplanations.A: Neutrophilic bronchiolitis suggests asthma or chronic bronchitis.
optionExplanations.B: Honeycombing indicates chronic interstitial fibrosis.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Hyaline membranes characterize diffuse alveolar damage.
optionExplanations.D: Noncaseating granulomas indicate sarcoidosis.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: Cold agglutinins in Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection
memoryAnchor: Walking pneumonia, cold clumping.
commonTrap: Treating atypical pneumonia with a beta-lactam.
stem: A 19-year-old college student has 10 days of low-grade fever, headache, and dry cough. Chest radiograph shows bilateral patchy interstitial infiltrates that look worse than his mild symptoms. Sputum Gram stain shows no organisms. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely?

options.text: Elevated serum galactomannan
Cold agglutinins (IgM against the I antigen)
Acid-fast bacilli on sputum smear
Gram-positive diplococci on culture

explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes atypical (walking) pneumonia in young adults, with a prolonged mild course and bilateral interstitial infiltrates. It lacks a cell wall, so it does not Gram stain. IgM cold agglutinins against the I antigen on red cells can cause hemolysis. Macrolides or doxycycline treat it, and beta-lactams are ineffective.
pearl: Mycoplasma: no cell wall, no Gram stain, cold agglutinins, treat with azithromycin.

optionExplanations.A: Galactomannan is a marker of invasive aspergillosis.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Cold agglutinins support Mycoplasma pneumonia.
optionExplanations.C: Acid-fast bacilli indicate tuberculosis.
optionExplanations.D: Gram-positive diplococci would suggest typical pneumococcal pneumonia.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Paraneoplastic syndromes of small cell carcinoma
memoryAnchor: Small cell: central, SIADH.
commonTrap: Assigning hypercalcemia of squamous cancer to SIADH.
stem: A 62-year-old man with a 45-pack-year smoking history has a central hilar mass on chest radiograph. Serum sodium is 122 mEq/L and urine osmolality is 520 mOsm/kg despite clinical euvolemia. Which of the following is the most likely tumor type?

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma
Adenocarcinoma
Bronchial carcinoid
Small cell carcinoma

explanation: Small cell carcinoma is a central tumor strongly associated with smoking that secretes ADH (SIADH) and ACTH (Cushing syndrome). Lambert-Eaton syndrome is another paraneoplastic effect. Histology shows small blue cells with scant cytoplasm, neuroendocrine markers, and is treated with chemotherapy rather than surgery.
pearl: Small cell: central, SIADH, ACTH, Lambert-Eaton; squamous: PTHrP; adenocarcinoma: peripheral.

optionExplanations.A: Squamous cell carcinoma is central but causes hypercalcemia via PTHrP.
optionExplanations.B: Adenocarcinoma is typically peripheral and is common in nonsmokers.
optionExplanations.C: Bronchial carcinoid can cause carcinoid syndrome rather than SIADH.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Small cell carcinoma is a central tumor that causes SIADH.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Rightward shift of the oxyhemoglobin curve during exercise
memoryAnchor: CADET faces right.
commonTrap: Confusing right shift (unloading) with left shift (loading).
stem: A 25-year-old marathon runner exercises vigorously. Her skeletal muscle temperature rises and tissue pH falls. Which of the following changes in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve best facilitates oxygen delivery to her muscles?

options.text: Upward shift with higher oxygen-carrying capacity
Leftward shift with increased affinity for oxygen
Rightward shift with decreased affinity for oxygen
No shift because delivery depends only on cardiac output

explanation: Increased temperature, increased PCO2, decreased pH (Bohr effect), and increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate shift the curve to the right, lowering hemoglobin affinity for oxygen and promoting unloading in metabolically active tissues. The P50 increases. A leftward shift occurs with fetal hemoglobin, carbon monoxide, and alkalosis.
pearl: Right shift: CADET face right (CO2, Acid, DPG, Exercise, Temperature). Left shift: CO, HbF, alkalosis.

optionExplanations.A: Oxygen-carrying capacity depends on hemoglobin concentration, not on the curve shift.
optionExplanations.B: A left shift would hold oxygen more tightly and impair delivery.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Right shift unloads oxygen at active tissues.
optionExplanations.D: The curve shifts with local conditions in addition to cardiac output.

subject: Genetics
testedConcept: CFTR chloride channel defect and sweat chloride testing
memoryAnchor: CF: Chloride stuck, thick mucus.
commonTrap: Confusing cystic fibrosis with primary ciliary dyskinesia.
stem: A 4-year-old boy has recurrent Pseudomonas pneumonia, chronic diarrhea with foul-smelling bulky stools, and poor weight gain. Sweat chloride is 85 mEq/L (normal less than 30). Which of the following best describes the underlying defect?

options.text: Defect in dynein arm assembly
Defective chloride channel regulation due to misfolded CFTR protein
Deficiency of the cystic duct enzyme lipase
Defective sodium channel in the collecting duct

explanation: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive and most often results from the delta F508 deletion in CFTR on chromosome 7, causing misfolding and degradation of the chloride channel. Thick secretions cause chronic sinopulmonary infection, pancreatic insufficiency with fat malabsorption, meconium ileus, and male infertility. Sweat chloride above 60 mEq/L confirms the diagnosis.
pearl: CF: delta F508, sweat chloride over 60, pancreatic insufficiency, Pseudomonas; treat with CFTR modulators.

optionExplanations.A: Dynein defects cause primary ciliary dyskinesia with situs inversus.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Misfolded CFTR protein impairs chloride transport.
optionExplanations.C: Lipase deficiency does not explain the multisystem disease.
optionExplanations.D: ENaC defects cause Liddle syndrome with hypertension.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Restrictive pattern and honeycombing in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
memoryAnchor: Fibrosis: stiff lungs, honeycomb, crackles.
commonTrap: Interpreting a high FEV1/FVC as normal rather than restrictive.
stem: A 66-year-old man has progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough for 18 months. Examination shows fine bibasilar end-inspiratory crackles and digital clubbing. Pulmonary function testing shows an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.88 and a decreased total lung capacity. Which of the following HRCT findings is most likely?

options.text: Subpleural honeycombing with traction bronchiectasis
Upper lobe cavitary nodules
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with perilymphatic nodules
Hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms

explanation: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis causes a restrictive pattern with an increased or normal FEV1/FVC ratio, decreased TLC and DLCO, and subpleural basal honeycombing on HRCT. Pathology shows usual interstitial pneumonia with temporally heterogeneous fibrosis and fibroblast foci. Antifibrotic agents such as pirfenidone and nintedanib slow progression.
pearl: Restrictive: FEV1/FVC normal or high, low TLC; obstructive: FEV1/FVC low, high TLC.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Honeycombing is the hallmark of usual interstitial pneumonia.
optionExplanations.B: Upper lobe cavities suggest tuberculosis.
optionExplanations.C: Hilar adenopathy with perilymphatic nodules suggests sarcoidosis.
optionExplanations.D: Hyperinflation indicates obstructive lung disease.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Asbestos exposure, pleural plaques, and mesothelioma risk
memoryAnchor: Asbestos in the Base; silica in the Summit.
commonTrap: Overlooking that asbestos also increases bronchogenic carcinoma risk, especially with smoking.
stem: A 68-year-old retired shipyard worker has progressive exertional dyspnea. Chest radiograph shows calcified pleural plaques and lower lobe interstitial fibrosis. Sputum contains golden-brown fusiform rods with iron coating. Which of the following malignancies is he most at risk for?

options.text: Small cell lung carcinoma only
Hepatocellular carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus
Pleural mesothelioma

explanation: Asbestosis causes lower lobe fibrosis, ferruginous bodies, and pleural plaques. Asbestos exposure increases the risk of both bronchogenic carcinoma (especially in smokers) and pleural mesothelioma, which is nearly specific for asbestos exposure. Calcified pleural plaques are benign markers of exposure.
pearl: Asbestos: lower lobes, pleural plaques, ferruginous bodies, mesothelioma; silica: upper lobes, eggshell calcification.

optionExplanations.A: Asbestos increases risk of lung cancers generally, not only small cell carcinoma, and mesothelioma is the hallmark.
optionExplanations.B: Hepatocellular carcinoma relates to hepatitis, cirrhosis, and aflatoxin.
optionExplanations.C: Esophageal squamous cancer relates to alcohol, smoking, and hot liquids.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Mesothelioma is characteristic of asbestos exposure.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Renal compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis
memoryAnchor: Kidneys need days to compensate.
commonTrap: Reading high bicarbonate as a primary metabolic alkalosis.
stem: A 66-year-old man with severe COPD and chronic hypercapnia is evaluated for increased dyspnea. Arterial blood gas on room air shows pH 7.34, PaCO2 70 mmHg, and HCO3 37 mEq/L. His serum sodium is 140 mEq/L and chloride is 92 mEq/L. His blood pressure is 128/80 mmHg and heart rate is 94 bpm. Which of the following best describes his acid-base status?

options.text: Acute respiratory acidosis with minimal compensation
Mixed respiratory acidosis and primary metabolic alkalosis
Chronic respiratory acidosis with appropriate renal compensation
Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation

explanation: In chronic respiratory acidosis, retained carbon dioxide lowers pH, and the kidneys compensate over days by increasing bicarbonate reabsorption and generation, so bicarbonate rises about 3.5 to 4 mEq/L for each 10 mmHg increase in PaCO2. With a PaCO2 of 70 (30 above normal), the expected bicarbonate is roughly 24 plus 10.5 to 12, or about 35 to 36, which matches the measured 37 mEq/L and the near-normal pH of 7.34. In acute respiratory acidosis bicarbonate rises only about 1 mEq/L per 10 mmHg because renal compensation has not occurred. Therefore the diagnosis reflects chronic CO2 retention, and supplemental oxygen must be given cautiously because a decrease in hypoxic drive can raise PaCO2 further.
pearl: Chronic respiratory acidosis: HCO3 rises 3.5-4 per 10 mmHg PaCO2; acute: 1 per 10.

optionExplanations.A: Acute respiratory acidosis would show a much lower pH of about 7.20 and a bicarbonate near 27, whereas this patient has a high bicarbonate and a nearly normal pH.
optionExplanations.B: A second primary metabolic alkalosis would push bicarbonate well above the expected compensated value, whereas this value is appropriate for the degree of hypercapnia.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The bicarbonate rise matches the expected renal compensation for a PaCO2 of 70 mmHg over days.
optionExplanations.D: Metabolic acidosis would present with a low bicarbonate, not a bicarbonate of 37 mEq/L, and the primary disturbance here is respiratory.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: Isoniazid neuropathy prevention with pyridoxine during tuberculosis therapy
memoryAnchor: Isoniazid eats vitamin B6: give B6.
commonTrap: Attributing neuropathy to ethambutol rather than isoniazid.
stem: A 36-year-old man with HIV and a CD4 count of 180/mm3 is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis after 3 months of cough, night sweats, and weight loss. Temperature is 38.2 C, heart rate is 96 bpm, hemoglobin is 11.2 g/dL, and serum alanine aminotransferase is 30 U/L. Chest radiograph shows an apical cavitary lesion and sputum smear is acid-fast positive. He is started on isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. His physician also prescribes a vitamin supplement. Which of the following best explains the reason for this supplement?

options.text: Rifampin depletes folate and can cause megaloblastic anemia
Isoniazid inhibits pyridoxine activation and can cause peripheral neuropathy
Ethambutol causes thiamine deficiency and Wernicke encephalopathy
Pyrazinamide causes riboflavin deficiency and cheilosis

explanation: Isoniazid inhibits the conversion of pyridoxine (vitamin B6) to its active form and increases urinary pyridoxine excretion, which causes peripheral neuropathy, particularly in HIV, diabetes, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, and pregnancy. Pyridoxine supplementation decreases the risk. Isoniazid also causes hepatitis, so liver enzymes are monitored, and a lupus-like reaction can occur in slow acetylators. Rifampin induces cytochrome P450 and colors secretions orange, ethambutol causes optic neuritis with red-green color blindness, and pyrazinamide causes hyperuricemia and hepatotoxicity, so each requires distinct monitoring.
pearl: RIPE: Rifampin (orange fluids, CYP inducer), Isoniazid (neuropathy, hepatitis; give B6), Pyrazinamide (hyperuricemia), Ethambutol (optic neuritis).

optionExplanations.A: Rifampin induces cytochrome P450 enzymes and causes orange secretions, but it does not cause folate depletion and megaloblastic anemia.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Isoniazid interferes with pyridoxine and can cause neuropathy, which supplementation helps to prevent.
optionExplanations.C: Ethambutol causes optic neuritis rather than thiamine deficiency, so Wernicke encephalopathy is not its mechanism.
optionExplanations.D: Pyrazinamide causes hyperuricemia and hepatotoxicity, not riboflavin deficiency with cheilosis.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Foot process effacement in minimal change disease
memoryAnchor: Minimal change: invisible on light microscopy, effaced on EM.
commonTrap: Expecting abnormal findings on light microscopy.
stem: A 5-year-old boy has periorbital edema and frothy urine 2 weeks after an upper respiratory infection. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein, and serum albumin is 1.9 g/dL. Light microscopy of a renal biopsy appears normal. Which of the following findings is expected on electron microscopy?

options.text: Effacement of podocyte foot processes
Tram-track basement membrane splitting
Subepithelial humps
Spike-and-dome pattern of the basement membrane

explanation: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. Light microscopy and immunofluorescence are normal, and electron microscopy shows effacement of podocyte foot processes. Proteinuria is selective for albumin, and the disease responds to corticosteroids.
pearl: Minimal change: child, post-infection, normal light microscopy, steroid-responsive, selective proteinuria.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Foot process effacement is the hallmark of minimal change disease.
optionExplanations.B: Tram-track splitting is seen in membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.
optionExplanations.C: Subepithelial humps are seen in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
optionExplanations.D: Spike-and-dome pattern is seen in membranous nephropathy.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Low C3 and subepithelial humps in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
memoryAnchor: Humps on the epithelial side, low C3.
commonTrap: Confusing granular and linear immunofluorescence.
stem: An 8-year-old girl has cola-colored urine, periorbital edema, and blood pressure of 145/92 mmHg 2 weeks after a skin infection. Urinalysis shows red blood cell casts. Serum C3 is low and antistreptolysin O is elevated. Biopsy electron microscopy would most likely show which of the following?

options.text: Splitting of the basement membrane with mesangial interposition
Foot process effacement only
Linear IgG deposition along the basement membrane
Subepithelial immune complex humps

explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune complex disease producing a nephritic picture with hematuria, hypertension, edema, and low C3. Biopsy shows enlarged hypercellular glomeruli, granular IgG, IgM, and C3 on immunofluorescence, and subepithelial humps on electron microscopy. Most children recover with supportive care.
pearl: PSGN: lumpy-bumpy granular IF, subepithelial humps, low C3, ASO elevated.

optionExplanations.A: Basement membrane splitting describes membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.
optionExplanations.B: Foot process effacement alone describes minimal change disease.
optionExplanations.C: Linear IgG describes anti-GBM disease.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Subepithelial humps characterize poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Muddy brown casts distinguishing acute tubular necrosis from prerenal azotemia
memoryAnchor: Brown casts, high sodium: tubules are dead.
commonTrap: Treating established ATN as prerenal with fluids alone.
stem: A 60-year-old man develops oliguria 3 days after a prolonged hypotensive episode during cardiac surgery. Serum creatinine rises from 1.0 to 3.4 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows muddy brown granular casts, and urine sodium is 55 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Postrenal obstruction
Prerenal azotemia
Acute tubular necrosis
Acute interstitial nephritis

explanation: Ischemic or toxic injury to tubular epithelial cells causes acute tubular necrosis, with muddy brown casts, elevated urine sodium, fractional excretion of sodium above 2 percent, and poor urine concentration. Prerenal azotemia has low urine sodium and FENa below 1 percent and responds to volume repletion. Biopsy shows tubular cell necrosis, and recovery occurs over days to weeks.
pearl: ATN: muddy brown casts, FENa over 2%; prerenal: FENa under 1%, BUN:Cr over 20.

optionExplanations.A: Postrenal obstruction would show hydronephrosis on ultrasonography.
optionExplanations.B: Prerenal azotemia has concentrated urine and low urine sodium.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Muddy brown casts with high urine sodium indicate ATN.
optionExplanations.D: Interstitial nephritis shows white blood cell casts and eosinophils after a drug exposure.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Type 1 distal renal tubular acidosis with hypokalemia and stones
memoryAnchor: Type 1 is Distal and Dissolves bones into stones.
commonTrap: Confusing the potassium patterns of type 1 and type 4 RTA.
stem: A 30-year-old woman with Sjogren syndrome has muscle weakness and recurrent kidney stones. Serum bicarbonate is 15 mEq/L, potassium is 2.9 mEq/L, and chloride is 112 mEq/L with a normal anion gap. Urine pH is 6.6. Which of the following is the most likely defect?

options.text: Impaired ammonium excretion from hypoaldosteronism
Aldosterone deficiency in the collecting duct
Impaired bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Impaired hydrogen ion secretion in the collecting duct

explanation: Type 1 (distal) renal tubular acidosis results from failure of alpha-intercalated cells to secrete hydrogen ions, so urine cannot acidify below pH 5.5 despite systemic acidosis. Hypokalemia, hypercalciuria, and calcium phosphate stones occur, and autoimmune diseases such as Sjogren syndrome are causes. Treatment is bicarbonate or citrate.
pearl: RTA 1: distal H+ secretion defect, low K, stones; RTA 2: proximal HCO3 wasting; RTA 4: low aldosterone, high K.

optionExplanations.A: Type 4 RTA features high potassium rather than low potassium.
optionExplanations.B: Aldosterone deficiency causes type 4 RTA with hyperkalemia.
optionExplanations.C: Proximal bicarbonate wasting is type 2 RTA, where urine pH falls below 5.5 once bicarbonate is depleted.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Failed distal hydrogen ion secretion causes type 1 RTA.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Thiazide use to reduce urinary calcium in recurrent stones
memoryAnchor: Thiazides: you gain calcium; loops: you lose calcium.
commonTrap: Using a loop diuretic in a patient with calcium stones.
stem: A 45-year-old man has had three episodes of calcium oxalate kidney stones. A 24-hour urine collection shows hypercalciuria. Which of the following drugs would most appropriately reduce his urinary calcium excretion?

options.text: Hydrochlorothiazide
Acetazolamide
Spironolactone
Furosemide

explanation: Thiazides block the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, increasing calcium reabsorption and decreasing urinary calcium, so they reduce calcium stone formation. Adverse effects include hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia, and hypercalcemia. Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion.
pearl: Loops lose calcium; thiazides gain calcium. Citrate and hydration also prevent stones.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Hydrochlorothiazide lowers urinary calcium.
optionExplanations.B: Acetazolamide causes bicarbonaturia and can promote calcium phosphate stones.
optionExplanations.C: Spironolactone does not reduce urinary calcium meaningfully.
optionExplanations.D: Furosemide increases calcium excretion and can promote stones.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Struvite staghorn calculi with Proteus infection
memoryAnchor: Proteus: Pee turns alkaline, stones grow into antlers.
commonTrap: Attributing staghorn stones to E. coli.
stem: A 52-year-old woman with recurrent urinary tract infections has flank pain. Urine pH is 8.0 and imaging shows a large staghorn calculus in the right renal pelvis. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?

options.text: Enterococcus faecalis
Proteus mirabilis
Candida albicans
Escherichia coli

explanation: Urease-producing organisms such as Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella, and Staphylococcus saprophyticus hydrolyze urea to ammonia, raising urine pH and precipitating struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate), forming staghorn calculi. Treatment is surgical removal and antibiotics. Calcium oxalate is the most common stone type overall.
pearl: Struvite: urease-positive bugs, alkaline urine, staghorn; uric acid: acidic urine, radiolucent.

optionExplanations.A: Enterococcus does not typically produce urease.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Urease-positive Proteus raises urine pH and forms struvite stones.
optionExplanations.C: Candida is not associated with struvite stones.
optionExplanations.D: E. coli does not produce urease.

subject: Genetics
