testedConcept: Berry aneurysm risk in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
memoryAnchor: Cysts in kidneys and bubbles in the brain arteries.
commonTrap: Confusing ADPKD with von Hippel-Lindau disease.
stem: A 38-year-old man with bilateral flank masses, hypertension, and hematuria has a family history of kidney failure. Ultrasonography shows enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts. He asks about associated conditions. Which of the following is most likely associated with his disease?

options.text: Wilms tumor
Pheochromocytoma only
Renal cell carcinoma with cerebellar hemangioblastoma
Berry aneurysms of the circle of Willis

explanation: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, most often from PKD1 mutations on chromosome 16, causes progressive cystic enlargement of the kidneys, hypertension, hematuria, and eventual renal failure. Extrarenal manifestations include hepatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse, and berry aneurysms with risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage. Tolvaptan can slow progression.
pearl: ADPKD: PKD1/PKD2, berry aneurysms, hepatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse; ARPKD presents in infancy.

optionExplanations.A: Wilms tumor occurs in children and is not linked to ADPKD.
optionExplanations.B: Pheochromocytoma occurs in MEN2 or VHL, not ADPKD.
optionExplanations.C: RCC with cerebellar hemangioblastoma suggests von Hippel-Lindau disease.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Berry aneurysms are associated with ADPKD.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules and ACE inhibitor renal protection
memoryAnchor: ACE inhibitors relax the exit door.
commonTrap: Choosing any antihypertensive as equally renoprotective.
stem: A 58-year-old man with 20 years of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has persistent albuminuria and hypertension. Renal biopsy shows nodular glomerulosclerosis with hyalinization of efferent arterioles. Which of the following drug classes most effectively slows progression of his kidney disease?

options.text: Alpha blockers
Loop diuretics
ACE inhibitors
Calcium channel blockers

explanation: Diabetic nephropathy results from nonenzymatic glycosylation of the glomerular basement membrane and efferent arteriole, leading to hyperfiltration and Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules. ACE inhibitors and ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole, decreasing intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria, and slow progression. SGLT2 inhibitors also provide renal protection.
pearl: Diabetic nephropathy: early hyperfiltration, microalbuminuria, nodular glomerulosclerosis; treat with ACEi/ARB and SGLT2 inhibitors.

optionExplanations.A: Alpha blockers lower blood pressure without a renoprotective effect.
optionExplanations.B: Loop diuretics relieve edema but do not slow nephropathy.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. ACE inhibitors reduce intraglomerular pressure by dilating the efferent arteriole.
optionExplanations.D: Calcium channel blockers lower blood pressure but dilate the afferent arteriole and are less protective.

subject: Immunology
testedConcept: Anti-GBM antibodies against type IV collagen in Goodpasture syndrome
memoryAnchor: Linear like a line along the basement membrane.
commonTrap: Mistaking granular for linear immunofluorescence.
stem: A 24-year-old man who smokes has hemoptysis and dark urine. Serum creatinine is 3.2 mg/dL and urinalysis shows red cell casts. Renal biopsy immunofluorescence is expected to show which of the following patterns?

options.text: Pauci-immune staining
Linear IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane
Mesangial IgA deposition
Granular immune complex deposition

explanation: Goodpasture syndrome is a type II hypersensitivity with antibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. Biopsy shows crescents and linear IgG deposition. Treatment is plasmapheresis, corticosteroids, and cyclophosphamide.
pearl: Goodpasture: lung and kidney, linear IgG, type IV collagen; treat with plasma exchange.

optionExplanations.A: Pauci-immune staining suggests ANCA-associated vasculitis.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Linear IgG indicates anti-GBM antibodies.
optionExplanations.C: Mesangial IgA suggests IgA nephropathy.
optionExplanations.D: Granular deposits suggest immune complex diseases such as lupus or poststreptococcal GN.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Calcium gluconate for membrane stabilization in hyperkalemia
memoryAnchor: Calcium protects the heart; insulin shifts the potassium.
commonTrap: Starting with potassium-lowering therapy while ignoring membrane stabilization.
stem: A 64-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease who missed dialysis has weakness. Serum potassium is 7.6 mEq/L, and ECG shows peaked T waves and a widened QRS. Which of the following is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate
Intravenous furosemide only
Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate only
Observation with repeat potassium in 6 hours

explanation: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes is a medical emergency. Intravenous calcium gluconate stabilizes the cardiac myocyte membrane within minutes without lowering potassium. Insulin with glucose and albuterol shift potassium into cells, and dialysis or binders remove it. Calcium is given first when ECG changes are present.
pearl: Hyperkalemia ECG: peaked T, wide QRS, sine wave; treat with calcium, insulin and glucose, albuterol, then removal.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Calcium gluconate protects the myocardium immediately.
optionExplanations.B: Furosemide is slow and ineffective in anuric patients.
optionExplanations.C: Binders act slowly and do not protect against arrhythmia.
optionExplanations.D: Observation risks fatal arrhythmia.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Calculation of creatinine clearance from urine and plasma values
memoryAnchor: U times V over P.
commonTrap: Dividing urine flow by the concentration ratio.
stem: A 45-year-old woman has a urine flow rate of 1.5 mL/min. Her urine creatinine concentration is 80 mg/dL and her plasma creatinine concentration is 1.0 mg/dL. Assuming creatinine is freely filtered and not reabsorbed, what is her approximate glomerular filtration rate?

options.text: 53 mL/min
1.5 mL/min
80 mL/min
120 mL/min

explanation: Clearance equals urine concentration times urine flow divided by plasma concentration: (80 mg/dL x 1.5 mL/min) / 1.0 mg/dL = 120 mL/min, which is the normal glomerular filtration rate. Creatinine is slightly secreted, so creatinine clearance slightly overestimates true GFR, while inulin is the gold standard.
pearl: Clearance = (U x V) / P. Inulin measures GFR exactly; creatinine slightly overestimates it.

optionExplanations.A: 53 mL/min results from dividing instead of multiplying.
optionExplanations.B: 1.5 mL/min is the urine flow rate alone.
optionExplanations.C: 80 mL/min is the urine concentration alone.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. 80 x 1.5 / 1.0 = 120 mL/min.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Clear cell renal carcinoma with erythropoietin production and VHL loss
memoryAnchor: Clear cells, 3p loss, extra red cells.
commonTrap: Attributing polycythemia to smoking alone.
stem: A 62-year-old man who smokes has gross hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable mass. Hemoglobin is 18.6 g/dL. CT shows a 7-cm mass in the upper pole of the right kidney with invasion into the renal vein. Biopsy shows polygonal cells with clear cytoplasm. Which of the following best explains his elevated hemoglobin?

options.text: Bone marrow hyperplasia from the JAK2 mutation
Increased plasma volume contraction from hematuria
Ectopic erythropoietin secretion by the tumor
Chronic hypoxia from smoking

explanation: Renal cell carcinoma, most commonly clear cell type, arises from proximal tubule cells and is associated with loss of the VHL gene on chromosome 3. It can secrete erythropoietin, causing secondary polycythemia, as well as renin and PTHrP. It spreads through the renal vein into the inferior vena cava and is treated with nephrectomy.
pearl: RCC: hematuria, flank pain, palpable mass; paraneoplastic EPO, renin, PTHrP; spreads via renal vein.

optionExplanations.A: A JAK2 mutation causes polycythemia vera with low erythropoietin.
optionExplanations.B: Hematuria would lower rather than raise hemoglobin.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Tumor erythropoietin production causes polycythemia.
optionExplanations.D: Smoking can cause secondary polycythemia, but the renal mass is the likely source of EPO here.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Anti-PLA2R antibodies and spike-and-dome pattern in membranous nephropathy
memoryAnchor: Membranous: spikes and domes, PLA2R.
commonTrap: Mistaking subepithelial deposits for minimal change disease.
stem: A 55-year-old man has leg edema, urine protein of 6 g/day, and serum albumin of 2.1 g/dL. Hepatitis B and malignancy screens are negative. Renal biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the capillary walls, and electron microscopy shows subepithelial deposits with a spike-and-dome pattern. Which of the following is the most likely target antigen?

options.text: Nephrin
Phospholipase A2 receptor
Complement factor H
Type IV collagen

explanation: Primary membranous nephropathy is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in white adults and is mediated by autoantibodies against the phospholipase A2 receptor on podocytes, forming subepithelial immune complexes. Secondary causes include hepatitis B, lupus, drugs, and solid tumors. Patients are at risk of renal vein thrombosis.
pearl: Membranous: adult nephrotic, spike and dome, anti-PLA2R, renal vein thrombosis risk.

optionExplanations.A: Nephrin mutations cause congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Anti-PLA2R antibodies cause primary membranous nephropathy.
optionExplanations.C: Factor H abnormalities are linked to C3 glomerulopathy and atypical HUS.
optionExplanations.D: Type IV collagen is the target in Goodpasture syndrome.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Osmotic demyelination from overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia
memoryAnchor: Slow correction saves the pons.
commonTrap: Correcting severe chronic hyponatremia too quickly.
stem: A 52-year-old woman with chronic alcohol use is admitted with confusion. Serum sodium is 108 mEq/L, serum osmolality is 226 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality is 410 mOsm/kg, and urine sodium is 60 mEq/L. She is given hypertonic saline, and sodium rises to 124 mEq/L within 12 hours. Two days later she develops quadriparesis, dysarthria, and difficulty swallowing. Heart rate is 82 bpm and blood pressure is 120/76 mmHg. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her new neurologic findings?

options.text: Osmotic demyelination of the pons from rapid correction of hyponatremia
Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency
Cerebral edema from continued water intoxication
Cerebral infarction from hypotension

explanation: In chronic hyponatremia, brain cells adapt by losing intracellular osmolytes to prevent swelling. If serum sodium is corrected too quickly (more than 8 to 10 mEq/L in 24 hours), water leaves these adapted cells and causes osmotic demyelination syndrome, classically central pontine myelinolysis, which appears 2 to 6 days later with quadriparesis, dysarthria, dysphagia, and locked-in syndrome. Risk factors include alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, and liver disease. Because the demyelination results from rapid osmotic shifts, treatment of chronic hyponatremia must be slow, and if overcorrection occurs, relowering sodium with desmopressin and free water can decrease injury.
pearl: Correct chronic hyponatremia by no more than 8 mEq/L per day; overcorrection causes central pontine myelinolysis.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia causes pontine osmotic demyelination days later.
optionExplanations.B: Wernicke encephalopathy causes confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia, not delayed quadriparesis with dysphagia after sodium correction.
optionExplanations.C: Cerebral edema occurs with rapid development of hyponatremia, whereas here the deficit followed correction and not a fall in sodium.
optionExplanations.D: Hemodynamics are stable, and infarction from hypotension would not follow a pattern of locked-in syndrome after a sodium shift.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Induction immunosuppression for class IV lupus nephritis
memoryAnchor: Wire loops mean treat hard and early.
commonTrap: Relying on supportive therapy alone for diffuse proliferative disease.
stem: A 27-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has new edema, hypertension, and hematuria. Blood pressure is 156/98 mmHg, serum creatinine is 2.2 mg/dL, urine protein is 4.1 g/day, and serum C3 and C4 are low with elevated anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies. Renal biopsy shows diffuse endocapillary proliferation with wire-loop lesions and subendothelial immune deposits. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for joint pain
High-dose glucocorticoids with mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide
Observation with ACE inhibitor therapy only
Rituximab as the only initial agent for all patients

explanation: Diffuse proliferative (class IV) lupus nephritis is the most severe and common form, caused by immune complex deposition with complement consumption, producing nephritic and nephrotic features. Wire-loop lesions on light microscopy reflect subendothelial deposits, and immunofluorescence shows a full-house pattern. Untreated disease leads to kidney failure, so induction therapy with high-dose glucocorticoids plus mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide is indicated, followed by maintenance immunosuppression. ACE inhibitors reduce proteinuria as an adjunct, and NSAIDs should be avoided because they decrease renal blood flow.
pearl: Class IV lupus nephritis: wire loops, full-house IF, low complement; induce with steroids plus MMF or cyclophosphamide.

optionExplanations.A: NSAIDs decrease renal perfusion and would worsen kidney injury, whereas they do not treat the cause of the nephritis.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Glucocorticoids with mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide are the induction treatment for class IV lupus nephritis.
optionExplanations.C: ACE inhibitors alone do not control the immune-mediated glomerular inflammation, and delay increases the risk of kidney failure.
optionExplanations.D: Rituximab is an alternative in refractory disease and is not standard monotherapy for every patient at initial presentation.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: HLA-DQ2 association and IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies in celiac disease
memoryAnchor: Gluten in, villi out.
commonTrap: Testing IgA antibodies in a patient with total IgA deficiency without checking total IgA.
stem: A 29-year-old woman has chronic diarrhea, bloating, weight loss, and iron deficiency anemia. She also has an itchy vesicular rash on the elbows. Which of the following is the most likely HLA association and the best initial serologic test?

options.text: HLA-B27; antinuclear antibodies
HLA-DR4; anti-smooth muscle antibodies
HLA-DQ2 or DQ8; IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies
HLA-DR3; anti-mitochondrial antibodies

explanation: Celiac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten and associated with HLA-DQ2 and DQ8. The best initial screening test is IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody, confirmed by small bowel biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytes. Dermatitis herpetiformis is the associated skin disease and responds to dapsone and a gluten-free diet.
pearl: Celiac: IgA anti-tTG, villous atrophy, dermatitis herpetiformis, increased risk of T-cell lymphoma.

optionExplanations.A: HLA-B27 is associated with spondyloarthropathies.
optionExplanations.B: HLA-DR4 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 and IgA anti-tTG antibodies are characteristic of celiac disease.
optionExplanations.D: HLA-DR3 is associated with primary biliary cholangitis and other autoimmune disease.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Transmural inflammation and skip lesions in Crohn disease
memoryAnchor: Crohn: Cobblestones, Skip lesions, Creeping fat.
commonTrap: Mixing the depth and continuity of Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.
stem: A 23-year-old woman has chronic right lower quadrant pain, diarrhea, and an anal fistula. Colonoscopy shows patchy ulcerations separated by normal mucosa in the terminal ileum. Which of the following histologic features is most likely?

options.text: Transmural inflammation with noncaseating granulomas
Continuous mucosal and submucosal inflammation with crypt abscesses
Pseudomembranes with neutrophils
Villous atrophy with intraepithelial lymphocytes

explanation: Crohn disease can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, most often the terminal ileum, with skip lesions, transmural inflammation, noncaseating granulomas, fistulas, strictures, and a cobblestone appearance. Complications include malabsorption of vitamin B12 and bile salts and calcium oxalate kidney stones. Ulcerative colitis, in contrast, is continuous and limited to mucosa and submucosa.
pearl: Crohn: skip lesions, transmural, fistulas, terminal ileum, string sign; UC: continuous from rectum, pANCA.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Transmural inflammation and granulomas characterize Crohn disease.
optionExplanations.B: Continuous mucosal inflammation with crypt abscesses describes ulcerative colitis.
optionExplanations.C: Pseudomembranes describe Clostridioides difficile colitis.
optionExplanations.D: Villous atrophy describes celiac disease.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Triple therapy for Helicobacter pylori with proton pump inhibitor
memoryAnchor: PPI plus two antibiotics.
commonTrap: Treating an H. pylori ulcer with acid suppression only.
stem: A 46-year-old man has epigastric pain that improves with meals and awakens him at night. Endoscopy shows a duodenal ulcer, and a urea breath test is positive. Which of the following regimens is most appropriate?

options.text: Famotidine alone
Sucralfate alone
Misoprostol and aspirin
Proton pump inhibitor, clarithromycin, and amoxicillin

explanation: Helicobacter pylori is associated with duodenal ulcers, gastric ulcers, and gastric cancer and lymphoma. Eradication regimens combine a proton pump inhibitor with two antibiotics such as clarithromycin and amoxicillin (or metronidazole), or bismuth quadruple therapy where clarithromycin resistance is high. Eradication heals ulcers and prevents recurrence.
pearl: H. pylori: urease-positive, treat with PPI plus two antibiotics; test of cure after therapy.

optionExplanations.A: Famotidine reduces acid but does not eradicate H. pylori.
optionExplanations.B: Sucralfate is a mucosal protectant and does not eradicate the organism.
optionExplanations.C: Misoprostol protects against NSAID ulcers, and aspirin would worsen injury.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Triple therapy eradicates the organism.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: Interpreting hepatitis B serology after vaccination
memoryAnchor: Vaccine gives surface antibody, not core antibody.
commonTrap: Reading anti-HBs as evidence of past infection.
stem: A 25-year-old health care worker has hepatitis B serology tests drawn after completing a vaccination series. Results show negative HBsAg, positive anti-HBs antibody, and negative anti-HBc antibody. Which of the following best describes his status?

options.text: Acute hepatitis B infection
Immune due to vaccination
Chronic hepatitis B infection
Window period of infection

explanation: Vaccination induces antibodies against the surface antigen only, so a vaccinated patient has anti-HBs positivity with negative HBsAg and negative anti-HBc. Natural immunity after resolved infection shows anti-HBs and anti-HBc positivity. The window period shows negative HBsAg and anti-HBs with positive IgM anti-HBc. He is therefore immune due to vaccination.
pearl: Vaccinated: anti-HBs only; resolved infection: anti-HBs plus anti-HBc; chronic: HBsAg over 6 months.

optionExplanations.A: Acute infection shows positive HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Isolated anti-HBs reflects vaccine-induced immunity.
optionExplanations.C: Chronic infection shows persistent HBsAg for more than 6 months.
optionExplanations.D: The window period has positive IgM anti-HBc and negative anti-HBs.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Ascitic fluid neutrophil count diagnostic of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
memoryAnchor: Two-fifty neutrophils means treat for SBP.
commonTrap: Waiting for culture results before treating.
stem: A 58-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and ascites has fever, abdominal pain, and confusion. Temperature is 38.4 C. Paracentesis shows 620 neutrophils/mm3 in ascitic fluid. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Large-volume paracentesis only
Oral lactulose only
Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt
Intravenous ceftriaxone with albumin

explanation: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed by an ascitic fluid neutrophil count of 250/mm3 or more, most often from Escherichia coli or Klebsiella. Treatment is a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone, with intravenous albumin to reduce the risk of hepatorenal syndrome. Secondary prophylaxis with a fluoroquinolone follows.
pearl: SBP: PMN of 250 or more, treat with ceftriaxone and albumin, prophylaxis after an episode.

optionExplanations.A: Paracentesis alone does not treat infection.
optionExplanations.B: Lactulose treats hepatic encephalopathy but not the infection.
optionExplanations.C: TIPS is for refractory ascites or variceal bleeding and may worsen encephalopathy.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Ceftriaxone with albumin treats SBP.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Ultrasonographic findings and treatment of acute cholecystitis
memoryAnchor: Stone in the cystic duct, wall gets thick.
commonTrap: Confusing cholecystitis with ascending cholangitis.
stem: A 44-year-old woman has 12 hours of right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder, nausea, and fever. Temperature is 38.5 C and inspiration during palpation of the right upper quadrant causes her to stop breathing. Which of the following ultrasonographic findings is most likely?

options.text: Pancreatic pseudocyst
Hepatic abscess
Gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid
Dilated common bile duct without gallstones

explanation: Acute cholecystitis is caused by cystic duct obstruction by a gallstone, causing gallbladder inflammation with a positive Murphy sign, fever, and leukocytosis. Ultrasonography shows stones, wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid. Treatment is intravenous fluids, antibiotics, and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
pearl: Cholecystitis: Murphy sign, ultrasound first, HIDA if equivocal; cholangitis adds jaundice and confusion (Charcot and Reynolds).

optionExplanations.A: A pseudocyst is a pancreatitis complication.
optionExplanations.B: A hepatic abscess presents with fever and a liver lesion.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Stones with wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid indicate cholecystitis.
optionExplanations.D: A dilated duct without stones suggests another cause of biliary obstruction.

subject: Genetics
testedConcept: HFE C282Y mutation and phlebotomy in hemochromatosis
memoryAnchor: Too much iron: bleed it out.
commonTrap: Choosing chelation before phlebotomy.
stem: A 48-year-old man has fatigue, arthralgias of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints, bronze skin, and new diabetes. Serum ferritin is 2,400 ng/mL and transferrin saturation is 85%. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Therapeutic phlebotomy
Deferoxamine as first-line therapy for all patients
Liver transplantation immediately
Iron supplementation

explanation: Hereditary hemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive disorder, most often from the C282Y mutation in the HFE gene on chromosome 6, causing excessive intestinal iron absorption. Iron deposition causes cirrhosis, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, arthropathy, hypogonadism, and bronze skin, and raises the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Therapeutic phlebotomy is first-line treatment.
pearl: Hemochromatosis: HFE C282Y, high ferritin and transferrin saturation, bronze diabetes; phlebotomy.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Phlebotomy removes iron and prevents organ damage.
optionExplanations.B: Chelation is reserved for patients who cannot tolerate phlebotomy.
optionExplanations.C: Transplant is reserved for end-stage liver disease.
optionExplanations.D: Iron supplementation would worsen overload.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Loss of myenteric plexus neurons causing failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation
memoryAnchor: Achalasia: gate will not open, nerves gone.
commonTrap: Confusing achalasia with peptic stricture.
stem: A 38-year-old woman has progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, and weight loss. Barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus tapering to a narrow segment at the gastroesophageal junction. Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.text: Weakness of the upper esophageal sphincter
Loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus
Compression of the esophagus by an aberrant subclavian artery
Fibrosis of the esophageal submucosa from reflux

explanation: Achalasia results from degeneration of inhibitory (nitric oxide and VIP) neurons in the myenteric plexus, causing incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter and absent peristalsis. Barium swallow shows a bird-beak appearance, and manometry confirms the diagnosis. Chagas disease causes secondary achalasia, and patients have an increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma.
pearl: Achalasia: dysphagia to solids and liquids, bird beak, manometry; treat with pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy, or botulinum toxin.

optionExplanations.A: Upper sphincter weakness causes oropharyngeal dysphagia.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Loss of myenteric inhibitory neurons impairs sphincter relaxation.
optionExplanations.C: An aberrant subclavian artery causes dysphagia lusoria, which is rare and compressive.
optionExplanations.D: Submucosal fibrosis from reflux causes peptic stricture with solid-food dysphagia.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Initial management of acute variceal bleeding in cirrhosis
memoryAnchor: Constrict, cover, and clip.
commonTrap: Transfusing to a normal hemoglobin and raising portal pressure.
stem: A 54-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis presents with vomiting of bright red blood. Blood pressure is 88/54 mmHg, heart rate is 124 bpm, hemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL, platelet count is 78,000/mm3, and INR is 1.9. Examination shows ascites, spider angiomata, and caput medusae. Intravenous access and fluids have been started. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional management?

options.text: Vasopressin infusion without endoscopy
Transfusion to a hemoglobin target above 12 g/dL
Octreotide, intravenous ceftriaxone, and urgent endoscopic band ligation
Propranolol and discharge with outpatient endoscopy

explanation: Esophageal varices form from portal hypertension through portosystemic collaterals at the gastroesophageal junction. Acute variceal bleeding is a medical emergency with high mortality. Management includes resuscitation with a restrictive transfusion strategy (hemoglobin target about 7 to 8 g/dL, because overtransfusion raises portal pressure and increases rebleeding), a splanchnic vasoconstrictor such as octreotide, prophylactic antibiotics such as ceftriaxone to decrease infection and mortality, and endoscopic band ligation within 12 hours. Nonselective beta blockers such as propranolol are used for secondary prophylaxis after the bleed, not during hypotension, and TIPS is rescue therapy.
pearl: Variceal bleed: ABCs, octreotide, antibiotics, endoscopic banding; beta blockers and banding for prophylaxis.

optionExplanations.A: Vasopressin has more adverse effects than octreotide, and endoscopy is needed for definitive control.
optionExplanations.B: A liberal transfusion target increases portal pressure and rebleeding, whereas a restrictive target of about 7 g/dL is advised.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Octreotide, ceftriaxone, and band ligation are the standard care for acute variceal bleeding.
optionExplanations.D: Propranolol would worsen hypotension during an acute bleed and discharge is unsafe for an unstable patient.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Lactulose mechanism in hepatic encephalopathy
memoryAnchor: Lactulose traps ammonia as ammonium in the colon.
commonTrap: Giving diuretics or sedatives, which can precipitate encephalopathy.
stem: A 62-year-old man with hepatitis C cirrhosis is brought in with confusion, asterixis, and day-night sleep reversal after a week of constipation. Temperature is 37.0 C, blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, heart rate is 88 bpm, serum sodium is 136 mEq/L, and serum creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. Serum ammonia is elevated at 150 micromol/L. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of the first-line treatment for his condition?

options.text: Propranolol decreases portal pressure and hepatic ammonia production
Neomycin increases urea cycle activity in hepatocytes
Furosemide increases renal excretion of ammonia
Lactulose acidifies colonic contents and traps ammonia as ammonium

explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy results from failure of the cirrhotic liver and portosystemic shunting to clear gut-derived ammonia, which causes astrocyte swelling and neurotransmitter dysfunction. Precipitants include constipation, infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, electrolyte disturbance, and sedatives, and these should be sought and corrected. Lactulose is a nonabsorbable disaccharide metabolized by colonic bacteria to acids, which lowers the colonic pH and converts ammonia to ammonium that cannot be absorbed, and it also causes osmotic diarrhea that decreases ammonia absorption. Rifaximin is added to decrease the ammonia-producing bacterial load and reduce recurrence.
pearl: Hepatic encephalopathy: find the trigger, give lactulose, add rifaximin to prevent recurrence.

optionExplanations.A: Propranolol is used to prevent variceal bleeding, and it does not lower ammonia or treat encephalopathy.
optionExplanations.B: Neomycin is an antibiotic that decreases ammonia-producing bacteria and does not increase urea cycle activity.
optionExplanations.C: Furosemide does not treat hepatic encephalopathy and can worsen it by causing hypokalemia and alkalosis, which increase renal ammonia production.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Lactulose acidifies the colon, trapping ammonia as ammonium, and speeds its elimination.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Fixed splitting of S2 and right ventricular volume overload in atrial septal defect
memoryAnchor: Fixed split: the atrium is always open.
commonTrap: Expecting a holosystolic murmur in an atrial septal defect.
stem: A 26-year-old woman has exertional dyspnea and palpitations. Examination shows a widely split S2 that does not vary with respiration and a soft systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border. Echocardiography shows right atrial and ventricular enlargement. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Atrial septal defect
Patent ductus arteriosus
Coarctation of the aorta
Ventricular septal defect

explanation: An atrial septal defect causes left-to-right shunting at atrial level, producing right heart volume overload, increased pulmonary flow, and fixed splitting of the second heart sound. Paradoxical embolism can occur if the shunt reverses, and untreated disease may cause pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome. Treatment is percutaneous or surgical closure.
pearl: ASD: fixed split S2, ostium secundum most common, associated with paradoxical embolism.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Fixed split S2 with right heart enlargement indicates an atrial septal defect.
optionExplanations.B: A patent ductus arteriosus causes a continuous machinery murmur.
optionExplanations.C: Coarctation causes arm-leg blood pressure differences and rib notching.
optionExplanations.D: A ventricular septal defect causes a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Left atrial myxoma presenting with positional obstruction and constitutional symptoms
memoryAnchor: Myxoma swings like a pendulum in the left atrium.
commonTrap: Confusing adult myxoma with pediatric rhabdomyoma.
stem: A 52-year-old woman has episodic dyspnea and presyncope when she changes position, along with fever, weight loss, and elevated interleukin-6. Examination shows a low-pitched diastolic sound that varies with position. Echocardiography shows a pedunculated mass in the left atrium attached to the interatrial septum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Rhabdomyoma
Angiosarcoma
Cardiac myxoma
Mural thrombus

explanation: Myxoma is the most common primary adult cardiac tumor and usually arises in the left atrium near the fossa ovalis. A mobile mass can intermittently obstruct the mitral valve, causing positional symptoms and a tumor plop, and it can release interleukin-6, causing fever and weight loss, or embolize. Histology shows stellate cells in a gelatinous matrix, and surgical excision is curative.
pearl: Myxoma: left atrium, tumor plop, constitutional symptoms; rhabdomyoma: children, tuberous sclerosis.

optionExplanations.A: Rhabdomyoma is the most common pediatric cardiac tumor and is associated with tuberous sclerosis.
optionExplanations.B: Angiosarcoma is a rare, aggressive malignant tumor typically in the right atrium.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A pedunculated left atrial mass attached to the septum is typical of a myxoma.
optionExplanations.D: A mural thrombus is not usually attached by a stalk to the septum and does not release interleukin-6.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Diagnostic criteria and definitive treatment of preeclampsia
memoryAnchor: Placenta out, preeclampsia out.
commonTrap: Relying on antihypertensives alone to treat the disease.
stem: A 29-year-old primigravid woman at 36 weeks of gestation has headache and ankle swelling. Blood pressure is 156/102 mmHg on two readings 6 hours apart, and urine protein is 2+ on dipstick. She had normal blood pressure before 20 weeks. Which of the following is the definitive treatment for her condition?

options.text: Long-term oral hydralazine alone
Delivery of the fetus and placenta
Diuretic therapy
Bed rest until term

explanation: Preeclampsia is new hypertension (140/90 mmHg or higher) after 20 weeks with proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction, caused by abnormal placental implantation with endothelial dysfunction. Delivery is the definitive treatment, and at or beyond 37 weeks or with severe features delivery is indicated. Magnesium sulfate prevents seizures, and labetalol or hydralazine treats severe hypertension.
pearl: Preeclampsia: HTN after 20 weeks plus proteinuria; severe features need magnesium; cure is delivery.

optionExplanations.A: Antihypertensives treat blood pressure but not the underlying disease.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Delivery removes the placenta and cures the disease.
optionExplanations.C: Diuretics can worsen reduced intravascular volume and are not indicated.
optionExplanations.D: Bed rest does not prevent progression and is not curative.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Fetal complications of gestational diabetes
memoryAnchor: Sugar in, big baby, then low sugar out.
commonTrap: Attributing first-trimester malformations to gestational diabetes.
stem: A 33-year-old woman at 28 weeks of gestation has an abnormal glucose tolerance test. Her fasting glucose is 98 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely complication in her newborn?

options.text: Macrosomia with neonatal hypoglycemia
Caudal regression only in the third trimester
Microcephaly with hydrops
Intrauterine growth restriction with polycythemia only

explanation: Maternal hyperglycemia crosses the placenta, causing fetal hyperinsulinemia, macrosomia, and risk of shoulder dystocia. After birth, abrupt loss of maternal glucose leads to neonatal hypoglycemia. Respiratory distress, polycythemia, hypocalcemia, and hyperbilirubinemia also occur. Pregestational diabetes in the first trimester raises the risk of congenital malformations such as caudal regression and neural tube defects.
pearl: GDM: macrosomia, hypoglycemia, shoulder dystocia; screen at 24-28 weeks.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Fetal hyperinsulinemia causes macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycemia.
optionExplanations.B: Caudal regression results from first-trimester hyperglycemia in pregestational diabetes.
optionExplanations.C: Microcephaly with hydrops suggests infection, not gestational diabetes.
optionExplanations.D: Growth restriction is not typical of gestational diabetes with adequate control.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Methotrexate for stable unruptured ectopic pregnancy
memoryAnchor: Stable and small: methotrexate; unstable: scalpel.
commonTrap: Operating on a stable patient with a small unruptured ectopic pregnancy.
stem: A 26-year-old woman with prior pelvic inflammatory disease has 7 weeks of amenorrhea, mild left lower quadrant pain, and light vaginal spotting. She is hemodynamically stable. Serum beta-hCG is 2,800 mIU/mL and transvaginal ultrasonography shows no intrauterine pregnancy and a small left adnexal mass without free fluid. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oxytocin infusion
Immediate laparotomy
Expectant management with no follow-up
Methotrexate

explanation: Ectopic pregnancy occurs most often in the fallopian tube, with risk factors including prior PID, tubal surgery, and previous ectopic pregnancy. A stable patient with an unruptured mass, low hCG, and no fetal cardiac activity can be treated with methotrexate, a folate antagonist that stops trophoblast proliferation. Hemodynamic instability or rupture requires surgery.
pearl: Ectopic: positive hCG with no intrauterine pregnancy at hCG over 1,500-2,000; methotrexate if stable.

optionExplanations.A: Oxytocin is used to induce labor and does not treat ectopic pregnancy.
optionExplanations.B: Laparotomy is for instability or rupture.
optionExplanations.C: Expectant management without follow-up risks rupture.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Methotrexate is used for stable unruptured ectopic pregnancy.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Painless bleeding in placenta previa and avoidance of digital examination
memoryAnchor: Previa: Painless; do not touch the cervix.
commonTrap: Performing a pelvic examination before ultrasonography.
stem: A 32-year-old multiparous woman at 33 weeks of gestation has sudden painless bright red vaginal bleeding. Her uterus is soft and nontender, fetal heart tones are normal, and she is hemodynamically stable. Which of the following should be avoided until the diagnosis is established?

options.text: Digital cervical examination
Transabdominal ultrasonography
Intravenous access
Fetal heart rate monitoring

explanation: Placenta previa is implantation of the placenta over the cervical os, presenting with painless bright red bleeding in the second or third trimester. Digital examination can provoke massive hemorrhage and must be avoided until ultrasonography excludes previa. Management includes monitoring, steroids, and cesarean delivery. Placental abruption instead causes painful bleeding with a tender, rigid uterus.
pearl: Previa: painless, bright red; abruption: painful, dark, DIC risk, associated with cocaine and hypertension.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A digital examination can cause severe bleeding in placenta previa.
optionExplanations.B: Ultrasonography is the diagnostic test and is safe.
optionExplanations.C: IV access is appropriate for a bleeding patient.
optionExplanations.D: Fetal monitoring is indicated and safe.

subject: Immunology
testedConcept: Rh immune globulin prophylaxis in Rh-negative pregnancy
memoryAnchor: Give anti-D before the immune system learns Rh.
commonTrap: Assuming a first pregnancy requires no prophylaxis.
stem: A 28-year-old Rh-negative woman, gravida 1, is at 28 weeks of gestation. Her husband is Rh-positive and her antibody screen is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate step?

options.text: No treatment because this is her first pregnancy
Administer Rh immune globulin now and after delivery if the newborn is Rh-positive
Start high-dose steroids to prevent sensitization
Wait and give Rh immune globulin only after delivery

explanation: Fetomaternal hemorrhage can sensitize an Rh-negative mother to Rh-positive fetal red cells, producing IgG anti-D that crosses the placenta in later pregnancies and causes hemolytic disease of the newborn. Rh immune globulin given at 28 weeks and within 72 hours of delivery of an Rh-positive infant, and after bleeding events, prevents sensitization. It is not useful once the mother is already sensitized.
pearl: Rh-negative mother: RhoGAM at 28 weeks and within 72 hours postpartum; test for sensitization first.

optionExplanations.A: Sensitization can occur in a first pregnancy, so prophylaxis is still needed.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Prophylaxis at 28 weeks and postpartum prevents sensitization.
optionExplanations.C: Steroids do not prevent alloimmunization.
optionExplanations.D: Giving it only after delivery misses sensitization that can occur during pregnancy.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Uterine atony as the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage
memoryAnchor: Boggy uterus, massage and oxytocin.
commonTrap: Missing that a firm uterus with bleeding suggests trauma.
stem: A 34-year-old woman, gravida 4, has heavy vaginal bleeding 20 minutes after vaginal delivery of a 4,300-g infant after a prolonged labor. The uterus is boggy and enlarged above the umbilicus, and the placenta appears intact. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.text: Cervical laceration
Uterine inversion
Retained placental fragments
Uterine atony

explanation: Uterine atony is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage, with risk factors including macrosomia, prolonged labor, high parity, and polyhydramnios. A soft, boggy uterus is typical. Treatment includes uterine massage, oxytocin, and second-line uterotonics such as methylergonovine and carboprost, and surgery if needed.
pearl: PPH 4 Ts: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin; atony is most common.

optionExplanations.A: A cervical laceration produces bleeding with a firm uterus.
optionExplanations.B: Uterine inversion presents with a mass in the vagina and shock.
optionExplanations.C: Retained placenta fragments produce a firm uterus with continued bleeding.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A boggy uterus after a prolonged labor with macrosomia indicates atony.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Genetics and presentation of complete hydatidiform mole
memoryAnchor: Complete mole: empty egg, paternal only.
commonTrap: Assigning triploidy to a complete mole.
stem: A 22-year-old woman at 11 weeks of amenorrhea has vaginal bleeding, hyperemesis, and a uterus larger than expected. Serum beta-hCG is 280,000 mIU/mL and TSH is suppressed. Ultrasonography shows a snowstorm pattern without a fetus. Which of the following describes the most likely karyotype?

options.text: 45,X of maternal origin
46,XX of entirely paternal origin
69,XXY with maternal and paternal contribution

explanation: Complete mole results from fertilization of an empty ovum by a haploid sperm that duplicates, giving a 46,XX karyotype that is entirely paternal. It causes diffuse villous swelling, markedly elevated hCG with hyperthyroidism from TSH-like activity, theca lutein cysts, and risk of choriocarcinoma. Treatment is suction curettage with hCG follow-up, and methotrexate for persistent disease.
pearl: Complete mole: 46,XX paternal, no fetus, snowstorm; partial mole: triploid with fetus.

optionExplanations.A: Trisomy 18 is a fetal aneuploidy with a fetus present.
optionExplanations.B: A 45,X karyotype is Turner syndrome.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A complete mole is diploid and paternal.
optionExplanations.D: A partial mole is triploid (69,XXY) and often has fetal parts.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Neural tube defect risk with valproate exposure
memoryAnchor: Valproate leaves the tube open.
commonTrap: Attributing Ebstein anomaly to valproate.
stem: A 27-year-old woman with epilepsy taking valproic acid plans pregnancy. She asks about fetal risks. Which of the following birth defects is most strongly associated with first-trimester valproate exposure?

options.text: Neural tube defects
Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina
Ebstein anomaly
Phocomelia

explanation: Valproate inhibits histone deacetylase and interferes with folate metabolism, increasing the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida, along with cardiac and craniofacial anomalies. Women of childbearing age should take folic acid, and alternatives such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam are preferred when possible. Lithium causes Ebstein anomaly, thalidomide causes phocomelia, and diethylstilbestrol causes vaginal clear cell carcinoma.
pearl: Valproate: neural tube defects; carbamazepine: also NTD; phenytoin: fetal hydantoin syndrome.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Valproate is associated with neural tube defects.
optionExplanations.B: Clear cell vaginal adenocarcinoma is associated with in utero diethylstilbestrol exposure.
optionExplanations.C: Ebstein anomaly is associated with lithium.
optionExplanations.D: Phocomelia is associated with thalidomide.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Loss of deep tendon reflexes as the first sign of magnesium toxicity
memoryAnchor: Check the knee jerk before the next dose.
commonTrap: Confusing preeclampsia hyperreflexia with magnesium toxicity.
stem: A 30-year-old woman with severe preeclampsia at 35 weeks is receiving magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis. Which of the following is the earliest clinical sign of magnesium toxicity?

options.text: Hypertension
Tachycardia
Hyperreflexia
Loss of patellar reflexes

explanation: Magnesium sulfate blocks neuromuscular transmission, so toxicity first causes loss of deep tendon reflexes, followed by respiratory depression and cardiac arrest at higher levels. Monitoring includes reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output, because magnesium is renally cleared. Calcium gluconate is the antidote.
pearl: Magnesium toxicity: loss of DTRs, respiratory depression; antidote calcium gluconate.

optionExplanations.A: Magnesium tends to lower blood pressure slightly rather than raise it.
optionExplanations.B: Tachycardia is not the characteristic early sign.
optionExplanations.C: Hyperreflexia occurs in preeclampsia, whereas toxicity causes hyporeflexia.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Loss of patellar reflexes is the earliest sign.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: Polymicrobial endometritis after cesarean delivery treated with clindamycin and gentamicin
memoryAnchor: Cesarean plus prolonged labor, then fever: cover anaerobes and gram negatives.
commonTrap: Using narrow oral therapy for severe polymicrobial infection.
stem: A 31-year-old woman has fever, lower abdominal pain, and foul-smelling lochia 3 days after cesarean delivery that followed 20 hours of ruptured membranes and prolonged labor. Temperature is 39.1 C, heart rate is 116 bpm, and blood pressure is 112/68 mmHg. The uterus is tender and enlarged, wound is clean, and white blood cell count is 21,000/mm3. Lungs are clear and urinalysis is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Observation with acetaminophen
Oral amoxicillin alone
Intravenous clindamycin plus gentamicin
Oral fluconazole for fungal infection

explanation: Postpartum endometritis is a polymicrobial ascending infection of the endometrium, most common after cesarean delivery, with risk factors including prolonged labor, prolonged rupture of membranes, and multiple cervical examinations. Organisms include anaerobes, gram-negative rods, group B streptococci, and enterococci. Treatment is broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering anaerobes and gram-negative bacteria, such as clindamycin with gentamicin. Failure to improve in 48 to 72 hours should prompt evaluation for abscess or septic pelvic thrombophlebitis because the risk of complications increases with delay.
pearl: Endometritis: fever, uterine tenderness, foul lochia; treat with clindamycin plus gentamicin.

optionExplanations.A: Observation risks sepsis, and acetaminophen would treat fever without treating the infection.
optionExplanations.B: Oral amoxicillin alone lacks adequate anaerobic and gram-negative coverage and is not appropriate for severe infection.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Clindamycin and gentamicin cover polymicrobial anaerobic and gram-negative flora.
optionExplanations.D: Fluconazole treats fungal infection, whereas this process is bacterial.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Endometrial hyperplasia risk and oral contraceptive treatment in polycystic ovary syndrome
usmleContentArea: Female and Transgender Reproductive System & Breast
memoryAnchor: PCOS: protect the lining with progestin.
commonTrap: Using clomiphene when pregnancy is not desired.
stem: A 24-year-old woman with obesity has oligomenorrhea, acne, and hirsutism. LH to FSH ratio is elevated and ultrasonography shows enlarged ovaries with multiple peripheral follicles. She does not desire pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her menstrual irregularity and hyperandrogenism?

options.text: Clomiphene citrate
Combined oral contraceptive pills
Danazol
Estrogen-only therapy

explanation: Polycystic ovary syndrome causes chronic anovulation and hyperandrogenism with insulin resistance. Combined oral contraceptives suppress LH and androgen production, increase sex hormone-binding globulin, and provide progestin to protect the endometrium from unopposed estrogen, which otherwise raises the risk of hyperplasia and endometrial cancer. Weight loss and metformin improve insulin resistance, and clomiphene or letrozole is used to induce ovulation when pregnancy is desired.
pearl: PCOS: Rotterdam criteria; OCPs for cycles and hirsutism; letrozole for ovulation induction.

optionExplanations.A: Clomiphene induces ovulation and is for patients who desire fertility.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. OCPs regulate cycles, reduce androgens, and protect the endometrium.
optionExplanations.C: Danazol is an androgenic agent that would worsen hirsutism.
optionExplanations.D: Estrogen alone increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Ectopic endometrial tissue causing dysmenorrhea and chocolate cysts
usmleContentArea: Female and Transgender Reproductive System & Breast
memoryAnchor: Endometriosis: Endometrium Everywhere.
commonTrap: Confusing endometriosis with adenomyosis.
stem: A 31-year-old woman has severe dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, and 2 years of infertility. Examination shows fixed retroverted uterus and nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments. Laparoscopy shows dark brown cysts on the ovary. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Pelvic inflammatory disease
Leiomyoma
Endometriosis
Adenomyosis

explanation: Endometriosis is the presence of functional endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus, causing cyclic pelvic pain, dyspareunia, infertility, and ovarian endometriomas ("chocolate cysts"). Treatment includes NSAIDs, hormonal suppression, and surgery. Adenomyosis is endometrial tissue within the myometrium causing a globular, tender uterus.
pearl: Endometriosis: ectopic endometrium, chocolate cysts, laparoscopy; adenomyosis: inside the myometrium.

optionExplanations.A: PID presents with fever, cervical motion tenderness, and discharge.
optionExplanations.B: Leiomyoma causes an enlarged irregular uterus and menorrhagia.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Dysmenorrhea, infertility, and chocolate cysts indicate endometriosis.
optionExplanations.D: Adenomyosis presents with menorrhagia and a diffusely enlarged, boggy uterus.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: HPV E6 and E7 oncoproteins inactivate p53 and Rb
usmleContentArea: Female and Transgender Reproductive System & Breast
memoryAnchor: E6 = p53 (six letters), E7 = Rb.
commonTrap: Reversing the targets of E6 and E7.
stem: A 35-year-old woman has an abnormal Pap smear showing high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. HPV genotyping is positive for type 16. Which of the following best explains the oncogenic mechanism of this virus?

options.text: Integration near MYC causing overexpression
E6 inactivates Rb and E7 degrades p53
Insertion of a viral tyrosine kinase
E6 degrades p53 and E7 inactivates Rb

explanation: High-risk HPV types 16 and 18 produce E6, which promotes degradation of p53, and E7, which inactivates the retinoblastoma protein. Loss of these tumor suppressors allows unchecked proliferation and progression from dysplasia to carcinoma. Vaccination and Pap screening with HPV testing prevent cervical cancer. In summary, E6 degrades p53 and E7 inactivates Rb.
pearl: HPV 16/18: E6 breaks p53, E7 blocks Rb; types 6/11 cause genital warts.

optionExplanations.A: MYC overexpression is characteristic of Burkitt lymphoma.
optionExplanations.B: This reverses the roles of E6 and E7.
optionExplanations.C: Viral tyrosine kinases are not the mechanism of HPV.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. E6 targets p53 and E7 targets Rb.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Estrogen-secreting granulosa cell tumor and endometrial hyperplasia
usmleContentArea: Female and Transgender Reproductive System & Breast
memoryAnchor: Granulosa: Grows the endometrium.
commonTrap: Assigning androgen secretion to granulosa cell tumors.
stem: A 58-year-old woman has postmenopausal bleeding. Pelvic examination shows a 7-cm right adnexal mass. Serum inhibin is elevated, and endometrial biopsy shows hyperplasia. The ovarian tumor histology shows cells with coffee-bean nuclei and Call-Exner bodies. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the endometrial findings?

options.text: Tumor secretion of estrogen
Tumor secretion of alpha-fetoprotein
Tumor secretion of testosterone
Tumor secretion of beta-hCG

explanation: Granulosa cell tumors are sex cord-stromal tumors that secrete estrogen and inhibin, causing endometrial hyperplasia, postmenopausal bleeding, and precocious puberty in children. Call-Exner bodies are characteristic. Sertoli-Leydig tumors secrete androgens, dysgerminomas can secrete hCG, and yolk sac tumors secrete AFP.
pearl: Granulosa: estrogen, inhibin, Call-Exner bodies; endometrial hyperplasia risk.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Estrogen from the tumor stimulates the endometrium.
optionExplanations.B: AFP is secreted by yolk sac tumors.
optionExplanations.C: Testosterone secretion is typical of Sertoli-Leydig tumors.
optionExplanations.D: hCG secretion characterizes germ cell tumors such as choriocarcinoma and some dysgerminomas.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Tamoxifen mixed estrogen receptor activity and endometrial cancer risk
usmleContentArea: Female and Transgender Reproductive System & Breast
memoryAnchor: Tamoxifen: protects breast, stimulates uterus.
commonTrap: Confusing the skeletal effects of tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors.
stem: A 52-year-old woman with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer is started on tamoxifen after lumpectomy. Which of the following adverse effects should she be counseled about?

options.text: Osteoporosis and hot flashes only
Endometrial cancer and venous thromboembolism
Cardiotoxicity and heart failure
Hemorrhagic cystitis

explanation: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator that is an antagonist in breast tissue and an agonist in the endometrium and bone. It increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer and thromboembolism, and it causes hot flashes. It preserves bone density in postmenopausal women. Aromatase inhibitors have the opposite bone effect and cause osteoporosis.
pearl: Tamoxifen: breast antagonist, endometrium agonist; raloxifene does not stimulate the endometrium.

optionExplanations.A: Osteoporosis is a risk of aromatase inhibitors, not tamoxifen.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Endometrial cancer and clots are key risks of tamoxifen.
optionExplanations.C: Cardiotoxicity is associated with trastuzumab and anthracyclines.
optionExplanations.D: Hemorrhagic cystitis is associated with cyclophosphamide.

subject: Anatomy
testedConcept: Normal breast development with absent uterus in Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome
usmleContentArea: Female and Transgender Reproductive System & Breast
memoryAnchor: MRKH: normal hormones, missing womb.
commonTrap: Confusing MRKH with androgen insensitivity syndrome.
stem: A 16-year-old girl has primary amenorrhea. She has normal breast development, normal pubic and axillary hair, and a blind vaginal pouch. Pelvic ultrasonography shows normal ovaries and no uterus. Which of the following karyotypes is most likely?

options.text: 46,XY
47,XXY
46,XX

explanation: Mullerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome) results from failure of the paramesonephric ducts to develop, causing absent uterus and upper vagina with normal ovaries and 46,XX karyotype. Secondary sexual characteristics are normal because ovarian function is intact. Androgen insensitivity (46,XY) shows scant pubic hair and no ovaries.
pearl: MRKH: 46,XX, normal ovaries, normal pubic hair, absent uterus; check for renal anomalies.

optionExplanations.A: A 46,XY female with AIS would have testes and scant pubic hair.
optionExplanations.B: Turner syndrome has streak gonads and absent breast development.
optionExplanations.C: Klinefelter occurs in males.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Mullerian agenesis occurs in 46,XX females with normal hormone function.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Hormonal changes at menopause
usmleContentArea: Female and Transgender Reproductive System & Breast
memoryAnchor: No follicles, no estrogen, high FSH.
commonTrap: Expecting low gonadotropins when estradiol is low in primary ovarian failure.
stem: A 52-year-old woman has not menstruated for 14 months and has hot flashes and vaginal dryness. Which of the following hormone patterns is expected?

options.text: Low FSH with high estradiol
Low FSH and LH with low estradiol
High FSH and LH with low estradiol
High FSH with high estradiol

explanation: At menopause, ovarian follicles are depleted, estradiol and inhibin fall, and loss of negative feedback increases FSH and LH, with FSH rising first and most. Consequences include hot flashes, vaginal atrophy, and accelerated bone loss. Estrogen therapy relieves symptoms but increases the risk of thromboembolism and, without progestin, endometrial cancer. High FSH and LH with low estradiol is therefore the expected pattern.
pearl: Menopause: FSH up, estradiol down, bone loss, vaginal atrophy.

optionExplanations.A: Low FSH with high estradiol suggests an estrogen-secreting source.
optionExplanations.B: Low gonadotropins would suggest hypothalamic or pituitary failure.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Loss of estradiol raises FSH and LH.
optionExplanations.D: High estradiol is not seen in menopause.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Unopposed estrogen and postmenopausal bleeding in endometrial carcinoma
usmleContentArea: Female and Transgender Reproductive System & Breast
memoryAnchor: Bleeding after menopause: biopsy.
commonTrap: Observing postmenopausal bleeding without tissue diagnosis.
stem: A 61-year-old obese woman with diabetes has vaginal bleeding 10 years after menopause. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows an endometrial thickness of 14 mm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Initiation of estrogen therapy
Endometrial biopsy
Repeat ultrasonography in 6 months
Reassurance because bleeding is common after menopause

explanation: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Risk factors include obesity, diabetes, nulliparity, tamoxifen, and unopposed estrogen exposure, which causes endometrial hyperplasia. An endometrial biopsy is the initial test, and treatment is hysterectomy with salpingo-oophorectomy.
pearl: Endometrial cancer: postmenopausal bleeding, endometrial stripe over 4 mm, endometrioid type is most common.

optionExplanations.A: Estrogen would worsen hyperplasia.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Biopsy is the next step for postmenopausal bleeding with a thickened endometrium.
optionExplanations.C: Delaying follow-up could miss cancer.
optionExplanations.D: Postmenopausal bleeding is never normal.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: Tubo-ovarian abscess and ectopic pregnancy risk after pelvic inflammatory disease
usmleContentArea: Female and Transgender Reproductive System & Breast
memoryAnchor: Severe PID: admit, IV antibiotics, think abscess.
commonTrap: Treating a tubo-ovarian abscess as simple outpatient PID.
stem: A 22-year-old sexually active woman has 4 days of lower abdominal pain, fever, and purulent cervical discharge. Temperature is 38.9 C, heart rate is 112 bpm, and blood pressure is 108/66 mmHg. Cervical motion tenderness and right adnexal tenderness are present. White blood cell count is 18,500/mm3, urine hCG is negative, and transvaginal ultrasonography shows a 6-cm complex right adnexal mass. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Hospitalization with intravenous cefoxitin and doxycycline
Single-dose oral azithromycin only
Observation for 48 hours
Outpatient oral metronidazole only

explanation: Pelvic inflammatory disease results from ascending infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, often polymicrobial. A complex adnexal mass with fever suggests tubo-ovarian abscess, which requires hospitalization and intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics covering gonococci, chlamydia, and anaerobes, with drainage if the mass fails to respond. Complications include infertility, chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy because of tubal scarring, and perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome). Delay increases the risk of rupture and sepsis. Because the infection ascends from the cervix, treatment must cover gonococci, chlamydia, and anaerobes, and failure to improve leads to drainage; delay will increase the risk of rupture and sepsis.
pearl: PID: cervical motion tenderness; complications: infertility, ectopic pregnancy, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis, TOA.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Hospitalization with intravenous cefoxitin and doxycycline treats severe PID with a tubo-ovarian abscess by covering gonococci, chlamydia, and anaerobes.
optionExplanations.B: A single oral dose lacks anaerobic coverage and is inadequate for a complex abscess, whereas severe disease requires parenteral therapy instead.
optionExplanations.C: Observation risks abscess rupture and sepsis, and the fever and mass show that the infection is not self-limited.
optionExplanations.D: Metronidazole alone does not cover gonococci and chlamydia, which are the main pathogens and would remain untreated.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Alpha-1 blocker and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor actions in benign prostatic hyperplasia
memoryAnchor: Finasteride Finishes DHT.
commonTrap: Confusing finasteride with alpha blockers.
stem: A 66-year-old man has urinary hesitancy, weak stream, and nocturia. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate. He is started on finasteride. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this drug?

options.text: Antagonism of androgen receptors in the prostate
Blockade of alpha-1 receptors in prostatic smooth muscle
Inhibition of conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone
Inhibition of phosphodiesterase type 5

explanation: Finasteride inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, preventing conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, which shrinks prostatic tissue over months. Alpha-1 blockers such as tamsulosin relax smooth muscle quickly. Adverse effects of finasteride include decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and gynecomastia, and it lowers PSA by about half.
pearl: BPH: tamsulosin for fast relief, finasteride to shrink the gland; finasteride halves PSA.

optionExplanations.A: Androgen receptor antagonism is the action of flutamide.
optionExplanations.B: Alpha-1 blockade is the action of tamsulosin.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Finasteride blocks the conversion of testosterone to DHT.
optionExplanations.D: PDE5 inhibition is the action of sildenafil and tadalafil.

subject: Anatomy
testedConcept: Left-sided varicocele from drainage of the left testicular vein into the renal vein
memoryAnchor: Left vein takes the long way round.
commonTrap: Missing that a right-sided varicocele needs imaging.
stem: A 24-year-old man has a dull ache in the left scrotum that worsens by the end of the day. Examination shows a soft mass above the left testis that feels like a bag of worms and decreases when he lies down. Which of the following best explains why this finding is usually on the left?

options.text: The left testicular artery is longer than the right
The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle
The right testicular vein drains into the right renal vein
The left testis descends later than the right

explanation: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, whereas the right drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The longer course and perpendicular entry increase venous pressure, predisposing to varicocele, a cause of male infertility. A new right-sided or non-decompressing varicocele should prompt evaluation for a retroperitoneal mass or renal cell carcinoma obstructing the vein.
pearl: Left testicular vein to left renal vein; right to IVC; sudden varicocele raises concern for renal tumor.

optionExplanations.A: The arterial supply does not explain venous varicosities.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The left testicular vein enters the left renal vein.
optionExplanations.C: The right testicular vein drains into the IVC.
optionExplanations.D: Testicular descent timing does not explain the left predominance.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Peripheral zone adenocarcinoma with osteoblastic metastases
memoryAnchor: Peripheral on exam, sclerotic on film.
commonTrap: Confusing the zones affected by BPH and cancer.
stem: A 72-year-old man has back pain and a hard, nodular prostate on examination. Serum PSA is 85 ng/mL. Radiograph of the lumbar spine shows dense sclerotic vertebral lesions. Which of the following best describes the primary tumor?

options.text: Transitional cell carcinoma of the urethra
Squamous cell carcinoma of the transition zone
Sarcoma of the central zone
Adenocarcinoma arising in the peripheral zone

explanation: Prostate adenocarcinoma usually arises in the peripheral zone, which is palpable on rectal examination, whereas benign hyperplasia affects the transition zone. It spreads hematogenously through the Batson venous plexus to bone, producing osteoblastic lesions and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Androgen deprivation therapy with leuprolide, abiraterone, or enzalutamide treats metastatic disease.
pearl: Prostate cancer: peripheral zone, osteoblastic mets, Batson plexus; BPH: transition zone.

optionExplanations.A: Urothelial carcinoma arises in the bladder and urethra.
optionExplanations.B: Squamous carcinoma of the prostate is rare.
optionExplanations.C: Sarcomas are rare in the prostate.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Peripheral zone adenocarcinoma commonly metastasizes to bone as sclerotic lesions.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Radiosensitivity and histology of testicular seminoma
memoryAnchor: Seminoma: Sheets, Sensitive, no AFP.
commonTrap: Expecting AFP elevation in pure seminoma.
stem: A 33-year-old man has a painless, firm 3-cm testicular mass. Serum AFP is normal and beta-hCG is mildly elevated. Orchiectomy specimen shows sheets of uniform cells with clear cytoplasm, fried-egg appearance, and lymphocytic infiltrate. Which of the following is the best description of this tumor?

options.text: Seminoma, highly radiosensitive
Yolk sac tumor with Schiller-Duval bodies
Leydig cell tumor with Reinke crystals
Embryonal carcinoma with glandular structures

explanation: Seminoma is the most common testicular germ cell tumor, with uniform cells in sheets and a fibrous septum with lymphocytes. It may produce mildly elevated hCG, does not produce AFP, and is very radiosensitive with an excellent prognosis. Yolk sac tumors secrete AFP, and Leydig cell tumors cause gynecomastia or precocious puberty.
pearl: Seminoma: radiosensitive, normal AFP; nonseminomatous tumors secrete AFP or hCG and are less radiosensitive.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Uniform fried-egg cells and normal AFP indicate seminoma.
optionExplanations.B: Yolk sac tumors secrete AFP and show Schiller-Duval bodies.
optionExplanations.C: Leydig tumors contain Reinke crystals and produce androgens or estrogens.
optionExplanations.D: Embryonal carcinoma is more aggressive with glandular architecture.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Contraindication of sildenafil with nitrates
memoryAnchor: Nitrates plus sildenafil: pressure falls off a cliff.
commonTrap: Overlooking nitrate use in a patient with coronary disease.
stem: A 58-year-old man with coronary artery disease takes sublingual nitroglycerin as needed and requests a prescription for sildenafil for erectile dysfunction. Which of the following is the most important reason to avoid prescribing it?

options.text: Risk of agranulocytosis
Risk of tendon rupture
Risk of severe hypotension when combined with nitrates
Risk of hepatic necrosis

explanation: Sildenafil inhibits phosphodiesterase type 5, increasing cyclic GMP in the corpus cavernosum and prolonging nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation. Nitrates also raise cGMP through nitric oxide, so combining the two causes profound hypotension and can precipitate myocardial ischemia. Other adverse effects include headache, flushing, and blue-tinged vision.
pearl: PDE5 inhibitors: contraindicated with nitrates; headache, flushing, blue vision.

optionExplanations.A: Agranulocytosis is a risk of drugs such as clozapine and dapsone.
optionExplanations.B: Tendon rupture is a fluoroquinolone adverse effect.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. PDE5 inhibitors plus nitrates cause dangerous hypotension.
optionExplanations.D: Hepatic necrosis is not characteristic of PDE5 inhibitors.

subject: Anatomy
testedConcept: Para-aortic lymph node drainage of the testis versus inguinal drainage of the scrotum
memoryAnchor: Testes drain where they were born.
commonTrap: Assuming testicular tumors spread to inguinal nodes.
stem: A 29-year-old man has a testicular germ cell tumor. Imaging is planned to look for early nodal spread. Which of the following lymph node groups is most likely to be involved first?

options.text: Femoral lymph nodes
Superficial inguinal lymph nodes
Internal iliac lymph nodes
Para-aortic lymph nodes

explanation: The testes develop near the kidneys and retain their lymphatic drainage to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes along the renal vessels, so germ cell tumors spread to retroperitoneal nodes. The scrotal skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, so scrotal cancers and infections involve inguinal nodes. Orchiectomy should use an inguinal approach to avoid altering lymphatic drainage.
pearl: Testis: para-aortic; scrotum: superficial inguinal; ovary: para-aortic.

optionExplanations.A: Femoral nodes receive deep lower limb drainage.
optionExplanations.B: Superficial inguinal nodes drain the scrotum, penis skin, and lower limb.
optionExplanations.C: Internal iliac nodes drain the pelvic viscera, including the prostate and cervix.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Testicular lymph drains to the para-aortic nodes.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: Painless chancre and benzathine penicillin treatment of primary syphilis
memoryAnchor: Painless ulcer: penicillin.
commonTrap: Confusing a painless syphilitic chancre with painful herpes or chancroid.
stem: A 27-year-old man has a 1-cm painless, indurated genital ulcer with a clean base and nontender inguinal lymphadenopathy for 2 weeks. Dark-field microscopy shows spirochetes. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral azithromycin for 7 days only
Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G
Topical podophyllin
Oral acyclovir

explanation: Primary syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum and presents with a painless chancre. Treatment for primary, secondary, and early latent disease is a single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G. A Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can follow treatment due to release of endotoxin-like substances. Herpes causes painful grouped vesicles, and chancroid causes a painful ulcer.
pearl: Syphilis: painless chancre, then rash with condylomata lata, then gummas; penicillin G is the treatment.

optionExplanations.A: Azithromycin is not first-line therapy for syphilis.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Benzathine penicillin G is first-line for primary syphilis.
optionExplanations.C: Podophyllin treats genital warts.
optionExplanations.D: Acyclovir treats herpes simplex infection.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: Avoiding prostate massage and treating acute bacterial prostatitis with a fluoroquinolone
memoryAnchor: Hot, tender prostate: antibiotics, not massage.
commonTrap: Performing prostate massage in acute infection.
stem: A 45-year-old man has 2 days of fever, perineal pain, dysuria, and urinary frequency. Temperature is 39.0 C. Digital rectal examination shows a tender, warm, swollen prostate. Urinalysis shows pyuria. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Ciprofloxacin
Observation without antibiotics
Finasteride
Prostatic massage

explanation: Acute bacterial prostatitis is caused by gram-negative rods such as Escherichia coli, and presents with fever, dysuria, and a tender boggy prostate. Treatment is a fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which penetrate prostatic tissue, for several weeks. Vigorous prostatic massage is avoided because it can cause bacteremia. Ciprofloxacin is therefore the most appropriate treatment.
pearl: Acute prostatitis: E. coli; treat with fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX; avoid massage.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A fluoroquinolone with prostatic penetration treats acute prostatitis.
optionExplanations.B: Untreated acute prostatitis can lead to abscess and sepsis.
optionExplanations.C: Finasteride treats BPH, not infection.
optionExplanations.D: Massage risks bacteremia.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Radical inguinal orchiectomy and tumor markers in nonseminomatous germ cell tumor
memoryAnchor: Take it out through the groin.
commonTrap: Biopsying a suspected testicular tumor through the scrotum.
stem: A 24-year-old man has a 4-cm painless, firm left testicular mass for 6 weeks. Serum AFP is 640 ng/mL and beta-hCG is 1,200 mIU/mL. Ultrasonography shows a heterogeneous intratesticular mass with calcifications. Chest radiograph is normal, and abdominal CT shows no retroperitoneal adenopathy. Temperature is 36.9 C, heart rate is 74 bpm, and hemoglobin is 14.2 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Scrotal incision and drainage
Observation with repeat ultrasonography in 3 months
Radical inguinal orchiectomy
Transscrotal biopsy of the mass

explanation: A solid intratesticular mass with elevated AFP indicates a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor (such as a yolk sac component), because pure seminoma does not secrete AFP. Diagnosis and treatment begin with radical inguinal orchiectomy with high ligation of the spermatic cord, which removes the tumor and avoids violating the scrotum, where lymphatic drainage goes to the inguinal nodes rather than the para-aortic nodes and could increase the risk of local spread. After surgery, tumor markers, staging imaging, and risk-adapted treatment such as surveillance, retroperitoneal lymph node dissection, or bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin follow. Biopsy through the scrotum is avoided because it can cause tumor seeding.
pearl: Testicular mass: inguinal orchiectomy, never scrotal biopsy; AFP means nonseminoma; seminoma is radiosensitive.

optionExplanations.A: Incision and drainage treats an abscess and is not appropriate for a solid mass with elevated markers.
optionExplanations.B: Observation delays treatment of a likely malignancy, and the high AFP indicates an aggressive nonseminomatous tumor.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Radical inguinal orchiectomy is both diagnostic and therapeutic and avoids scrotal violation.
optionExplanations.D: A transscrotal biopsy can seed tumor cells into the scrotum and alter lymphatic drainage, whereas an inguinal approach does not.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins in Graves disease
memoryAnchor: Graves: the antibody is a fake TSH.
commonTrap: Confusing stimulating and destructive thyroid antibodies.
stem: A 34-year-old woman has weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance, and palpitations. Examination shows a diffusely enlarged nontender thyroid, proptosis, and pretibial myxedema. Which of the following is the underlying mechanism?

options.text: Autonomous hyperfunctioning thyroid nodule
Antibodies that destroy thyroid peroxidase-containing cells
Viral destruction of follicular cells with release of hormone
IgG antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor

explanation: Graves disease is a type II hypersensitivity in which thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins activate the TSH receptor, causing hyperthyroidism, a diffuse goiter, and orbitopathy and pretibial myxedema from fibroblast activation. Radioiodine uptake is diffusely increased, and treatment includes methimazole or propylthiouracil, radioiodine ablation, or thyroidectomy.
pearl: Graves: TSI, diffuse uptake, ophthalmopathy; thyroid storm treated with propranolol, PTU, steroids, iodine.

optionExplanations.A: A hyperfunctioning nodule causes toxic adenoma with a focal uptake pattern.
optionExplanations.B: Destruction of cells by antibodies describes Hashimoto thyroiditis.
optionExplanations.C: Viral destruction describes subacute thyroiditis with low uptake.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies cause Graves disease.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Hurthle cells and lymphoid follicles in Hashimoto thyroiditis
memoryAnchor: Hashimoto: Hurthle and Hordes of lymphocytes.
commonTrap: Confusing Hashimoto with Riedel thyroiditis.
stem: A 44-year-old woman has fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, and a firm, painless goiter. TSH is elevated and free T4 is low. Which of the following histologic findings is expected on thyroid biopsy?

options.text: Granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells
Lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centers and Hurthle cells
Papillae with psammoma bodies
Fibrous replacement with a stony hard consistency

explanation: Hashimoto thyroiditis is autoimmune destruction of the thyroid associated with anti-thyroid peroxidase and antithyroglobulin antibodies, HLA-DR5, and a lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centers and Hurthle cells. It can transiently cause hyperthyroidism and increases the risk of primary thyroid B-cell lymphoma. Levothyroxine replaces the hormone.
