pearl: Hashimoto: anti-TPO, Hurthle cells, lymphoma risk; de Quervain: painful, post-viral, granulomas.

optionExplanations.A: Granulomatous inflammation is subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Lymphoid follicles with Hurthle cells characterize Hashimoto thyroiditis.
optionExplanations.C: Papillae with psammoma bodies describe papillary carcinoma.
optionExplanations.D: Fibrous replacement describes Riedel thyroiditis.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Laboratory pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism
memoryAnchor: High PTH with high calcium: gland is at fault.
commonTrap: Missing that malignancy-related hypercalcemia suppresses PTH.
stem: A 56-year-old woman has recurrent kidney stones, constipation, and bone pain. Serum calcium is 11.8 mg/dL, phosphate is 2.1 mg/dL, and parathyroid hormone is elevated. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.text: Parathyroid adenoma
Vitamin D toxicity
Parathyroid carcinoma associated with PTHrP
Chronic kidney disease

explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism is most often from a solitary parathyroid adenoma, causing hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and elevated PTH. Classic features are stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones. Surgical parathyroidectomy treats symptomatic disease. Secondary hyperparathyroidism occurs in chronic kidney disease and differs by its phosphate pattern.
pearl: Primary hyperparathyroidism: high Ca, low phosphate, high PTH; malignancy: high Ca, low PTH.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. High calcium, low phosphate, and high PTH indicate an adenoma.
optionExplanations.B: Vitamin D toxicity raises calcium and phosphate with a low PTH.
optionExplanations.C: PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia has a low PTH.
optionExplanations.D: CKD causes low calcium and high phosphate.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia in primary adrenal insufficiency
memoryAnchor: Addison: Always dark, ACTH high.
commonTrap: Expecting hyperpigmentation in secondary adrenal insufficiency.
stem: A 38-year-old woman has fatigue, weight loss, salt craving, and darkening of the skin creases. Blood pressure is 90/58 mmHg. Serum sodium is 128 mEq/L, potassium is 5.9 mEq/L, and glucose is 62 mg/dL. Which of the following explains her skin changes?

options.text: Decreased cortisol directly stimulating melanin
Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes
Excess aldosterone
Elevated ACTH acting on melanocytes

explanation: Primary adrenal insufficiency, most commonly autoimmune adrenalitis in developed countries, reduces cortisol and aldosterone. Loss of negative feedback raises ACTH, which is cleaved from pro-opiomelanocortin along with melanocyte-stimulating hormone, causing hyperpigmentation. Aldosterone deficiency causes hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension. Treatment is hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. Elevated ACTH acting on melanocytes causes the hyperpigmentation.
pearl: Primary: high ACTH, pigmentation, hyperkalemia; secondary: low ACTH, no pigmentation, normal potassium.

optionExplanations.A: Cortisol deficiency removes feedback but does not directly stimulate melanin.
optionExplanations.B: Melanocyte destruction causes vitiligo.
optionExplanations.C: Aldosterone excess would cause hypokalemia and hypertension.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. High ACTH and MSH from POMC darken the skin.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: High-dose dexamethasone suppression distinguishing pituitary from ectopic ACTH
memoryAnchor: Pituitary responds to high-dose dex; ectopic ignores it.
commonTrap: Attributing a suppressible, ACTH-dependent syndrome to an adrenal source.
stem: A 45-year-old woman has central obesity, purple striae, hypertension, and glucose intolerance. Serum ACTH is elevated. Low-dose dexamethasone does not suppress cortisol, but high-dose dexamethasone suppresses cortisol production by more than 50%. Which of the following is the most likely source of ACTH?

options.text: Small cell lung carcinoma
Adrenal adenoma
Pituitary adenoma
Exogenous glucocorticoid administration

explanation: In Cushing disease, a pituitary adenoma secretes ACTH but retains partial sensitivity to negative feedback, so high-dose dexamethasone suppresses cortisol. Ectopic ACTH, as from small cell carcinoma, is not suppressed. Adrenal tumors cause low ACTH. Exogenous steroids also produce low ACTH and low cortisol.
pearl: High ACTH plus suppression on high-dose dex = pituitary; no suppression = ectopic.

optionExplanations.A: Ectopic ACTH does not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone.
optionExplanations.B: An adrenal adenoma has suppressed ACTH.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Suppression with high-dose dexamethasone indicates a pituitary source.
optionExplanations.D: Exogenous steroids suppress both ACTH and endogenous cortisol.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Alpha blockade before beta blockade in pheochromocytoma
memoryAnchor: Alpha before beta.
commonTrap: Starting a beta blocker first.
stem: A 40-year-old man has episodic headaches, sweating, palpitations, and blood pressure of 210/120 mmHg during attacks. Plasma metanephrines are elevated and CT shows a 4-cm adrenal mass. Before surgery, which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic management?

options.text: Hydrochlorothiazide
Phenoxybenzamine
Propranolol alone
Lisinopril

explanation: Pheochromocytoma secretes catecholamines from chromaffin cells. Preoperative management begins with alpha blockade (phenoxybenzamine, an irreversible nonselective alpha antagonist) to control blood pressure and allow volume expansion. A beta blocker is added only after alpha blockade, because unopposed alpha stimulation from beta blockade can precipitate a hypertensive crisis.
pearl: Pheochromocytoma: alpha blocker first, then beta blocker, then surgery; associated with MEN2 and VHL.

optionExplanations.A: Thiazides do not control catecholamine-mediated hypertension adequately.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Alpha blockade comes first.
optionExplanations.C: A beta blocker alone causes unopposed alpha stimulation and a hypertensive crisis.
optionExplanations.D: ACE inhibitors are not first-line for catecholamine excess.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Metformin reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and carries lactic acidosis risk
memoryAnchor: Metformin: liver sugar down, lactic acid watch.
commonTrap: Confusing metformin with sulfonylureas.
stem: A 52-year-old man with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes and normal renal function is started on metformin. Which of the following best describes its mechanism and a major contraindication?

options.text: Decreases hepatic gluconeogenesis; avoid in severe renal impairment
Increases urinary glucose excretion; avoid with recurrent genital infection
Delays carbohydrate absorption in the gut; avoid in bowel obstruction
Stimulates insulin release from beta cells; avoid in sulfa allergy

explanation: Metformin activates AMP-activated protein kinase, reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis and improving insulin sensitivity, without causing hypoglycemia or weight gain. Its main serious adverse effect is lactic acidosis, so it is avoided in severe renal impairment, hepatic failure, and acute illness with hypoperfusion. Gastrointestinal upset and vitamin B12 deficiency can occur.
pearl: Metformin: first-line, weight neutral, lactic acidosis, B12 deficiency; hold for contrast and AKI.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Metformin lowers gluconeogenesis, and renal failure raises lactic acidosis risk.
optionExplanations.B: This describes SGLT2 inhibitors.
optionExplanations.C: This describes alpha-glucosidase inhibitors such as acarbose.
optionExplanations.D: This describes sulfonylureas, which increase insulin release and cause hypoglycemia.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Water deprivation test distinguishing central from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
memoryAnchor: Desmopressin works only if the kidney can listen.
commonTrap: Confusing central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
stem: A 30-year-old man has polyuria and polydipsia. Serum sodium is 147 mEq/L. During a water deprivation test, urine osmolality remains 140 mOsm/kg, and it rises to 480 mOsm/kg after desmopressin administration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Primary polydipsia
Central diabetes insipidus
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
SIADH

explanation: Diabetes insipidus causes inability to concentrate urine. In central DI, the pituitary fails to release ADH, and urine osmolality rises after exogenous desmopressin. In nephrogenic DI, the collecting duct is resistant to ADH and there is no response. Primary polydipsia raises urine osmolality with water deprivation.
pearl: Central DI: responds to desmopressin; nephrogenic DI: does not (lithium, hypercalcemia).

optionExplanations.A: Primary polydipsia would raise urine osmolality with water deprivation.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A response to desmopressin indicates central DI.
optionExplanations.C: Nephrogenic DI shows no response to desmopressin.
optionExplanations.D: A syndrome of excess ADH would produce hyponatremia rather than hypernatremia.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: RET mutation and prophylactic thyroidectomy in MEN2
memoryAnchor: C cells, calcitonin, amyloid, RET.
commonTrap: Assuming all thyroid cancers share BRAF mutations.
stem: A 28-year-old woman has a thyroid nodule. Biopsy shows polygonal cells in an amyloid stroma that stains positive for calcitonin. Her father had a pheochromocytoma and her brother had a thyroid cancer. Which of the following is the most likely genetic abnormality?

options.text: RET proto-oncogene mutation
PAX8-PPAR gamma rearrangement
RAS mutation with follicular architecture
BRAF V600E mutation

explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, secretes calcitonin, and deposits amyloid. Familial cases occur in MEN2A and MEN2B from germline RET gain-of-function mutations. Carriers are offered prophylactic thyroidectomy, and pheochromocytoma must be excluded before surgery. Papillary carcinoma is associated with BRAF and RET/PTC rearrangements and shows psammoma bodies. The responsible defect is a RET proto-oncogene mutation.
pearl: MEN2A: medullary thyroid, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia; MEN2B: medullary, pheo, mucosal neuromas.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Germline RET mutations cause MEN2-associated medullary carcinoma.
optionExplanations.B: PAX8-PPAR gamma is associated with follicular carcinoma.
optionExplanations.C: RAS mutations are associated with follicular neoplasms.
optionExplanations.D: BRAF V600E is associated with papillary carcinoma.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Fluid resuscitation first in hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
memoryAnchor: Fluids first, insulin second.
commonTrap: Treating HHS with insulin alone.
stem: A 74-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is brought in with 4 days of polyuria and progressive confusion after a urinary tract infection. Blood pressure is 92/58 mmHg, heart rate is 118 bpm, and temperature is 38.1 C. Serum glucose is 920 mg/dL, sodium is 134 mEq/L, potassium is 4.6 mEq/L, bicarbonate is 22 mEq/L, and serum osmolality is 365 mOsm/kg. Urine ketones are trace and arterial pH is 7.36. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Intravenous insulin bolus without fluids
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
Oral metformin and outpatient follow-up
Aggressive intravenous isotonic saline resuscitation

explanation: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state occurs in type 2 diabetes with severe hyperglycemia (above 600 mg/dL), marked hyperosmolality, and profound dehydration with minimal ketosis and near-normal pH. Osmotic diuresis causes a large volume deficit, so the most important initial step is aggressive isotonic saline to restore perfusion, followed by insulin infusion once potassium is confirmed above 3.3 mEq/L, and potassium replacement as needed. The precipitant, here infection, must be treated. Rapid insulin without fluids can shift water into cells and worsen hypotension, and bicarbonate is not indicated with normal pH.
pearl: HHS: glucose over 600, osmolality over 320, minimal ketones; fluids first, then insulin, replace potassium.

optionExplanations.A: Insulin without fluids can worsen hypotension by shifting water into cells and does not correct the volume deficit.
optionExplanations.B: Bicarbonate is reserved for severe acidosis, whereas this patient has a normal pH.
optionExplanations.C: Outpatient treatment is unsafe for an altered, hypotensive patient with severe hyperosmolality.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Volume resuscitation with isotonic saline is the first priority in HHS.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Hypokalemia with low renin in aldosterone-producing adenoma
memoryAnchor: Low renin plus high aldosterone: find the nodule.
commonTrap: Treating bilateral hyperplasia surgically or unilateral adenoma medically only.
stem: A 45-year-old woman has resistant hypertension, muscle weakness, and polyuria. Blood pressure is 168/104 mmHg on three medications and heart rate is 78 bpm. Serum sodium is 144 mEq/L, potassium is 2.9 mEq/L, and bicarbonate is 31 mEq/L. Plasma renin activity is suppressed and the plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio is elevated. CT shows a 1.5-cm left adrenal nodule. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Lisinopril alone with dietary potassium restriction
Bilateral adrenalectomy with lifelong replacement
Laparoscopic unilateral adrenalectomy
Long-term loop diuretic monotherapy

explanation: Primary aldosteronism (Conn syndrome) causes hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis from excess aldosterone, which increases sodium reabsorption and potassium and hydrogen ion secretion in the collecting duct. Renin is suppressed because volume expansion inhibits the juxtaglomerular apparatus, which distinguishes it from secondary hyperaldosteronism. Confirmatory testing and adrenal vein sampling establish unilateral disease, and an aldosterone-producing adenoma is treated with unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy, which can cure hypertension. Bilateral hyperplasia is treated with spironolactone or eplerenone because surgery does not help.
pearl: Conn: high BP, low K, alkalosis, low renin; adenoma: surgery; hyperplasia: spironolactone.

optionExplanations.A: Lisinopril would not correct aldosterone excess, and potassium restriction is inappropriate in a patient with hypokalemia.
optionExplanations.B: Bilateral adrenalectomy is reserved for rare cases and would require lifelong steroid replacement, whereas unilateral disease needs only one gland removed.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Unilateral adrenalectomy treats an aldosterone-producing adenoma.
optionExplanations.D: Loop diuretics would worsen hypokalemia and alkalosis, which are already present.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Ryanodine receptor defect and dantrolene treatment in malignant hyperthermia
memoryAnchor: Dantrolene dampens the ryanodine receptor.
commonTrap: Using antipyretics for malignant hyperthermia.
stem: A 22-year-old man develops a temperature of 40.8 C, muscle rigidity, and tachycardia 30 minutes after induction of anesthesia with sevoflurane and succinylcholine. End-tidal carbon dioxide is markedly elevated and serum potassium is 6.4 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Dantrolene
Acetaminophen
Bromocriptine
Cyproheptadine

explanation: Malignant hyperthermia is an autosomal dominant disorder of the ryanodine receptor (RYR1) in skeletal muscle. Volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine trigger uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, causing sustained contraction, hypermetabolism, hyperthermia, hypercapnia, and rhabdomyolysis. Dantrolene blocks the ryanodine receptor and is the treatment, along with stopping the trigger and cooling.
pearl: Malignant hyperthermia: RYR1, volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine, treat with dantrolene.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Dantrolene blocks calcium release through the ryanodine receptor.
optionExplanations.B: Acetaminophen does not treat hypermetabolic hyperthermia from calcium release.
optionExplanations.C: Bromocriptine is used for neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
optionExplanations.D: Cyproheptadine treats serotonin syndrome.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Mixed respiratory alkalosis and anion-gap metabolic acidosis in salicylate toxicity
memoryAnchor: Ionized salicylate stays in the urine.
commonTrap: Missing the respiratory alkalosis component of salicylate toxicity.
stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought in after ingesting a large number of aspirin tablets. She has tinnitus, vomiting, tachypnea, and fever. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.46, PaCO2 22 mmHg, and HCO3 15 mEq/L, with an elevated anion gap. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Fomepizole
Intravenous acetylcysteine
Flumazenil
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize the urine

explanation: Salicylates stimulate the medullary respiratory center, causing respiratory alkalosis, and uncouple oxidative phosphorylation, causing anion-gap metabolic acidosis, hyperthermia, and tinnitus. Sodium bicarbonate alkalinizes the serum and urine, trapping salicylate in its ionized form and increasing renal elimination. Severe cases need hemodialysis.
pearl: Salicylates: tinnitus, mixed acid-base disorder, uncoupling; treat with bicarbonate and dialysis if severe.

optionExplanations.A: Fomepizole treats methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning.
optionExplanations.B: Acetylcysteine is the antidote for acetaminophen.
optionExplanations.C: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Alkalinization enhances salicylate excretion.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Atropine and pralidoxime for organophosphate poisoning
memoryAnchor: Atropine dries it up; pralidoxime frees the enzyme.
commonTrap: Giving cholinesterase inhibitors for cholinergic toxicity.
stem: A 38-year-old farmer is brought in after spraying insecticide. He has salivation, lacrimation, diarrhea, urination, bronchorrhea, miosis, and muscle fasciculations. Heart rate is 48 bpm. Which of the following drug combinations is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Dimercaprol and succimer
Physostigmine and neostigmine
Atropine and pralidoxime
Naloxone and flumazenil

explanation: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing cholinergic excess with muscarinic (SLUDGE, bronchorrhea, bradycardia, miosis) and nicotinic (fasciculations, weakness) effects. Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and reverses secretions and bradycardia, and pralidoxime regenerates acetylcholinesterase before aging occurs. Skin decontamination is also essential.
pearl: Organophosphates: SLUDGE, miosis, fasciculations; atropine plus pralidoxime.

optionExplanations.A: Dimercaprol and succimer are chelators for heavy metals.
optionExplanations.B: Physostigmine and neostigmine are cholinesterase inhibitors that would worsen toxicity.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Atropine and pralidoxime reverse muscarinic effects and reactivate the enzyme.
optionExplanations.D: Naloxone and flumazenil reverse opioids and benzodiazepines.

subject: Physiology
testedConcept: Normal PaO2 with reduced oxygen content in carbon monoxide poisoning
memoryAnchor: CO: oximeter lies, oxygen content falls.
commonTrap: Trusting pulse oximetry in suspected CO poisoning.
stem: A 35-year-old woman is found confused with headache and nausea in a house heated by a faulty furnace. Pulse oximetry reads 98% on room air, and PaO2 is 95 mmHg. Skin appears pink. Which of the following best explains her symptoms?

options.text: Reduced PaO2 from alveolar hypoventilation
Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity because carboxyhemoglobin shifts the curve to the left
Inhibition of cytochrome oxidase by cyanide only
Ferric iron in hemoglobin preventing oxygen binding

explanation: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with about 200-fold higher affinity than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin, which lowers oxygen content and shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin curve to the left, impairing release to tissues. PaO2 and pulse oximetry readings remain falsely normal because the oximeter cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin. Treatment is 100% oxygen, or hyperbaric oxygen in severe cases.
pearl: CO poisoning: normal PaO2, falsely normal SpO2, cherry-red skin; treat with 100% oxygen.

optionExplanations.A: PaO2 is normal in CO poisoning.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Carboxyhemoglobin reduces oxygen content and impairs unloading.
optionExplanations.C: Cyanide poisoning inhibits cytochrome oxidase and can coexist in fires, but is not the mechanism here.
optionExplanations.D: Ferric iron describes methemoglobinemia.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Basophilic stippling and enzyme inhibition in lead poisoning
memoryAnchor: Lead blocks heme at two steps.
commonTrap: Confusing the enzyme defects of lead poisoning and acute intermittent porphyria.
stem: A 3-year-old boy living in an old house with peeling paint has irritability, abdominal pain, constipation, and microcytic anemia. Peripheral smear shows basophilic stippling. Blood lead level is 65 micrograms/dL. Which of the following enzymes are inhibited by this toxin?

options.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Porphobilinogen deaminase only
Ferrochelatase and delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase
Pyruvate kinase

explanation: Lead inhibits ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase in heme synthesis, causing accumulation of protoporphyrin and ALA, microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling from inhibition of ribosomal RNA degradation, and neurologic effects. Features include lead lines on gums and metaphyseal bands, wrist and foot drop, and encephalopathy. Treatment is chelation with succimer or EDTA, and dimercaprol for severe cases.
pearl: Lead: ferrochelatase and ALAD inhibition, basophilic stippling, abdominal colic; succimer for children.

optionExplanations.A: G6PD deficiency causes oxidant hemolysis.
optionExplanations.B: Porphobilinogen deaminase is deficient in acute intermittent porphyria.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Lead inhibits ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase.
optionExplanations.D: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic hemolysis.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis for Pneumocystis at CD4 below 200
memoryAnchor: Under 200: Pneumocystis, TMP-SMX.
commonTrap: Choosing azithromycin for Pneumocystis prophylaxis.
stem: A 34-year-old man with HIV infection has a CD4 count of 150/mm3 and no current symptoms. He has no known drug allergies. Which of the following is the most appropriate prophylaxis?

options.text: Valganciclovir
Azithromycin alone
Fluconazole
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole

explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis is started at a CD4 count below 200/mm3, using trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which also protects against toxoplasmosis when the CD4 count is below 100. Azithromycin prophylaxis for Mycobacterium avium complex is no longer routinely required when antiretroviral therapy is started. Antiretroviral therapy should begin in all patients.
pearl: HIV prophylaxis: CD4 under 200 TMP-SMX; under 100 add toxoplasmosis coverage; start ART in all patients.

optionExplanations.A: Valganciclovir treats cytomegalovirus and is not used as routine prophylaxis.
optionExplanations.B: Azithromycin prevents MAC and is not first for Pneumocystis.
optionExplanations.C: Fluconazole is for cryptococcal or Candida infection.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. TMP-SMX prevents Pneumocystis pneumonia.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: Primaquine for hypnozoites of Plasmodium vivax
memoryAnchor: Primaquine for the persisting liver stage.
commonTrap: Forgetting to test G6PD before primaquine.
stem: A 30-year-old man returns from a trip to India with recurrent cyclic fever, chills, and splenomegaly. Blood smear shows enlarged red cells with Schuffner dots and ring forms. He has received treatment for the acute blood stage. Which of the following drugs is needed to prevent relapse?

options.text: Quinidine
Primaquine
Doxycycline
Artesunate

explanation: Plasmodium vivax and ovale form dormant hypnozoites in the liver that cause relapse after the blood stage is treated. Primaquine kills hypnozoites, but G6PD deficiency should be excluded before treatment because it causes hemolysis. Plasmodium falciparum causes severe malaria with high parasitemia, cerebral disease, and no hypnozoite stage.
pearl: P. vivax and ovale: hypnozoites, need primaquine; check G6PD first.

optionExplanations.A: Quinidine is used for severe malaria in some settings and does not eradicate hypnozoites.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Primaquine eradicates liver hypnozoites.
optionExplanations.C: Doxycycline is used for prophylaxis and adjunct therapy.
optionExplanations.D: Artesunate treats the blood stage of severe malaria.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: Doxycycline for early localized Lyme disease with erythema migrans
memoryAnchor: Bullseye rash: doxycycline.
commonTrap: Using intravenous therapy for uncomplicated early disease.
stem: A 42-year-old woman who hiked in Connecticut 10 days ago has an expanding 12-cm annular erythematous rash with central clearing on the thigh, fatigue, and low-grade fever. She is not pregnant. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral doxycycline
Oral fluconazole
Intravenous ceftriaxone for all patients
Topical corticosteroids

explanation: Lyme disease is caused by Borrelia burgdorferi transmitted by Ixodes ticks. Early localized disease presents with erythema migrans, and oral doxycycline is the treatment, with amoxicillin for pregnant women and children under 8. Late manifestations include arthritis, facial nerve palsy, and heart block. Intravenous ceftriaxone is used for neurologic or cardiac involvement.
pearl: Lyme: erythema migrans, Facial palsy, Arthritis, AV block; doxycycline for early disease.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Doxycycline treats early Lyme disease.
optionExplanations.B: Fluconazole treats fungal infection.
optionExplanations.C: Ceftriaxone is reserved for neurologic or cardiac manifestations.
optionExplanations.D: Topical steroids do not treat the infection.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Metabolic derangements of tumor lysis syndrome and rasburicase prophylaxis
memoryAnchor: Cells burst, labs go wild.
commonTrap: Missing the hypocalcemia in tumor lysis syndrome.
stem: A 12-year-old boy with Burkitt lymphoma begins chemotherapy. Two days later he has oliguria, muscle cramps, and a prolonged QT interval. Laboratory results show potassium 6.8 mEq/L, phosphate 8.2 mg/dL, calcium 6.9 mg/dL, and uric acid 15 mg/dL. Which of the following drugs would have reduced the risk of this complication?

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate only
Calcium gluconate before chemotherapy
Furosemide only
Rasburicase with aggressive hydration

explanation: Tumor lysis syndrome follows rapid cell death of highly proliferative tumors, releasing potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids, which causes hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and hyperuricemia with acute kidney injury. Prevention uses intravenous hydration and a uric acid lowering agent, allopurinol or rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase). Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.
pearl: TLS: high K, phosphate, uric acid; low calcium; prevent with fluids and rasburicase or allopurinol.

optionExplanations.A: Bicarbonate alone does not lower uric acid effectively.
optionExplanations.B: Calcium is not given prophylactically and can precipitate with phosphate.
optionExplanations.C: Furosemide alone does not address uric acid production.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Rasburicase breaks down uric acid and hydration protects the kidney.

subject: Genetics
testedConcept: Knudson two-hit hypothesis in hereditary retinoblastoma
memoryAnchor: Hereditary means the first hit is already there.
commonTrap: Assuming familial retinoblastoma requires two new mutations.
stem: A 14-month-old boy has leukocoria in the left eye. His father had retinoblastoma as a child and later developed osteosarcoma. Which of the following best explains why hereditary retinoblastoma develops in early childhood?

options.text: A germline RB1 mutation requires only one additional somatic hit
Activation of the RAS oncogene by a point mutation
Amplification of N-myc in retinal cells
Two somatic RB1 mutations are needed in the same retinal cell

explanation: Knudson two-hit hypothesis states that both RB1 alleles must be inactivated for tumorigenesis. In hereditary retinoblastoma, one defective allele is inherited in every cell, so only one somatic mutation is needed, causing bilateral, multifocal, earlier disease and increased risk of osteosarcoma. Sporadic disease requires two somatic hits and is usually unilateral.
pearl: RB1 loss: retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma; Rb binds E2F to restrain the G1 to S transition.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. An inherited first hit leaves only one somatic hit to occur.
optionExplanations.B: RAS activation is an oncogene mechanism and not the cause of retinoblastoma.
optionExplanations.C: N-myc amplification occurs in neuroblastoma.
optionExplanations.D: Two somatic hits describe sporadic retinoblastoma, which is later and unilateral.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: TSST-1 superantigen crosslinks MHC class II and T-cell receptors
memoryAnchor: Superantigen: glues T cells to MHC II outside the groove.
commonTrap: Confusing superantigen action with ADP-ribosylating toxins.
stem: A 21-year-old woman has fever, hypotension, diffuse erythematous rash, and vomiting on the fourth day of her menstrual period while using a highly absorbent tampon. Two weeks later her palms and soles desquamate. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the widespread cytokine release?

options.text: ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2
Direct lysis of erythrocytes by a pore-forming hemolysin
Crosslinking of MHC class II molecules with T-cell receptors outside the antigen-binding site
Activation of adenylate cyclase through Gs

explanation: Staphylococcus aureus toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 is a superantigen that binds MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells and the T-cell receptor beta chain outside the antigen groove, activating up to 20 percent of T cells polyclonally. This causes massive release of interleukin-1, interleukin-2, interferon-gamma, and TNF, producing shock and rash. Treatment includes fluids, removal of the tampon, and antistaphylococcal antibiotics with clindamycin.
pearl: Superantigens: TSST-1 (S. aureus) and pyrogenic exotoxins (S. pyogenes) activate T cells nonspecifically.

optionExplanations.A: ADP-ribosylation of EF-2 is the mechanism of diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A.
optionExplanations.B: Pore-forming hemolysins lyse cells but do not drive superantigen-mediated cytokine storm.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Superantigens crosslink MHC II and T-cell receptors nonspecifically.
optionExplanations.D: Gs activation with increased cAMP is the mechanism of cholera toxin and heat-labile ETEC toxin.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: N-myc amplification and urinary catecholamine metabolites in neuroblastoma
memoryAnchor: Neuroblastoma: N-myc, VMA, crosses the line.
commonTrap: Confusing neuroblastoma with Wilms tumor.
stem: A 2-year-old girl has an abdominal mass that crosses the midline, periorbital ecchymoses, and rapid, irregular eye movements. Urinary homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid are elevated. Biopsy shows small round blue cells forming rosettes. Which of the following genetic abnormalities is associated with a poor prognosis?

options.text: BCR-ABL translocation
N-myc amplification
RB1 deletion
WT1 deletion

explanation: Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest cells of the adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain and is the most common extracranial solid tumor in young children. Elevated urinary catecholamine metabolites, Homer-Wright rosettes, opsoclonus-myoclonus, and bone marrow involvement are typical. Amplification of N-myc predicts aggressive disease. Wilms tumor, by contrast, is a unilateral flank mass that does not cross the midline.
pearl: Neuroblastoma: crosses midline, high HVA and VMA, N-myc; Wilms: does not cross midline, WT1.

optionExplanations.A: BCR-ABL translocation is associated with chronic myeloid leukemia.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. N-myc amplification is associated with aggressive neuroblastoma.
optionExplanations.C: RB1 deletion is associated with retinoblastoma.
optionExplanations.D: WT1 deletion is associated with Wilms tumor.

subject: Microbiology
testedConcept: Initial sepsis resuscitation with crystalloids, early antibiotics, and norepinephrine
memoryAnchor: Fluids first, norepinephrine next.
commonTrap: Choosing dopamine as the first-line vasopressor.
stem: A 70-year-old woman with diabetes is brought in with fever, confusion, and flank pain. Temperature is 39.3 C, heart rate is 124 bpm, respiratory rate is 28/min, and blood pressure is 74/40 mmHg. Serum lactate is 5.2 mmol/L, white blood cell count is 22,000/mm3, and creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. After 30 mL/kg of crystalloid and broad-spectrum antibiotics, her mean arterial pressure remains 58 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start dopamine as the preferred first-line pressor
Restrict further fluids and observe
Give oral fludrocortisone alone
Start norepinephrine infusion

explanation: This patient has septic shock from urosepsis, defined by infection with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg despite adequate fluid resuscitation, and lactate above 2 mmol/L. Initial management includes blood cultures, antibiotics within the first hour, source control, and 30 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid. Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor because it raises blood pressure through alpha-1 vasoconstriction with modest beta-1 inotropy, and it results in lower arrhythmia risk than dopamine. Vasopressin or hydrocortisone is added if hypotension persists despite increasing doses. The next step is therefore to start norepinephrine infusion.
pearl: Septic shock: cultures, antibiotics in 1 hour, 30 mL/kg fluid, norepinephrine for MAP under 65.

optionExplanations.A: Dopamine causes more tachyarrhythmia and has worse outcomes than norepinephrine, so it is not the preferred first-line agent.
optionExplanations.B: Restricting fluids and observing would risk further organ injury, because the patient remains hypotensive with hypoperfusion.
optionExplanations.C: Fludrocortisone alone does not reverse hypotension, whereas it can serve as an adjunct in refractory shock.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock after fluid resuscitation.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: N-acetylcysteine for acetaminophen overdose guided by the Rumack-Matthew nomogram
memoryAnchor: Replace glutathione early.
commonTrap: Waiting for transaminase elevation before giving the antidote.
stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought in 6 hours after ingesting approximately 30 acetaminophen tablets (500 mg each) in a suicide attempt. She has nausea but is alert. Blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg, heart rate is 96 bpm, aspartate aminotransferase is 40 U/L, INR is 1.0, and serum acetaminophen concentration is 220 micrograms/mL, which is above the treatment line on the nomogram. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer flumazenil as the antidote
Administer intravenous N-acetylcysteine
Wait for liver enzyme elevation before treatment
Perform hemodialysis as the first-line antidote

explanation: In overdose, acetaminophen is metabolized by CYP2E1 to the toxic metabolite NAPQI, which depletes hepatic glutathione and causes centrilobular necrosis. Liver enzymes are normal in the first 24 hours, so treatment decisions rely on the serum level plotted against time on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is most effective when started within 8 to 10 hours, which decreases the risk of hepatotoxicity. Activated charcoal is used if within a few hours of ingestion. Waiting for symptoms or liver injury increases the risk of fulminant hepatic failure. The next step is therefore to administer intravenous N-acetylcysteine.
pearl: Acetaminophen: NAPQI depletes glutathione; give NAC based on the nomogram, ideally within 8 hours.

optionExplanations.A: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and has no effect on acetaminophen toxicity.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione and prevents liver injury when started early.
optionExplanations.C: Waiting for enzyme elevation delays treatment and increases the risk of fulminant hepatic failure, whereas treatment is guided by the nomogram.
optionExplanations.D: Hemodialysis is reserved for massive overdose with severe acidosis, whereas the antidote is the first-line treatment.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: HER2-targeted therapy and cardiotoxicity monitoring
memoryAnchor: Trastuzumab hits HER2 and can hurt the heart.
commonTrap: Overlooking cardiac monitoring with HER2-targeted therapy.
stem: A 49-year-old woman with invasive breast cancer that overexpresses HER2 receives trastuzumab after surgery. Which of the following should be monitored during her treatment?

options.text: Left ventricular ejection fraction
Absolute neutrophil count for agranulocytosis
Urinary calcium excretion
Serum creatine kinase for myopathy

explanation: Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody against the extracellular domain of HER2, a receptor tyrosine kinase overexpressed in some breast cancers. Its major adverse effect is cardiotoxicity with decreased left ventricular ejection fraction, which is generally reversible but increased by anthracyclines, so cardiac function is monitored with echocardiography. Imatinib and other kinase inhibitors have distinct toxicities.
pearl: Trastuzumab: HER2 antibody, cardiotoxicity; doxorubicin: dilated cardiomyopathy.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Trastuzumab can reduce left ventricular ejection fraction.
optionExplanations.B: Agranulocytosis is associated with drugs such as clozapine.
optionExplanations.C: Urinary calcium is not monitored with trastuzumab.
optionExplanations.D: Creatine kinase monitoring relates to statin myopathy.

subject: Biochemistry
testedConcept: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causing tyrosine to become essential
memoryAnchor: No hydroxylase, no tyrosine.
commonTrap: Missing that tyrosine becomes conditionally essential.
stem: A 6-month-old boy has developmental delay, fair skin, eczema, and a musty body odor. Newborn screening was not performed. Plasma phenylalanine is markedly elevated. Which of the following amino acids becomes essential in his diet?

options.text: Methionine
Tryptophan
Tyrosine
Leucine

explanation: Phenylketonuria is most often caused by phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency (or less often tetrahydrobiopterin defects), preventing conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine. Tyrosine therefore becomes essential, and phenylalanine accumulates and is diverted to phenylketones, causing intellectual disability, hypopigmentation from reduced melanin, and a musty odor. Treatment is a phenylalanine-restricted diet with tyrosine supplementation, and maternal PKU is teratogenic if uncontrolled.
pearl: PKU: low phenylalanine diet, tyrosine becomes essential, musty odor, avoid aspartame.

optionExplanations.A: Methionine is essential, and homocystinuria involves cystathionine synthase, not PKU.
optionExplanations.B: Tryptophan is already essential and is not specifically affected.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Without phenylalanine hydroxylase, tyrosine cannot be synthesized and must be supplied.
optionExplanations.D: Leucine is an essential amino acid unaffected by this block.

subject: Biochemistry
testedConcept: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency with fasting hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis
memoryAnchor: Type I: fasting crash, lactate, gout.
commonTrap: Confusing von Gierke disease with Cori disease.
stem: A 9-month-old boy has hepatomegaly, a doll-like face, fasting hypoglycemia, and lactic acidosis. Serum uric acid and triglycerides are elevated. Fasting glucose does not rise after glucagon administration. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient?

options.text: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase
Acid alpha-glucosidase
Glucose-6-phosphatase
Debranching enzyme

explanation: Von Gierke disease (glycogen storage disease type I) is deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase, preventing the final step of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Glucose-6-phosphate accumulates, causing severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia. Treatment is frequent feeding with cornstarch.
pearl: Von Gierke: hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia, hepatomegaly; treat with cornstarch.

optionExplanations.A: Muscle phosphorylase deficiency is McArdle disease with exercise intolerance.
optionExplanations.B: Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency is Pompe disease with cardiomegaly.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency causes type I glycogen storage disease.
optionExplanations.D: Debranching enzyme deficiency is Cori disease with milder hypoglycemia and no lactic acidosis.

subject: Biochemistry
testedConcept: Hexosaminidase A deficiency with cherry-red macula and no hepatosplenomegaly
memoryAnchor: Tay-Sachs: Tay is Tiny: no big liver.
commonTrap: Confusing Tay-Sachs and Niemann-Pick disease.
stem: A 7-month-old boy of Ashkenazi Jewish descent has regression of motor skills, hypotonia, an exaggerated startle response, and a cherry-red spot on the macula. There is no hepatosplenomegaly. Which of the following enzymes is deficient?

options.text: Hexosaminidase A
Glucocerebrosidase
Alpha-galactosidase A
Sphingomyelinase

explanation: Tay-Sachs disease is an autosomal recessive deficiency of hexosaminidase A, causing accumulation of GM2 ganglioside in neurons, with progressive neurodegeneration, cherry-red macula, and lamellar onion-skin lysosomes. There is no hepatosplenomegaly, distinguishing it from Niemann-Pick disease, which also has a cherry-red spot but with organomegaly.
pearl: Tay-Sachs: no organomegaly; Niemann-Pick: organomegaly; both have a cherry-red spot.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease.
optionExplanations.B: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher disease with hepatosplenomegaly and bone lesions.
optionExplanations.C: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease with neuropathic pain.
optionExplanations.D: Sphingomyelinase deficiency causes Niemann-Pick disease with hepatosplenomegaly.

subject: Biochemistry
testedConcept: Impaired collagen hydroxylation in vitamin C deficiency
memoryAnchor: Vitamin C helps collagen hold hands.
commonTrap: Attributing bleeding gums to vitamin K deficiency.
stem: A 67-year-old man who lives alone and eats a diet of tea and toast has gingival bleeding, perifollicular hemorrhages, and corkscrew hairs. Old surgical scars have reopened. Which of the following is the most likely biochemical defect?

options.text: Impaired conversion of homocysteine to methionine
Impaired hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen
Impaired hydroxylation of vitamin D in the kidney
Impaired gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors

explanation: Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, which hydroxylate proline and lysine residues of procollagen, necessary for stable triple-helix formation. Deficiency causes scurvy with weak collagen, bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhage, poor wound healing, and impaired iron absorption. Vitamin K deficiency instead impairs gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors.
pearl: Scurvy: weak collagen, bleeding gums, poor healing; treat with vitamin C.

optionExplanations.A: Homocysteine conversion requires B12 and folate.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Vitamin C is needed for collagen hydroxylation.
optionExplanations.C: Renal hydroxylation of vitamin D is a separate pathway.
optionExplanations.D: Gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors requires vitamin K.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Congo red apple-green birefringence in amyloid deposits
memoryAnchor: AL for light chains and plasma cells.
commonTrap: Confusing AL with AA amyloid.
stem: A 64-year-old man with multiple myeloma has macroglossia, nephrotic-range proteinuria, and restrictive cardiomyopathy. Abdominal fat pad biopsy stained with Congo red shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Which of the following is the major protein component of these deposits?

options.text: Beta-2 microglobulin
Serum amyloid A
Transthyretin
Immunoglobulin light chains

explanation: Primary (AL) amyloidosis is caused by deposition of misfolded immunoglobulin light chains from a plasma cell clone, as in myeloma, and affects the heart, kidney, tongue, liver, and nerves. Congo red staining with apple-green birefringence reveals beta-pleated sheet fibrils. AA amyloid comes from serum amyloid A in chronic inflammation.
pearl: AL: myeloma; AA: chronic inflammation; transthyretin: senile cardiac; beta-2 microglobulin: dialysis.

optionExplanations.A: Beta-2 microglobulin forms dialysis-related amyloidosis.
optionExplanations.B: Serum amyloid A forms secondary (AA) amyloid in chronic inflammatory diseases.
optionExplanations.C: Transthyretin forms senile systemic and hereditary amyloidosis.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. AL amyloid is derived from light chains.

subject: Immunology
testedConcept: Anti-centromere antibodies in limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis
memoryAnchor: CREST: Centromere.
commonTrap: Pairing anti-topoisomerase I with limited disease.
stem: A 47-year-old woman has Raynaud phenomenon, calcinosis of the fingertips, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasias. Which of the following antibodies is most associated with this disease form?

options.text: Anti-topoisomerase I
Anti-centromere
Anti-Smith
Anti-histone

explanation: Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome: calcinosis, Raynaud, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia) is associated with anti-centromere antibodies and a risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension. Diffuse systemic sclerosis is associated with anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) antibodies, with rapid skin involvement, interstitial lung disease, and scleroderma renal crisis.
pearl: CREST: anti-centromere; diffuse scleroderma: anti-Scl-70; renal crisis treated with ACE inhibitors.

optionExplanations.A: Anti-topoisomerase I marks diffuse systemic sclerosis.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Anti-centromere antibodies mark CREST syndrome.
optionExplanations.C: Anti-Smith is specific for lupus.
optionExplanations.D: Anti-histone antibodies are found in drug-induced lupus.

subject: Immunology
testedConcept: Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies with lymphoma risk in Sjogren syndrome
memoryAnchor: Sjogren: sicca, SSA, SSB.
commonTrap: Overlooking the lymphoma risk in Sjogren syndrome.
stem: A 52-year-old woman has dry eyes, dry mouth, and bilateral parotid enlargement. Schirmer test is abnormal. Which of the following autoantibodies and associated risks are expected?

options.text: Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies; risk of B-cell lymphoma
Anti-Jo-1 antibodies; risk of interstitial lung disease
Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies; risk of glomerulonephritis
Anti-centromere antibodies; risk of pulmonary hypertension

explanation: Sjogren syndrome is an autoimmune lymphocytic destruction of lacrimal and salivary glands, causing keratoconjunctivitis sicca and xerostomia, with anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies and rheumatoid factor. Patients have an increased risk of marginal zone B-cell (MALT) lymphoma, and mothers with anti-Ro antibodies risk neonatal lupus with congenital heart block.
pearl: Sjogren: dry eyes, dry mouth, parotid enlargement, anti-Ro and anti-La, MALT lymphoma.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies occur, with an increased risk of B-cell lymphoma.
optionExplanations.B: Anti-Jo-1 antibodies are associated with polymyositis and dermatomyositis.
optionExplanations.C: ANCA is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis.
optionExplanations.D: Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with CREST.

subject: Immunology
testedConcept: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency with low C4 and bradykinin-mediated swelling
memoryAnchor: Hereditary angioedema: bradykinin swelling, low C4.
commonTrap: Treating bradykinin-mediated angioedema as an allergic reaction.
stem: A 28-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of nonpruritic swelling of the face, lips, and bowel wall causing abdominal pain, without urticaria. Episodes are triggered by minor trauma. Her mother had similar symptoms. Serum C4 is low. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

options.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation
C3 deficiency
Deficiency of decay-accelerating factor
C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency

explanation: Hereditary angioedema is an autosomal dominant deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor, causing uncontrolled activation of the kallikrein-bradykinin and classical complement pathways. Bradykinin increases vascular permeability, producing nonpitting swelling without itching or urticaria, with low C4 even between attacks. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated, and treatment includes C1 inhibitor concentrate, icatibant, or ecallantide, not epinephrine or antihistamines.
pearl: Hereditary angioedema: low C4, no urticaria, ACE inhibitors contraindicated; treat with C1 inhibitor or icatibant.

optionExplanations.A: IgE-mediated degranulation causes allergic angioedema with urticaria and itching that responds to epinephrine.
optionExplanations.B: C3 deficiency causes recurrent bacterial infections.
optionExplanations.C: DAF deficiency causes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. C1 inhibitor deficiency causes bradykinin-mediated angioedema with low C4.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: ATP7B defect with low ceruloplasmin and Kayser-Fleischer rings
memoryAnchor: Wilson: copper in the liver, brain, and eye.
commonTrap: Treating Wilson disease like hemochromatosis.
stem: A 19-year-old man has tremor, dysarthria, personality change, and elevated liver enzymes. Slit-lamp examination shows a golden-brown ring at the corneal periphery. Serum ceruloplasmin is low and 24-hour urinary copper is elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Deferoxamine
Dimercaprol only
Penicillamine or trientine
Phlebotomy

explanation: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive defect in the copper-transporting ATPase ATP7B on chromosome 13, impairing biliary copper excretion and ceruloplasmin incorporation. Copper accumulates in the liver, basal ganglia, and cornea, causing hepatitis or cirrhosis, parkinsonian features, psychiatric symptoms, and Kayser-Fleischer rings. Treatment is a copper chelator such as penicillamine or trientine, and zinc, with liver transplantation for fulminant disease.
pearl: Wilson: ATP7B, low ceruloplasmin, Kayser-Fleischer rings, basal ganglia; treat with penicillamine.

optionExplanations.A: Deferoxamine chelates iron.
optionExplanations.B: Dimercaprol alone is not the standard chronic therapy for Wilson disease.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Copper chelation with penicillamine or trientine is the treatment.
optionExplanations.D: Phlebotomy treats hemochromatosis.

subject: Pharmacology
testedConcept: Fomepizole inhibition of alcohol dehydrogenase in ethylene glycol ingestion
memoryAnchor: Fomepizole blocks the first step.
commonTrap: Missing the toxic-metabolite mechanism of antifreeze ingestion.
stem: A 33-year-old man is brought in after drinking antifreeze. He is intoxicated and has flank pain and vomiting. Arterial pH is 7.18 with an anion gap of 28, serum creatinine is 2.0 mg/dL, and urinalysis shows envelope-shaped crystals. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Deferoxamine
Fomepizole
N-acetylcysteine
Hydroxocobalamin

explanation: Ethylene glycol is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to glycolic and oxalic acids, causing anion-gap metabolic acidosis, calcium oxalate crystal deposition in the kidney, and acute kidney injury. Fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing formation of toxic metabolites, and hemodialysis removes toxin in severe cases. Ethanol is an alternative competitive substrate.
pearl: Ethylene glycol: calcium oxalate crystals, AG acidosis, AKI; fomepizole and dialysis.

optionExplanations.A: Deferoxamine treats iron overload.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase.
optionExplanations.C: N-acetylcysteine is the antidote for acetaminophen.
optionExplanations.D: Hydroxocobalamin treats cyanide poisoning.

subject: Genetics
testedConcept: MEN1 mutation with pituitary, parathyroid, and pancreatic tumors
memoryAnchor: MEN1 = three Ps.
commonTrap: Confusing MEN1 with MEN2.
stem: A 34-year-old man has recurrent peptic ulcers and diarrhea, and hypercalcemia with elevated parathyroid hormone. MRI shows a pituitary adenoma, and CT shows a pancreatic mass. Serum gastrin is markedly elevated. His father had similar findings. Which of the following gene mutations is most likely?

options.text: MEN1 gene (menin)
RET proto-oncogene
NF1 tumor suppressor
VHL tumor suppressor

explanation: MEN1 (Wermer syndrome) is autosomal dominant from inactivating mutations in the tumor suppressor menin, causing tumors of the parathyroid (hypercalcemia), pancreatic islets (gastrinoma causing Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), and pituitary (prolactinoma). MEN2A and MEN2B involve RET and cause medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma. The responsible defect is therefore in the MEN1 gene (menin).
pearl: MEN1: 3 Ps (Pituitary, Parathyroid, Pancreas); MEN2A: medullary thyroid, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. MEN1 gene (menin) mutations cause parathyroid, pancreatic, and pituitary tumors.
optionExplanations.B: RET mutations cause MEN2A and MEN2B.
optionExplanations.C: NF1 causes neurofibromas and cafe-au-lait spots.
optionExplanations.D: VHL causes hemangioblastomas and renal cell carcinoma.

subject: Biochemistry
testedConcept: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency with bone and marrow involvement in Gaucher disease
memoryAnchor: Gaucher: glucocerebroside crumpled paper cells.
commonTrap: Treating hypersplenism with splenectomy rather than the enzyme defect.
stem: A 22-year-old woman of Ashkenazi Jewish descent has fatigue, easy bruising, and bone pain. Examination shows massive splenomegaly and hepatomegaly. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, platelet count is 62,000/mm3, and white blood cell count is 3,400/mm3. Radiograph of the femur shows an Erlenmeyer flask deformity. Bone marrow biopsy shows macrophages with a crumpled tissue paper appearance. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Splenectomy as the only treatment
Dietary restriction of galactose
Enzyme replacement therapy with imiglucerase
Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for all patients

explanation: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder, caused by an autosomal recessive deficiency of glucocerebrosidase, with accumulation of glucocerebroside in macrophages, producing wrinkled-paper cells. Hypersplenism and marrow infiltration cause pancytopenia, and bone involvement causes pain, osteonecrosis, and Erlenmeyer flask deformity. Enzyme replacement with imiglucerase or substrate reduction therapy reverses visceral and hematologic disease, and splenectomy is avoided when possible because it can accelerate bone and hepatic disease.
pearl: Gaucher: glucocerebrosidase, Erlenmeyer flask, crumpled tissue paper cells; enzyme replacement.

optionExplanations.A: Splenectomy alone does not correct the enzyme defect and can worsen bone disease, so it is not the sole treatment.
optionExplanations.B: Galactose restriction treats galactosemia, a different disorder with cataracts and liver injury in infancy.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Imiglucerase replaces the deficient enzyme and reverses organomegaly and cytopenias.
optionExplanations.D: Stem cell transplantation can cure the disease but carries high risk and is not first-line when effective enzyme therapy exists.

subject: Pathology
testedConcept: Saline hydration and bisphosphonate for hypercalcemia of malignancy
memoryAnchor: Fluids first, then block the bone.
commonTrap: Giving diuretics before the patient is volume replete.
stem: A 63-year-old man with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung has 1 week of confusion, constipation, polyuria, and abdominal pain. Blood pressure is 102/66 mmHg, heart rate is 104 bpm, serum calcium is 15.2 mg/dL, phosphate is 2.3 mg/dL, creatinine is 1.9 mg/dL, and parathyroid hormone is suppressed. ECG shows a shortened QT interval. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Furosemide before volume repletion
Urgent parathyroidectomy for an adenoma
Oral calcium restriction only
Aggressive intravenous normal saline followed by a bisphosphonate

explanation: Hypercalcemia of malignancy is most often caused by tumor secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP), as seen in squamous cell carcinomas, with suppressed PTH. Severe hypercalcemia causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and volume depletion, so the first step is aggressive isotonic saline to restore volume and increase renal calcium excretion. A bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid inhibits osteoclast resorption and decreases serum calcium over days, and calcitonin lowers calcium rapidly. Loop diuretics are used only after euvolemia, and parathyroid surgery treats primary hyperparathyroidism, which has an elevated PTH.
pearl: Malignancy hypercalcemia: PTHrP, low PTH; treat with saline, zoledronic acid, calcitonin.

optionExplanations.A: Furosemide before volume repletion would worsen dehydration and kidney injury, whereas saline must come first.
optionExplanations.B: Parathyroidectomy treats primary hyperparathyroidism, whereas this patient has suppressed PTH and a tumor source.
optionExplanations.C: Dietary calcium restriction has little effect because the source is bone resorption driven by PTHrP.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Saline and a bisphosphonate treat the volume deficit and block bone resorption.
